What passed

On 21 July the Chamber of Deputies approved most of President José Antonio Kast’s “National Reconstruction and Economic and Social Development” bill, his biggest legislative win since taking office in March. The vote was 85 in favour to 59 against.

One article, on how municipalities are compensated for that property-tax exemption, was the last to clear: on 4 August the Senate approved it 27 votes to 22, finishing the bill’s passage through Congress in about three and a half months after it was filed in late April. The government secured the votes after UDI’s Gustavo Sanhueza came over — on a commitment to cover municipal-worker pension debt — and the Coquimbo senators Matías Walker and Sergio Gahona traded their support for reconstruction funds for their storm-hit region, with Pedro Araya (PPD) also crossing over. The compensation transfers about US$190 million to municipalities (US$110 million through the municipal common fund and US$80 million directly), conditioned on councils cutting permit-processing times by 30 percent. It is not fully law yet: the government is sending three suppressive presidential vetoes — on an anatocismo (compound-interest) provision, a “financial right to be forgotten” and a 30-day payment rule for small firms — and the opposition has asked the Constitutional Court to strike the tax-stability guarantee and an environmental-restitution article, which cannot be promulgated until the court rules.

The corporate cut

The headline measure lowers the corporate income-tax rate from 27 percent toward 23 percent by 2029, phased through the intervening years (25.5 percent in 2027, 24 percent in 2028, 23 percent from 2029). The government framed it as restoring Chile’s tax competitiveness for investment.

The reform also introduces full reintegration — letting shareholders credit 100 percent of corporate tax — eliminates the capital-gains tax, and adds capital-repatriation incentives and a tax-stability guarantee for large investments. Most of it sits on the corporate and investment side rather than personal taxation.

The break for older homeowners

The change that reaches individuals most directly is the exemption of the first home of people over 65 from municipal property tax, the contribuciones. For older expats and retirees who own their home in Chile, that is a real annual saving.

The mechanism for compensating municipalities that lose the revenue is the piece still being finalised, so the exemption’s exact operation may be confirmed shortly.

What did not change

For arriving remote workers and new residents, the rules that matter most are untouched. Chile still taxes new arrivals only on Chilean-source income for their first three years. The law lets the tax authority extend that window in qualified cases on application; it does not set a fixed second three-year term.

Chile still has no wealth tax, and its income-tax treaty with the United States, which entered into force in December 2023 and has applied since 2024, remains. The reform does not alter the foreign-income runway that draws remote workers.

That combination is why the reform matters more for what it preserves than for what it changes. The headline corporate cut is aimed at foreign direct investment and large projects, while the levers that shape a typical expat’s tax bill — the three-year window on foreign income, the absence of a wealth tax and the US treaty — were deliberately left untouched. For a remote worker weighing Chile against a neighbour, the package removes a reason to hesitate without adding a new personal cost.

What it means for foreign residents

The net effect is a friendlier investment climate and a modest, concrete win for older homeowners, with nothing lost for new arrivals. It reinforces rather than changes the case for moving to Chile.

The corporate cut is phased and the municipal-compensation detail is unfinished, so confirm timing and any personal impact with a Chilean accountant. This is general information, not tax advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Chile’s tax reform change? It cuts corporate tax from 27 to 23 percent by 2029 and exempts first homes of people over 65 from municipal property tax, among other measures. Does it affect new residents’ taxes? No. The three-year exemption on foreign income, which the tax authority may extend on application, is unchanged, as is the absence of a wealth tax. Who gains from the property-tax change? Owners over 65, including older expats and retirees, whose first home is exempted from municipal property tax. Is the reform final? Not fully. Congress cleared it on 4 August, when the Senate passed the last article 27–22, but three presidential vetoes go back to Congress and the Constitutional Court must still rule on a challenge to the tax-stability guarantee before those parts can be promulgated. Does Chile still have the US tax treaty? Yes. The income-tax treaty with the United States, which entered into force in December 2023 and has applied since 2024, is unaffected.

World.title: Argentina Monotributo Tax Brackets Rise 16.8% by Aug 5
World.content:
Argentina · Money

Key Facts The update. Monotributo brackets rise 16.8 percent in August, tracking first-half inflation.

Monotributo brackets rise 16.8 percent in August, tracking first-half inflation. The deadline. Registered taxpayers must recategorise by today, Wednesday, August 5.

Registered taxpayers must recategorise by today, Wednesday, August 5. The top ceiling. The annual billing cap rises to about 126.6 million pesos (~US$85,000).

The annual billing cap rises to about 126.6 million pesos (~US$85,000). The entry band. Category A’s ceiling rises to about 12 million pesos (~US$8,060) a year.

Category A’s ceiling rises to about 12 million pesos (~US$8,060) a year. Who cares. Foreign freelancers billing local clients through Monotributo should check their band.

Argentina’s Monotributo brackets rise 16.8 percent in August, tracking first-half inflation, with a recategorisation deadline of August 5 and the top annual billing cap reaching about 126.6 million pesos (~US$85,000).

If you are a foreigner registered as a monotributista in Argentina, billing local clients under the simplified small-taxpayer regime, the mid-year update is here. The brackets rise 16.8 percent in August, and you have until today, Wednesday, August 5 to recategorise.

Argentina’s Monotributo brackets rise 16.8 percent for August, in line with first-half inflation. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What is changing

The Monotributo is Argentina’s simplified regime for small taxpayers, bundling tax and social contributions into a single monthly payment. The law updates its brackets twice a year, in January and July, using the preceding half-year’s inflation.

With first-half 2026 inflation at 16.8 percent, every band — from billing ceilings to income limits and monthly payments — rises by that amount for August. This mechanism is designed to stop inflation from silently pushing small taxpayers into higher tax brackets or out of the regime entirely, a problem that plagued Argentina for years before the automatic adjustment was introduced.

For a foreign reader, it helps to think of the Monotributo as a ladder. Each rung, or category, has a maximum annual billing limit and a fixed monthly fee that covers income tax, VAT, and pension contributions all at once. When the ladder shifts upward, the rungs move with it, so your place on the ladder should reflect your real earning power, not just the erosion of the currency.

The new numbers

The top annual billing ceiling climbs to about 126.6 million pesos (~US$85,000), from roughly 108 million (~US$72,500). Category A, the entry band, sees its ceiling rise to about 12 million pesos (~US$8,060) a year.

Monthly payments step up across every category in line with the 16.8 percent adjustment. The new amounts apply from the August due date and hold until the next update in January 2027.

These figures matter because crossing a ceiling without recategorising can trigger an automatic exclusion from the simplified system. Once excluded, a taxpayer falls into the general regime, which requires separate filings for income tax and VAT, a far heavier administrative burden for a solo freelancer or a small shop.

The deadline to recategorise

Taxpayers have from July 15 to August 5 to review their billing over the past twelve months, July 2025 to June 2026, and confirm or change their category. Those who have outgrown their band must move up; those who have billed less can move down.

Missing the window, or staying in the wrong category, risks penalties or exclusion from the regime. The recategorisation is done through ARCA’s online portal (formerly AFIP).

The process itself is straightforward: you log in with your tax ID, check your declared invoices for the twelve-month window, and the system suggests where you belong. Still, the portal’s interface can feel opaque if you are not fluent in Spanish or unfamiliar with Argentine tax terminology, which is why many foreigners lean on a local accountant even for this seemingly simple step.

Why it matters for foreigners

Many foreign freelancers and independent workers in Argentina bill local clients through Monotributo because it is simple and cheap. If your invoicing has grown, the higher ceilings may keep you inside the regime rather than pushing you into the general tax system.

Check where your last twelve months of billing lands against the new bands before August 5. Confirm the exact figures on the tax authority’s site, as amounts round differently by category.

There is also a less obvious benefit: staying inside the Monotributo means your monthly payment remains predictable. In the general regime, tax obligations can swing sharply with each billing cycle, which makes budgeting harder for someone earning in pesos while perhaps maintaining obligations in another currency.

The bigger picture

The update follows June inflation of 1.9 percent, the lowest monthly reading in about ten months. Slower inflation means smaller bracket jumps than in the recent past, but the twice-yearly adjustment still matters for anyone near a threshold.

None of this is tax advice. A local accountant can confirm your category and handle the recategorisation if you are unsure.

Looking ahead, the key question is whether the disinflation trend holds through the second half of the year. Today’s Focus Grain prices retreated across the board on Tuesday, with the soybean, corn and wheat tracker funds all closing lower. The broad decline was driven not by a single crop shock, but by a combination of improving harvest weather in the Americas, a firming US dollar, and cautious demand signals from China, the world’s top importer. The Teucrium Soybean Fund (SOYB) slipped 0.75% to US$25.05. The corn proxy, the Teucrium Corn Fund (CORN), eased a full percentage point to US$17.75. The weakest link was the Teucrium Wheat Fund (WEAT), which fell 1.65% to US$23.86, as solid Black Sea harvests compounded the broader downward pressure. For Latin America’s export titans, the moves highlight the tight link between Chicago futures and local profitability. Brazil, the world’s largest soybean exporter, and Argentina, a powerhouse in corn and soymeal, see their competitive edge sharpen when a weaker real or peso meets a strong dollar, but this same dynamic can exacerbate price slides for the US-dollar-denominated tracker funds. The session underscored that while crop conditions are the main weathervane, currency fluctuations are the sail. The strengthening dollar effectively raises the price for buyers holding other currencies, potentially cooling import demand just as record Latin American supplies prepare to flood global markets. What matters today. The triple decline in grain tracker funds reflects a fresh alignment of bearish factors—US weather, a firm dollar, and Chinese caution—threatening to shift the global supply-demand balance further in favour of buyers.

01 The session in one read

A basket of headwinds swept through grain markets on Tuesday, pushing all three major tracker funds into the red. The move was broad rather than isolated, reflecting a global recalibration of supply expectations that places Latin America’s vast export machine at centre stage.

The funds, which hold baskets of Chicago futures to give stock-like exposure to grain prices, fell in lockstep as the strengthening US dollar made benchmark contracts more expensive for international buyers. This currency effect amplified unease about swelling supply from both the US farm belt and the Black Sea region.

Assessment — Buyers gain the upper hand MEDIUM The grain complex is giving ground as temporary supply-side fears fade. With US corn and soybean crops thriving and the dollar creating a headwind, the onus shifts to demand. China’s next moves in the physical market are crucial, especially any acceleration in Brazilian soybean bookings or new-crop corn purchases. The variable to watch is the pace of Brazil’s next soybean harvest and whether early field reports confirm the stabilising yield expectations, which would remove the last bullish anchor from the market.

02 The board

The Teucrium Soybean Fund (SOYB) settled at US$25.05, a decline of 0.75% on the day. The fund holds multiple Chicago soybean futures contracts and its price drop reflects rising confidence that the US will harvest a bumper crop. The Teucrium Corn Fund (CORN) fell exactly 1.00% to US$17.75, weighed by weekly reports showing a high share of the US corn area in good-to-excellent condition.

Hardest hit was the Teucrium Wheat Fund (WEAT), which lost 1.65% to close at US$23.86. The decline in the wheat tracker was deepened by steady assessments of Russian and Ukrainian harvest volumes, which are proving solid despite persistent geopolitical risks in the Black Sea export corridor.

03 What moved it

The primary driver was improving crop weather across the US Midwest, where timely rains and moderate temperatures are supporting high yield potential for both soybeans and corn. When the US supply outlook brightens, global importers feel less urgency to bid aggressively, which directly pressures the futures that SOYB and CORN hold.

A second force was the firming dollar. Because grain futures are priced in US dollars, a stronger greenback makes these contracts more expensive for buyers in Europe, Asia and Latin America, potentially dampening their purchase appetite. For the wheat market, the fundamental picture was further clouded by solid Black Sea harvests, which ensure plenty of competitively-priced cargoes are available along traditional shipping routes, undercutting the case for higher Chicago prices tracked by WEAT.

04 The Latin American read

The price slide is a double-edged sword for Brazil and Argentina, the planet’s combined export engine for soybeans, corn and soymeal. Brazil has become the world’s largest soybean exporter, with the lion’s share of its fast-expanding Mato Grosso and Goiás production sailing directly to China’s coastal crushers. A dip in Chicago futures narrows dollar revenues, but exactly how this hits farmers depends on the local currency’s own trajectory.

A weaker Brazilian real can fully offset a fall in dollar prices, encouraging producers to sell by keeping local-currency returns elevated. Argentina’s Rosario-based crushing industry, which dominates global soymeal trade, faces the same calculus. Recent policy changes that reduced export taxes on grains have improved farmer incentives, increasing the likelihood that Argentina ships its surplus corn and wheat onto world markets, adding to global supply just as WEAT and CORN lose ground.

05 The names to watch

The three Teucrium funds—SOYB, CORN and WEAT—are commodity pools that hold a mix of futures contracts across different delivery months. This multi-contract structure smooths out the wildest swings of one specific expiry, but it also embeds a concept called roll yield. When markets are in contango, meaning future contracts cost more than the expiring ones, the funds pay a cost to roll their positions, creating a gradual drag on returns that investors should understand.

Beyond the fund mechanics, the giants of physical trade are the real-world levers. Brazil’s expanding export infrastructure in the Amazon and at Santos undergirds its status as China’s preferred soybean supplier, a relationship that drives demand-side swings for SOYB. For corn, the rise in Brazilian safrinha exports to China since Beijing approved key exporters marks a structural shift that can directly undercut CORN’s benchmarks. Argentina retains an outsized role in wheat cargos bound for Brazil and North Africa, meaning any Pampas weather scare or policy shift quickly echoes through WEAT.

06 The outlook

The grain complex enters the coming weeks with a heavier feel. Unless a fresh weather shock disrupts the favourable US outlook or the Black Sea export window unexpectedly tightens, bountiful supply is likely to anchor prices. The critical variable is Chinese demand as the country’s hog herd rebuild dictates soymeal and corn import volumes. Any sign that Beijing is stepping back from the physical market would remove the last major prop from a market already tilting in buyers’ favour.

07 What to watch

US weekly crop ratings: Watch the next set of US Department of Agriculture crop condition reports; a further rise in the good-to-excellent share for corn or soybeans would reinforce the bearish supply narrative and could push CORN and SOYB to fresh lows.

Watch the next set of US Department of Agriculture crop condition reports; a further rise in the good-to-excellent share for corn or soybeans would reinforce the bearish supply narrative and could push CORN and SOYB to fresh lows. USD/BRL exchange rate: The real’s movement against the dollar is crucial. A sustained weakening of the Brazilian real would encourage export selling and boost local farmer revenues, even if dollar-denominated futures tracked by the funds continue to slide.

The real’s movement against the dollar is crucial. A sustained weakening of the Brazilian real would encourage export selling and boost local farmer revenues, even if dollar-denominated futures tracked by the funds continue to slide. China’s soybean booking pace: Monitor daily export sales announcements for any pickup in Chinese purchase commitments. A slowdown in Brazilian cargo bookings would signal weak feed demand and directly undermine the floor in SOYB.

Monitor daily export sales announcements for any pickup in Chinese purchase commitments. A slowdown in Brazilian cargo bookings would signal weak feed demand and directly undermine the floor in SOYB. Argentina’s planting progress: Keep an eye on Pampas weather and farmer selling rates for wheat and early corn plantings. Solid moisture and expanded acreage, underpinned by lower export taxes, would add weight to global supply and pressure WEAT.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the grain tracker funds all fall on the same day?

A combination of three factors hit the complex simultaneously: improving crop weather in the US Midwest is boosting harvest prospects, a firming US dollar makes dollar-priced grain futures costlier for foreign buyers, and cautious Chinese demand is reducing the urgency for importers to bid up prices.

How does a strong dollar hurt soybean and corn prices?

Chicago grain futures are priced in US dollars. When the dollar strengthens against currencies like the Brazilian real, each contract becomes more expensive for buyers holding those other currencies, which can cool purchase demand and push futures lower.

Why is Brazil so important for global soybean and corn trade?

Brazil is the world’s largest soybean exporter and a rapidly growing corn supplier, with massive production expansion in central states and heavy investment in export terminals. The majority of its soybean exports flow directly to China, making Brazilian harvest prospects a key determinant of global grain supply tracked by SOYB and CORN.

What does the Teucrium Wheat Fund (WEAT) actually hold?

WEAT holds three Chicago wheat futures contracts across different delivery months. This structure provides broad exposure to US wheat prices while reducing volatility from any single contract expiry. Its performance also incorporates roll yield, which can be a drag on returns when futures markets are in contango.

Today’s Focus Oil equities across the Americas were hammered on Tuesday after the United States Oil Fund LP, the exchange-traded fund that tracks front-month WTI futures, fell 5.19% to US$115.78. The decline showed up in the wider commodity basket too, with the diversified Invesco DB Commodity Index Tracking Fund (DBC) down 1.97% on the session. For Latin America’s state-controlled giants and the new private-led boom in Guyana, the move instantly tightened the screws on revenue projections and share prices. Brazil’s Petrobras shed 1.78% to US$18.72, a comparatively mild loss that underscores how the deepwater pre-salt machine can absorb a single-day crude shock, even if political interference in fuel pricing prevents a perfect correlation with global benchmarks. Colombia’s Ecopetrol displayed similar resilience, falling 1.75% to US$16.31, but Argentina’s YPF took a sharper 2.78% hit, closing at US$49.64 as the investment case for the Vaca Muerta shale play is directly pegged to sustained high WTI levels. The sell-off reverberated beyond the listed producers. For Mexico’s Pemex, whose heavy debt load means its bonds act as a pure proxy for Mexican oil risk, lower crude threatens the cash-flow narrative that has kept creditors at bay, even though the company’s shares are not in our board. Conversely, Guyana’s Stabroek Block, operated by ExxonMobil, Hess and CNOOC, is adding low-political-risk barrels that become more valuable when higher-cost, state-run suppliers elsewhere in the region struggle, a dynamic that can accelerate the Atlantic basin’s supply shift away from legacy producers. What matters today. A sudden 5.19% plunge in the WTI tracker USO dragged down every major Latin American oil equity, but the damage was uneven, with shale-exposed YPF suffering most and pre-salt giant Petrobras proving stickier.

03 What moved it

The 5.19% plunge in USO signalled a sharp reassessment of demand prospects, with front-month WTI futures dragged lower by a combination of macroeconomic anxiety and a strengthening US dollar. Because USO rolls front-month contracts, it captures immediate shifts in futures positioning, and today’s move indicated that traders aggressively priced out near-term scarcity premiums.

The broader commodity complex confirmed the bearish tilt. The Invesco DB Commodity Index Tracking Fund, which holds a mix of crude, refined products and metals, saw its previous close rest at a multi-session low, while copper-tracking funds also retreated, severing any link between oil’s weakness and a rotation into industrial metals. This was a wholesale de-risking, not a targeted bet against energy.

04 The Latin American read

Brazil’s Petrobras, ending at US$18.72, absorbed the shock with relative composure thanks to the geological bounty of the pre-salt, where low lifting costs at the Santos and Campos basins insulate upstream margins even when WTI stumbles. However, the company’s discount to the crude move also reflects a persistent political risk premium, as the federal government’s influence over fuel pricing prevents a straightforward correlation with global benchmarks.

Argentina’s YPF, by contrast, cratered 2.78% to US$49.64 because the Vaca Muerta shale formation in the Neuquén Basin depends on sustained high WTI levels to justify the capital-intensive drilling and midstream infrastructure that investors have been betting on. Colombia’s Ecopetrol, at US$16.31, fell in sympathy, reminding the market that Andean producers cannot decouple from a broad Atlantic basin sell-off. Venezuela’s heavy crude, meanwhile, remains a latent supply variable: any US sanctions easing could suddenly release extra-heavy Orinoco Belt barrels, adding downward pressure to the heavy-light differential that already competes with Brazil’s and Guyana’s lighter offshore grades.

05 The names to watch

Petrobras is the bellwether for how pre-salt economics interact with volatile global benchmarks. Its ability to hold above US$18.70 in a down-5% crude session suggests that deepwater production margins provide a sturdy floor, but any sign of Brasília interfering in the dividend policy would test that support.

YPF stands as the highest-beta play in the region, amplifying WTI’s move in both directions. With shares now below US$50, the company’s ability to attract foreign partners for Vaca Muerta’s next drilling phase becomes a live question. In the Guyanas, ExxonMobil-led Stabroek Block production is the silent counterweight, adding low-cost, low-political-risk barrels that make the investment case for higher-cost state operators like Pemex and PDVSA even more challenging when prices fall.

06 The outlook

The immediate trajectory hinges on whether USO can find a floor near the US$115 mark or whether algorithmic selling extends the decline into a second session. For Latin American equities, a stabilisation in WTI would allow investors to refocus on company-level catalysts, such as Petrobras’s next pre-salt output report or YPF’s midstream capacity expansions. However, if the commodities complex continues to slide, the market will rapidly reprice the fiscal resilience of every state-controlled producer, from Mexico City to Buenos Aires.

07 What to watch

USO stabilisation: Watch whether USO rebounds above US$115.78 in the next session; a failure to hold that level would confirm a momentum break and could trigger a second wave of selling across YPF and Ecopetrol.

Watch whether USO rebounds above US$115.78 in the next session; a failure to hold that level would confirm a momentum break and could trigger a second wave of selling across YPF and Ecopetrol. Petrobras political risk: Monitor any news from Brasília on fuel-pricing policy or dividend distributions, because a political misstep could sever Petrobras’s relative resilience and push shares well below US$18.72.

Monitor any news from Brasília on fuel-pricing policy or dividend distributions, because a political misstep could sever Petrobras’s relative resilience and push shares well below US$18.72. YPF break-even stress: With YPF below US$50, track any statements from the company or Neuquén province on drilling activity, as a sustained low WTI environment would directly threaten the economics of new Vaca Muerta pads.

With YPF below US$50, track any statements from the company or Neuquén province on drilling activity, as a sustained low WTI environment would directly threaten the economics of new Vaca Muerta pads. Venezuela sanctions chatter: Any credible signal of US sanctions easing on PDVSA could immediately widen the heavy-light crude spread, pressuring Brazil’s and Guyana’s lighter grades and challenging the premium that pre-salt barrels currently command.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Latin American oil stocks fall on August 5?

A global crude sell-off drove the WTI-tracking USO down 5.19% to US$115.78, pulling Petrobras, Ecopetrol and YPF lower as investors repriced Latin America’s revenue outlook for cheaper oil.

Why did YPF fall more than Petrobras?

YPF dropped 2.78% to US$49.64 because the Vaca Muerta shale play requires consistently high WTI prices to justify drilling costs, whereas Petrobras’s low-cost pre-salt fields absorbed the crude shock with a milder 1.78% decline.

How does Guyana fit into this sell-off?

Guyana’s Stabroek Block, operated by ExxonMobil, Hess and CNOOC, is adding low-cost offshore barrels to the Atlantic basin; cheaper crude makes those projects even more competitive against higher-cost state producers like Pemex and PDVSA.

Is this a broader commodity problem or just oil?

It was mostly an energy story: the broad Invesco DB Commodity Index Tracking Fund (DBC) fell 1.97%, but copper-tracking funds actually rose, so investors were selling crude rather than the whole commodity complex.

Today’s Focus Latin America’s two most-watched zinc proxy stocks posted sharp gains on Tuesday. Nexa Resources, the integrated miner and smelter with operations in Peru and Brazil, added 5.06 per cent to close at US$13.50. Compañía de Minas Buenaventura jumped 5.87 per cent to US$32.26, lifted by zinc’s rally and its polymetallic concentrate output. Behind the move sits zinc’s structural reliance on galvanized steel, which absorbs about half of all refined supply. Construction beam orders, roof-panel demand in China and a fresh round of infrastructure spending signals gave traders a reason to bid up companies that can deliver mined concentrates and finished metal. Andean supply bottlenecks are amplifying the effect. In Peru, a top-five global producer, community protests and slower-than-expected environmental approvals have periodically choked concentrate flows out of the central Andes. Bolivia, a smaller but significant exporter, is dealing with persistent logistics and financing frictions for its medium-scale miners. Together these forces turned the session into a textbook zinc squeeze for Latin American producers. Investors used both Nexa and Buenaventura as liquid, regionally listed ways to express a view on the metal’s tightness without trading London contracts directly. What matters today. Zinc miner stocks surged because strong galvanized-steel demand collided with supply fears in Peru and Bolivia, lifting Latin America’s two main proxy plays.

01 The session in one read

Two of Latin America’s most liquid zinc proxy stocks surged on Tuesday, catching foreign investors who track the region’s base-metals exposure. Nexa Resources, which runs underground zinc mines in Peru and smelters in Brazil, closed at US$13.50, up 5.06 per cent. Buenaventura, the Peruvian polymetallic miner, gained 5.87 per cent to US$32.26.

The rally was driven by a confluence of firm galvanized-steel demand and anxiety about concentrate supply out of Peru and Bolivia. No single event triggered the move; instead, a steady drumbeat of construction-activity data and localised mining-capacity concerns provided the momentum.

Assessment — Supply jitters meet galvanizing demand HIGH The parallel rise in Nexa and Buenaventura points to a market that is pricing both a construction-led demand pulse and a credible threat of Andean concentrate disruptions. With Peru’s permitting delays and Bolivia’s logistical bottlenecks showing no quick fix, the zinc supply chain remains vulnerable to headline-driven rallies. The variable to watch is a further reduction in Peruvian concentrate shipments, which would test how quickly smelters can draw on accumulated stocks.

02 The board

The board shows zinc-linked equities delivering some of the strongest percentage gains among Latin American metal names. Nexa, the purest regional zinc play, and Buenaventura, with its precious- and base-metals mix, both moved higher on volume that suggested institutional buying rather than short covering.

Each price here represents a share of a listed company—not the raw metal spot—and the moves reflect earnings sensitivity to zinc. Nexa’s rise is the more direct read, given zinc contributes the largest slice of its revenue from mines such as Cerro Lindo and Vazante.

03 What moved it

The core driver was renewed evidence that construction—and therefore galvanizing—demand is holding up in several key markets. Approximately half of all refined zinc ends up coating steel against rust, so orders for beams, roofing and infrastructure components translate quickly into drawdowns on concentrate stocks.

At the same time, supply from Latin America is looking fragile. Peru, a top-five global mine supplier, has experienced periodic disruptions from community roadblocks and environmental-permit backlogs that slow the movement of zinc concentrates from the central Andes to port. Bolivia’s exports, meanwhile, are dominated by smaller operators facing tight credit and unreliable logistics, making every tonne of delayed shipment a marginal support for prices.

04 The Latin American read

For foreign investors, Nexa and Buenaventura are the two names that make zinc investable through a regional lens. Nexa’s integrated model—it mines in Peru and Brazil and smelts at Três Marias and Juiz de Fora—offers leverage to both the mined concentrate and the value-added metal that goes directly into galvanizers’ pots.

Buenaventura’s zinc exposure sits inside polymetallic mines such as Uchucchacua and Colquijirca, where the metal is produced alongside silver and lead. That means its share price responds to zinc, but the move on Tuesday was strong enough to suggest traders were using it as a liquid entry point for an Andean zinc bet.

05 The names to watch

Nexa Resources remains the headline proxy. Its Cerro Lindo mine in Ica is one of the world’s larger underground zinc operations, and the company’s quarterly output reports are closely watched for clues about Peruvian logistics and ore grades. Any sign of a grade shortfall or a shipping delay at the mine tends to move the share price sharply.

Buenaventura operates with a different risk profile because gold and silver still dominate its earnings, but the zinc-concentrate division has become a meaningful swing factor. Investors also keep an eye on Mexico’s Peñasquito and other polymetallic mines that feed the North American galvanizing chain, though those lack a liquid, pure local proxy.

06 The outlook

The short-term path for Latin American zinc equities will depend on whether China’s construction stimulus translates into actual steel-coating orders and on whether Peruvian and Bolivian concentrate flows face another disruption. A prolonged stand-off at a single large mine in the Peruvian highlands could rapidly tighten the spot market. For now, the zinc trade is running on the simple logic that galvanizing demand is real and the Andean supply chain sits on shaky ground.

07 What to watch

Peruvian concentrate shipments at risk: Any expansion of community protests or environmental permit freezes could delay supply from Cerro Lindo and other mines.

Any expansion of community protests or environmental permit freezes could delay supply from Cerro Lindo and other mines. Chinese galvanizing orders: Construction stimulus in China directly boosts demand for zinc-coated steel, lifting the price that Latin American miners receive.

Construction stimulus in China directly boosts demand for zinc-coated steel, lifting the price that Latin American miners receive. Bolivian logistics and credit: Tight financing for medium-scale miners in Potosí and Oruro may cap exports even when spot prices rise.

Tight financing for medium-scale miners in Potosí and Oruro may cap exports even when spot prices rise. Nexa quarterly production report: The company’s next output release will show whether ore grades and shipping volumes are tracking market expectations.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Nexa Resources jump 5.06 per cent to US$13.50?

Strong galvanizing demand combined with Peruvian supply worries lifted the zinc proxy, as zinc is Nexa’s primary revenue driver.

What does Buenaventura have to do with zinc?

Buenaventura’s Uchucchacua and Colquijirca mines produce zinc concentrates alongside precious metals, making its shares sensitive to the metal’s price moves.

How is galvanized steel connected to zinc prices?

Around half of refined zinc coats steel to prevent rust; when construction and manufacturing orders rise, demand for zinc jumps.

Why are Peru and Bolivia important for zinc supply?

Peru is a top-five global mine producer and Bolivia ships significant zinc concentrates, so disruptions there can tighten the world market.

Key Facts Vale’s ADR gained 1.71% to close at US$14.83 in New York, acting as a direct proxy for seaborne iron-ore prices and Chinese demand.

Today’s Focus Iron-ore proxies climbed decisively on Tuesday, with Vale’s New York-traded ADR rising to US$14.83 and CSN Mineração jumping to R$5.91, as fresh signals of Chinese credit easing revived bets on steel-intensive construction. Rio Tinto joined the move, advancing to US$99.01, confirming that the bid was broad-based across Western-listed mining equities. Behind the rally sat a concrete policy signal: China’s state council approved new special-bond issuance quotas for provincial governments, earmarked for stalled infrastructure works. That action directly lifted the outlook for rebar and structural steel orders, prompting North Asian traders to report a flurry of cargo inquiries for high-grade Brazilian ore from Vale’s northern system. Brazilian ore enjoys a structural advantage in this cycle because its higher iron content helps Chinese mills cut coke rates and carbon emissions per tonne of hot metal, a priority as Beijing tightens environmental compliance. Copper rose alongside it, with the copper-tracking fund CPER up 1.26%, so the day’s bid ran across the wider industrial-metals complex. For Latin American investors, the move reaffirms that Vale and CSN Mineração remain liquid barometers of Chinese policy sentiment, even when the underlying spot ore price is not on screen. The session’s rotation into iron-ore names while copper futures dipped suggests the market is pricing a China stimulus impulse concentrated in fixed-asset investment rather than broad manufacturing output. What matters today. Chinese credit easing triggered a concentrated bid for Brazilian iron-ore proxies, lifting Vale and CSN Mineração while copper futures slipped, signalling a construction-led rather than broad industrial recovery.

01 The session in one read

Iron-ore proxies surged on Tuesday after China’s state council authorised a new tranche of special-bond quotas for provincial infrastructure, handing investors a concrete reason to buy the steelmaking raw material. Vale’s New York ADR closed at US$14.83, a gain of 1.71%, while São Paulo-listed CSN Mineração jumped 3.14% to R$5.91.

The catalyst broke a two-week lull in China-linked commodity trades. Provincial governments had been sitting on approved but unfunded transport and water projects; the new bond quotas unlocked that pipeline, sending steel rebar futures higher during Asian hours and triggering follow-on buying in Western-listed mining shares throughout the European and American sessions.

Assessment — Construction stimulus, not broad reflation HIGH Tuesday’s move was clean and catalyst-driven: Chinese special-bond quotas unlocked a pipeline of infrastructure projects, directly boosting the marginal demand for seaborne ore. Vale’s ADR at US$14.83 and Rio Tinto at US$99.01 both broke above their 20-day moving averages on strong volume, while CSN Mineração’s R$5.91 close attracted local Brazilian fund flows rotating out of domestic rate-sensitive names. Copper advanced in the same session, with CPER up 1.26%, so this read as a broad industrial-metals bid rather than a narrow steel-and-concrete story. The variable to watch is the pace of special-bond disbursement over the next two weeks; any bureaucratic delay in project starts would unwind the premium built into Brazilian ore names.

02 The board

Vale’s ADR at US$14.83 acted as the session’s primary iron-ore bellwether, closely tracking the Brazil-to-China trade that defines the seaborne market. Rio Tinto confirmed the breadth of the move with a 3.24% advance to US$99.01, its Anglo-Australian shareholder base treating the Chinese credit signal as a marginal demand uplift for Pilbara ore as well.

CSN Mineração, the pure-play Brazilian iron-ore miner, outperformed with a 3.14% rally to R$5.91. Domestic Brazilian funds piled in, viewing the stock as the most direct equity exposure to a China construction cycle because CSN Mineração lacks the base-metal diversification that Vale carries through its nickel and copper divisions.

03 What moved it

China’s new special-bond allocation targeted the kind of steel-intensive fixed-asset investment that consumes large volumes of imported ore, from bridge pilings to high-speed rail track beds. Traders in Singapore and Shanghai reported a pick-up in floating cargo inquiries for high-grade Brazilian fines from Vale’s Carajás system, the very ore that traded at a widening premium during the session.

Chinese mills prefer Brazilian high-grade ore because its elevated iron content and lower alumina and phosphorus impurities allow them to operate blast furnaces with less coke and lower emissions per tonne of hot metal. That environmental calculus has gained weight since Beijing expanded its emissions-trading scheme to include the steel sector, making Vale’s product structurally advantaged when infrastructure approvals accelerate.

04 The Latin American read

Brazil’s equity market treated the move as a straightforward beta play on Chinese credit. CSN Mineração’s 3.14% surge outpaced the broader Ibovespa, which was weighted down by rate-sensitive utilities and consumer names, reflecting a clear rotation into the export-facing materials sector.

For Mexico and Chile, the session carried a reinforcing message: copper gained alongside iron ore, with CPER up 1.26% and Southern Copper adding 4.98%, signalling that the Chinese stimulus impulse reached beyond construction into the wider metals complex. That breadth matters for Latin American economies that export copper as well as iron ore, because it suggests the 2026 China recovery is running across commodity verticals rather than in one lane.

05 The names to watch

Vale remains the heavyweight proxy for any investor wanting dollar-denominated exposure to iron ore without navigating Brazilian onshore markets. Its ADR structure, with each receipt representing one common share listed on the NYSE, provides a liquid and familiar vehicle for foreign capital.

CSN Mineração offers a purer play on iron-ore prices than Vale because it lacks the base-metals earnings stream. Rio Tinto, while domiciled in London and Melbourne, provides a global comparator that often trades in sympathy with the Brazil–China route because its Pilbara operations compete for the same Chinese steel-mill customer base.

06 The outlook

The sustainability of this rally hinges on the speed with which provincial governments convert their new bond quotas into actual project starts. A rapid drawdown of funds into earthworks and concrete pours would tighten the physical iron-ore market into the fourth quarter, supporting Vale and CSN Mineração at current levels. Conversely, any sign that the quotas are being diverted to refinance existing local-government debt rather than fund new construction would reverse the demand narrative that drove Tuesday’s gains, making the bond-disbursement data the single most important variable for Latin American materials investors over the coming fortnight.

07 What to watch

Chinese special-bond disbursement pace: The speed at which provinces convert approved quotas into project starts will determine whether physical iron-ore purchases materialise or the rally fades.

Brazilian real trajectory: A strengthening real against the dollar compresses Vale’s export margins in local-currency terms; CSN Mineração’s São Paulo listing captures this dynamic more directly than the dollar-denominated ADR.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Vale’s shares move if iron ore isn’t on the price board?

Vale’s New York ADR acts as a liquid proxy for seaborne iron-ore prices, rising when investors expect higher Chinese steel demand to lift the miner’s earnings.

What makes Brazilian iron ore different from Australian ore?

Brazilian ore from Vale’s Carajás system carries higher iron content and fewer impurities, allowing Chinese mills to produce steel with lower coke consumption and emissions.

How does CSN Mineração differ from Vale?

CSN Mineração is a pure-play iron-ore exporter listed in São Paulo, without Vale’s base-metals divisions, making it a more concentrated bet on iron-ore prices in Brazilian reais.

Why did copper futures fall while iron-ore proxies rose?

China’s latest stimulus targeted construction and infrastructure, which are steel-intensive, while the broader manufacturing sector that drives copper demand saw no equivalent catalyst on Tuesday.

Today’s Focus Copper prices and mining equities vaulted higher on Tuesday as a powerful combination of fresh Chinese demand signals and a deepening global supply squeeze swept across the market. The United States Copper Index Fund, trading under the ticker CPER, settled at US$40.14, a daily gain of 1.26%. Because CPER tracks a portfolio of copper futures contracts rather than the spot price of physical metal, the move tells us traders are sharply upgrading their expectations for where copper is heading, not merely reacting to today’s cost of a delivered cathode. The equity response was even more emphatic. Shares of Southern Copper, a giant with vast Chilean and Peruvian operations, soared 4.98% to US$195.16. Freeport-McMoRan, another heavyweight producer with a globally diversified but LatAm-heavy portfolio, shot up 5.75%, closing at US$67.30. This magnified reaction in miners’ shares reflects the operational leverage that boosts profits faster when the commodity price outlook brightens, though academic research cautions the relationship is positive but inelastic over the long run. Behind the surge lies a fresh catalyst from Beijing, where new pledges for infrastructure spending and grid investment fanned expectations that the world’s largest consumer of refined copper will pull hard on global inventories. Investors read the announcements as a counterweight to months of sluggish manufacturing data. Coupled with the relentless structural demand from the global energy transition—where copper is essential for EV wiring, charging networks and solar farms—the Chinese move was enough to reignite the long-term thesis that a physical deficit is deepening just as supply from Chile and Peru faces persistent grade declines and permitting delays. What matters today. A sudden re-evaluation of Chinese demand for energy-transition metals is driving a broad, high-volume repricing of copper futures and LatAm-exposed mining equities.

01 The session in one read

Copper markets snapped higher on Tuesday, 4 August 2026, as a convergence of Chinese policy optimism and structural supply fears reset the board. The copper-tracking ETF CPER rose 1.26% to US$40.14, while the major producing stocks posted outsized gains: Southern Copper climbed 4.98% to US$195.16 and Freeport-McMoRan jumped 5.75% to US$67.30.

The session reveals a market that had been poised for a catalyst. The CPER fund, which tracks a portfolio of COMEX futures rather than physical metal, captures traders’ expectations, and its sharp upward lurch signals that market participants are pricing in a tighter supply-demand balance ahead.

Assessment — China bets clash with futures roll costs MEDIUM This rally is powerful but exposes a delicate fault line. The immediate trigger is genuine: a Chinese policy shift can rapidly tighten a copper market where visible inventories are already drawing. Yet CPER’s own structure introduces fragility. As a futures-based tracker, it incurs roll costs every time it shifts contracts to avoid physical delivery, which is why its longer-horizon returns often lag the equity miners it outpaced today. If Chinese stimulus scepticism returns or the US dollar strengthens, futures can deflate faster than the physical-backing narrative implies. Watch whether equity premiums on Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan hold into next week, as a reversal would signal that traders priced a policy pivot they have yet to see executed on the ground.

02 The board

The equity board flashed a classic risk-on rotation into materials. Southern Copper, the NYSE-listed producer with its deepest mines in Peru and Mexico, extended its post-earnings recovery, blasting through Tuesday’s marks to finish at US$195.16. Freeport-McMoRan, whose Grasberg operations in Indonesia sit alongside a massive South American portfolio, recorded the session’s biggest swing among the heavyweights, settling at US$67.30, a gain of 5.75%.

The gap between the 1.26% advance in the futures proxy and the near-5% surges in miner equities is instructive. It reflects how company earnings amplify commodity moves, especially when producers have reported strong second-quarter results, as Southern Copper did in recent weeks with net income above US$1.6 billion. Traders re-priced operational cash flows rapidly, betting that any sustained copper rally flows almost directly to the bottom line of firms with high fixed costs and long-life reserves.

03 What moved it

The immediate fuse was a new round of Chinese infrastructure and power-grid investment pledges. Because China consumes roughly half of the world’s refined copper, any decisive fiscal push is read as a direct bid on the metal. Traders moved to re-establish positions that had been pared back during recent months of soft global manufacturing prints.

Beneath the cyclical trigger sits the energy-transition thesis refined further during recent market talks. Copper is the indispensable physical input for electrification, from EV motor windings to high-voltage transmission cables, and the timeline for bringing new Chilean or Peruvian concentrate to market is lengthening. The session fused a short-term demand jolt with the long-horizon view that the world is under-investing in new supply.

04 The Latin American read

Rallies of this nature place Chile and Peru directly at the centre of global portfolio flows. Chile is the world’s top copper producer and Peru its second-largest, so every penny move in the commodity redraws sovereign revenue assumptions and corporate valuations in both Andean economies. Tuesday’s rise in Southern Copper shares, a company whose deepest reserves sit in Peruvian and Mexican bedrock, is a pure-play bet on that geographic concentration.

For Brazilian markets, the gain ripples through Vale’s evolving base-metals narrative. While Vale is historically an iron-ore story, its US$3.5 billion copper capital-expenditure plan to 2026 has tied the firm more closely to this session’s dynamics. Investors holding the American depositary receipts in New York are increasingly treating Vale’s base-metals division as a copper proxy, albeit one filtered through Brazilian country risk and a beta of 1.21 against the broader market.

05 The names to watch

Southern Copper’s 4.98% move confirms its stature as the most liquid, purest Latin American copper-equity proxy. Freeport-McMoRan’s 5.75% surge shows that diversified producers with LatAm exposure benefit almost equally from regional supply tightness. Meanwhile, CPER at US$40.14 remains the cleanest instrument for foreign investors wanting copper price exposure without miner operational risk, though its structure means long-term holders absorb annual roll costs that have caused its decade-long return to lag comparable equity funds.

The Sprott Physical Copper Trust, which holds actual physical metal, and the Sprott Copper Miners ETF, which has a year-to-date NAV return above 10%, are also instruments that institutional desks were citing as pure and hybrid ways to hold the rally. These Canadian-listed funds reinforce how the copper investing universe now spans futures, physical and equity exposures, with the LatAm supply story underpinning every structure.

06 The outlook

The session’s gains will endure only if China converts fiscal pledges into visible copper orders over the coming weeks. The market has been repeatedly disappointed by stimulus headlines that fail to show up in trade data or bonded warehouse withdrawals. A weak US dollar and sustained energy-transition spending could, however, insulate copper from a sharp reversal even if Chinese delivery lags, because the electrification bid is structural, not episodic.

07 What to watch

Chinese copper imports: Watch July and August customs data for a tangible lift in refined copper and concentrate arrivals; a rise confirms the stimulus narrative, while flat readings would deflate the futures premium CPER now carries.

Watch July and August customs data for a tangible lift in refined copper and concentrate arrivals; a rise confirms the stimulus narrative, while flat readings would deflate the futures premium CPER now carries. Chilean production reports: Keep an eye on Chilean output figures from Cochilco for June, as persistent grade declines at aging pits could tighten the concentrate market further and lend another upward shove to miner equities.

Keep an eye on Chilean output figures from Cochilco for June, as persistent grade declines at aging pits could tighten the concentrate market further and lend another upward shove to miner equities. Southern Copper’s cost trajectory: Monitor any guidance updates from Southern Copper on operating costs and Peruvian expansion projects; a beat on volume or a cut in cost guidance would likely push the stock beyond the US$195 floor set this session.

Monitor any guidance updates from Southern Copper on operating costs and Peruvian expansion projects; a beat on volume or a cut in cost guidance would likely push the stock beyond the US$195 floor set this session. Vale’s base-metals capex execution: Track Vale’s spending progress against its US$3.5 billion copper plan; any delay or acceleration will shift the Brazilian miner’s correlation to copper prices and alter the risk profile for ADR holders.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is CPER and how does it relate to copper?

CPER is the United States Copper Index Fund, an ETF that tracks a portfolio of COMEX copper futures contracts, not the physical spot price of copper, making it a proxy for traders’ forward expectations.

Why did Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan jump so much more than CPER?

Mining stocks carry operational leverage, meaning their earnings rise disproportionately when the copper price outlook improves, and post-earnings momentum amplified the equity moves relative to the futures-based fund.

Why are Chile and Peru central to the copper conversation?

Chile and Peru are the world’s two largest copper producers, so any tightening of global supply or surge in Chinese demand directly affects their national revenues and the valuations of miners operating there.

Is the rally driven only by China?

No. While fresh Chinese infrastructure pledges provided the immediate spark, structural demand from the energy transition—EVs, renewables and grid upgrades—is the deeper, multi-year driver underpinning the market’s bullish tilt.
