World.title: Carlos Alcaraz Withdraws From Cincinnati Open With Wrist Injury
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz has withdrawn from the 2026 Cincinnati Open as he continues to recover from the wrist injury that has kept him away from competition since April. The ATP Tour confirmed the decision Tuesday, ending hopes that the defending champion would make his long-awaited return at the Masters 1000 tournament in Ohio.

Alcaraz had entered Cincinnati as part of a planned comeback ahead of the US Open. Tournament organizers initially included him among a field led by Jannik Sinner, Alexander Zverev, Novak Djokovic, Taylor Fritz and Ben Shelton. However, the 23-year-old Spaniard has not recovered sufficiently to compete in the Cincinnati main draw, which begins August 13.

“We know Carlos is doing everything he can to get back to playing tournaments as soon as possible,” tournament director Bob Moran said in a statement. The withdrawal extends an absence that began at the Barcelona Open in April. Alcaraz has since missed several of the biggest tournaments on the calendar, including the French Open and Wimbledon.

Cincinnati would have provided his only scheduled competitive preparation before the US Open men’s singles tournament begins August 30 in New York. Alcaraz has not announced that he will miss the US Open, but his Cincinnati withdrawal raises further questions about whether he will be ready for the final Grand Slam of the season.

Returning directly at a best-of-five-set tournament would leave him without a competitive match in more than four months. The wrist injury interrupted what had been an outstanding start to the year. Alcaraz opened the season by winning the Australian Open, completing the career Grand Slam and becoming the youngest man to win all four major singles titles.

He has compiled a 22-3 record and won two ATP titles in 2026 despite playing his most recent match in April. The ATP Tour listed him as the world No. 2 when announcing his Cincinnati withdrawal. Alcaraz was due to defend 1,000 ranking points in Ohio after winning the 2025 Cincinnati title. He claimed the championship when Sinner was forced to retire from their final.

His absence removes one of the tournament’s leading attractions and eliminates the possibility of another Cincinnati meeting between the two biggest stars in men’s tennis. Sinner will now enter as the clear headline player in the men’s field. The Italian won Wimbledon earlier this summer and has been the dominant player at Masters 1000 level during the 2026 season.

The Cincinnati Open has not yet announced how Alcaraz’s place in the field will be filled. His withdrawal could allow the next eligible player into the main draw or create an additional opening for a qualifier or lucky loser, depending on when the draw is finalized. For Alcaraz, the immediate priority remains completing his recovery rather than rushing back before the US Open. His status for New York will now become one of the biggest questions in tennis over the coming weeks.

World.title: Guatemala’s Fuego Volcano Eruption Forces 1,700 Evacuations
World.content:
A powerful eruption of Guatemala’s Fuego Volcano has forced authorities to evacuate at least 1,700 residents from areas near the crater and declare the highest alert level Tuesday in zones exposed to falling ash. Fuego, considered the most active volcano in Central America and located near the capital, entered an eruptive phase Monday morning.

Its activity intensified overnight into Tuesday, with streams of lava flowing down its slopes and enormous columns of gas and ash rising into the sky. “The volcano is going through one of its most critical explosive phases,” producing mudflows, incandescent rocks, gases and ash, said Edwin Rojas, director of the Institute of Volcanology, known as Insivumeh.

Guatemala’s National Coordinator for Disaster Reduction, Conred, began evacuating communities near the volcano Monday evening and declared an orange danger alert nationwide. On Tuesday, the agency raised the alert to red in the departments of Sacatepéquez, Chimaltenango and Escuintla, which are home to 1.6 million people.

According to Conred Executive Secretary Claudinne Ogaldes, about 29,000 people are directly exposed to ashfall, making evacuations from the area essential. Ogaldes urged residents of nearby communities to wear masks and cover their water and food supplies. Conred said more than 1,700 people had been evacuated.

“We have become accustomed to living with a volcano that is always active, but this time it was simply too much,” said Sonia Vasquez, a 50-year-old resident of El Porvenir who spent the night in a shelter. Alejandro Garcia, another resident, also evacuated Monday evening after the alert was issued.

“We ran out, terrified,” he said, after seeing lava flowing down the volcano’s slopes. Despite the higher alert level, authorities reopened a road leading to the colonial city of Antigua, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Guatemala’s main tourist destinations. Operations at Guatemala City’s international airport have not been affected so far.

Lava Fountain

The Ministry of Education suspended in-person classes at schools in three communities near the volcano. “It would be better if we could move somewhere else because we live with this fear, since the volcano gives no warning,” said Lidia Ortiz, another evacuee. According to Insivumeh experts, a lava fountain reaching between 200 and 300 meters above the crater formed Monday, while the ash column rose to more than 7,000 meters.

As the ash dispersed at altitudes between 5,000 and 6,000 meters, it traveled as far as 130 kilometers westward. The institute said 34 earthquakes were recorded in Guatemala during the previous 24 hours, most with epicenters in the Pacific Ocean. Guatemala is located along the Pacific Ring of Fire and experiences significant seismic and volcanic activity.

Several mass evacuations have taken place in recent years because of eruptions at Fuego, which rises 3,763 meters above sea level and is located about 35 kilometers from Guatemala City in a straight line. In June 2025, around 800 people were evacuated because of eruptions at Fuego.

In 2018, 215 people were killed and about 200 others were reported missing after volcanic flows devastated a village on the slopes of the volcano.

World.title: Costa Rica Orders AyA to Compensate Customers Over Excess Water Charges
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Comptroller General has ordered the country’s national water utility and its public services regulator to identify customers who were billed more than they should have been for water, sewer and hydrant service, and to build a mechanism to pay them back. An audit released today put the improper charges at roughly ₡65.4 billion, about $144 million at the rate of ₡453.59 to the dollar.

The report concluded that our Instituto Costarricense de Acueductos y Alcantarillados (AyA) and the Autoridad Reguladora de los Servicios Públicos (Aresep) failed broadly to comply with the legal, technical and control framework that governs how rates are set. The findings reach into how tariffs are updated, how the money they raise is supervised, how the value of infrastructure is calculated, and whether the five services AyA bills for — drinking water, sewerage, hydrants, protection of water resources and related services — can be sustained. Aresep is the same regulator that sets fuel and electricity prices.

The largest single block of improper charges falls on sewer customers. The audit calculated that they paid ₡38.8 billion, about $86 million, for 5,909 assets that were already fully depreciated, meaning AyA had recovered its investment in them and kept billing for them anyway. Hydrant service accounted for ₡511 million, about $1.1 million, tied to 9,012 depreciated assets. In drinking water, auditors estimated improper charges of ₡26.1 billion, about $57 million, since 2023.

Auditors also questioned the values assigned to the infrastructure customers are charged for. A review of 3,761 assets revalued since 2019 found that 63.1 percent had risen in recorded value by more than 1,000 percent, and that some distribution networks were carried at up to 14,446 percent of their earlier value despite deteriorating in the ground.

The steepest increases involved infrastructure in the Huetar Caribe region, where AyA reports 70 percent unaccounted-for water, the share lost to leaks, metering errors and consumption that never produces revenue. The utility already loses more than half the water it produces in the Greater Metropolitan Area. Aresep declined in 2023 to recognize part of those revaluations in the rate base, on the grounds that they did not reflect the real condition of the pipes.

Along with overcharging, the Comptroller found rates that have gone years without formal review. AyA has not filed an ordinary tariff study for drinking water in eight years, for sewerage in nine, for hydrants in 11 and for related services in as long as 21, even though tariff income supplies roughly 70 percent of its budget.

Its own tariff unit prepared water and sewer studies that senior management saw in June 2025, but the institution neither sent them to Aresep nor documented a technical reason for holding them back. Aresep attempted several rate reviews on its own initiative and shelved them, saying AyA had not supplied reliable information. It never opened one for hydrants at all, and took 17 years to open one for related services.

The audit further found that AyA keeps the surpluses from its different services in a single common account without tracking where the money came from. In 2024, drinking water service lost ₡9.3 billion, about $20 million, while sewerage returned ₡3.7 billion and hydrants ₡243 million.

Because the funds are pooled, money paid by customers of one service covered losses in another. The Comptroller described this as unauthorized cross-subsidy that conflicts with the principle that each rate should finance only the service it belongs to, and noted that Aresep never carried out the financial reviews that would have caught it, despite receiving AyA’s regulatory accounting every quarter.

AyA’s own projections point to a shortfall of more than ₡34 billion, about $75 million, in drinking water service by 2027, driven largely by investment and debt payments. Even with a 15 percent rate increase, the institution calculated it would still lose more than ₡12 billion, about $26 million. The Comptroller warned that the financial position puts major works at risk, including the fifth stage of the Metropolitan Aqueduct and the sanitation program for urban areas.

Under the orders issued today, AyA and Aresep must identify the amounts collected in excess and define how customers will be compensated no later than June 30, 2027. New rate schedules must be published before December 31 of that year. AyA is required to put controls in place that keep each service’s revenue separate, and Aresep must establish procedures allowing it to act on its own when the operator fails to request a rate review.

What remains undefined is almost everything a customer would want to know. Neither institution has said whether repayment would arrive as a credit on future bills, a direct refund, or an adjustment folded into the next rate schedule, nor which billing periods would qualify, nor whether the account holder of record or the person who actually paid would receive it. The safest step for anyone who wants to be able to document what they paid is to keep their receipts.

AyA account numbers (NIS), appear on every bill, and billing history can be requested at agency offices. Landlords, condominium administrators and anyone who has moved between properties are the most likely to struggle to reconstruct a paper trail, particularly where several units share one meter, an arrangement that has generated separate billing complaints for more than a year.

Water is a small line item in most household budgets here compared with rent or transport, as our breakdown of what it costs to live in Costa Rica shows, but a refund calculated across several years would not be trivial. AyA said it is still analyzing the report and that it presented its position to the Comptroller last week, arguing that some findings were being interpreted differently from how the institution believes they should be read. Aresep said it is reviewing the scope and content of the orders.

The two halves of the audit sit awkwardly together. It says customers were charged for infrastructure they should not have been paying for, and in the same document says the rates they pay are too low to keep the system running and have been for the better part of a decade. Both things can be true at once, and the fix for one does not cancel the other. Whatever compensation is eventually defined is likely to come at the same period as higher bills.

World.title: Fisherman fined for possession of crack pipe, denies resisting arrest
World.content:
Fisherman fined for possession of crack pipe, denies resisting arrest

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City fisherman was fined after pleading guilty to possession of a utensil used for smoking a controlled drug but denied a separate charge of resisting lawful arrest.

Richard Slusher, 35, of West Canal, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday on charges stemming from an incident on Sunday, August 2.

Police allege that officers stopped Slusher at the corner of West and Basra streets and found a metal pipe, believed to be used for smoking crack cocaine, concealed in the waist of his pants.

Slusher initially pleaded guilty to both charges. However, after the prosecution’s facts were read, he disputed the allegation that he resisted arrest and a not-guilty plea was entered on his behalf.

He was fined $150 plus $5 court costs for possession of the pipe and was given until September 30, 2026, to pay. Failure to pay will result in one week’s imprisonment.

Slusher was offered bail of $300 with one surety for the resisting-arrest charge, which he met after settling an outstanding court fine.

He is scheduled to return to court on September 7, 2026.

World.title: Mediation set for ‘Trinibad’ man accused of leaving Golden Bay Hotel with unpaid $11,000 bill
World.content:
Mediation set for ‘Trinibad’ man accused of leaving Golden Bay Hotel with unpaid $11,000 bill

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A mediation session has been scheduled for a Trinidadian national accused of leaving the Golden Bay Hotel without paying a bill of more than $11,000.

Rubindra Rampersad, 46, remains at the Belize Central Prison after being unable to satisfy his bail conditions, which reportedly include providing proof of a residence in Belize and securing a Belizean surety.

Rampersad’s attorney, Darrell Bradley, informed the court that mediation is scheduled for Thursday, August 13, 2026. The criminal matter is expected to return before the Chief Magistrate on August 20.

A successful mediation could lead to a resolution of the dispute and the eventual withdrawal of the criminal charge. However, the outcome will depend on whether an agreement can be reached with the hotel.

Rampersad is charged with making off without payment. He has pleaded not guilty to allegations that he left the Golden Bay Hotel on May 29 without settling an outstanding bill of $11,470.24.

Police allege that Rampersad stayed at the Belize City hotel from May 1 to May 29 after booking a double room with a credit card. The card was reportedly declined several times, while Rampersad allegedly requested extensions to his stay without making payment.

Hotel management allegedly discovered at around 6:00 a.m. on May 29 that Rampersad had left the property. Police subsequently detained him at the Philip Goldson International Airport as he was preparing to leave Belize.

Rampersad was initially denied bail because he was considered a flight risk due to his foreign nationality and lack of ties to Belize. Earlier reports said the court later indicated that bail could be considered once suitable accommodation and other assurances were provided.

He was escorted back to the Belize Central Prison on Tuesday after again being unable to meet the requirements for his release.

World.title: Two police officers convicted of manslaughter in death of Andrew Dougal
World.content:
Two police officers convicted of manslaughter in death of Andrew Dougal

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two police officers have been convicted of manslaughter in connection with the 2022 death of 25-year-old Santa Cruz resident Andrew Dougal.

Justice Antoinette Moore delivered the guilty verdicts against officers John Lucas and Jaleel Lewis at around 12:30 p.m. on Tuesday, following their trial in the Belmopan High Court.

Both men were remanded pending sentencing, which has been scheduled for Tuesday, August 11, 2026.

Lucas was represented by attorney Audrey Matura, while attorney Hurl Hamilton represented Lewis. Crown Counsel Javier Chan prosecuted the case on behalf of the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. Both officers exercised their right to remain silent during the trial.

The case arose after Dougal was allegedly beaten and forcefully placed into the back of a police pickup truck during an encounter with the officers in Santa Cruz. Cellphone footage later emerged showing portions of the incident.

Dougal subsequently died at the hospital after reportedly suffering internal bleeding and other complications from his injuries.

Matura said a central issue during the trial was Dougal’s haemophilia, an inherited condition that prevents the blood from clotting normally. The court considered whether injuries sustained during the encounter were worsened by the condition and ultimately led to his death.

World.title: 24-year-old Lennox Gentle charged with murder of Kiffer McKenzie
World.content:
24-year-old Lennox Gentle charged with murder of Kiffer McKenzie

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged 24-year-old Lennox Linford Gentle, a Belizean labourer of Belize City, with the murder of Kiffer Alexander McKenzie.

Gentle was charged on Tuesday, August 4, following an investigation into McKenzie’s killing, which occurred on June 13, 2026.

McKenzie, 29, was shot shortly after 10:00 a.m. while inside his vehicle on Albert Street in downtown Belize City. Children were reportedly inside the vehicle when the gunman opened fire. After being wounded, McKenzie lost control of the vehicle and crashed near the former Scotiabank building.

He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries.

Police have not released further details regarding the evidence that led to Gentle’s arrest. He is expected to be arraigned in court on the murder charge.

World.title: One week after being busted in tourist’s stolen clothes, Collin Ramclam arrested for boisterous behavior over losing money in casino – Told police he was protected by God
World.content:
One week after being busted in tourist’s stolen clothes, Collin Ramclam arrested for boisterous behavior over losing money in casino – Told police he was protected by God

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A self-described Jehovah’s Witness who was convicted of theft last week returned to court on Tuesday, this time accused of behaving boisterously on Orange Street after allegedly losing his money gambling.

Collin Burton Ramclam, 37, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded not guilty to one count of boisterous behaviour. With no objection from the prosecution, he was offered bail of $200 plus one surety of the same amount. His next court appearance is scheduled for September 2, 2026.

Police allege that at around 2:30 a.m. on Tuesday, officers conducting foot patrols saw Ramclam walking from the direction of Albert Street toward the Pound Yard Bridge while shouting about money he had lost gambling at the Princess Casino on his birthday.

According to police, Ramclam continued shouting, used obscene language and refused instructions to leave the area quietly. He allegedly told officers that he was protected by God and could do whatever he wanted before he was detained and taken to the Precinct One Police Station.

Ramclam also allegedly confronted and threatened a court reporter while being escorted to court, accusing her of making him look foolish in a recent Breaking Belize News report.

His latest court appearance came one week after he pleaded guilty to stealing a suitcase belonging to 20-year-old French national Ange Cesar Cirnevin. Breaking Belize News previously reported that Ramclam admitted taking the unattended suitcase from a bus travelling from Belmopan to Belize City and was found wearing some of the tourist’s belongings.

Ramclam was subsequently fined $1,000 plus $5 cost of court, payable by October 30, 2026, or he will serve five months in prison in default.

World.title: Three men remanded after police find ammunition near abandoned vehicle
World.content:
Three men remanded after police find ammunition near abandoned vehicle

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Three Belize City men have been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after police allegedly found three live 9mm rounds in and around a vehicle abandoned on the Yabra Bridge.

Esmond Austin, 19, Devon Garcia, 21, and Isani Conorquie, 19, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where they were jointly charged with keeping ammunition without a gun licence. Garcia was additionally charged with obstruction.

Police say officers responded to the bridge at about 4:30 a.m. on Sunday, August 2, after receiving reports that a damaged black Ford Escape had been abandoned and several men were seen running from the area.

The three men were later detained and taken back to the scene. During a search, officers allegedly found one live round near the vehicle’s rear door, another inside the rear passenger area and a third inside a white cloth bag.

Police further allege that Garcia grabbed one of the rounds while officers were processing the vehicle and attempted to throw it into a nearby canal. The ammunition instead landed in an adjoining yard and was recovered.

Garcia initially pleaded guilty to obstruction but later disputed the facts presented by the prosecution. Austin and Conorquie also indicated that they wanted to plead guilty to the ammunition charge, but the Magistrate advised the men to seek legal advice before entering pleas.

Due to the nature of the ammunition charge, bail was denied and all three men were remanded until October 5, 2026.

World.title: Hold It In: Police alleged that man possessed firearm under the influence of alcohol but because he refused to give urine sample Court threw out the case
World.content:
Hold It In: Police alleged that man possessed firearm under the influence of alcohol but because he refused to give urine sample Court threw out the case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man walked free on Monday after the Chief Magistrate ruled that the facts presented by police did not support charges of possessing a firearm while under the influence of alcohol or drugs and failing to provide a specimen.

Dijon Jamaal Smith, 32, of Flamboyant Street, was initially remanded to the Belize Central Prison after pleading not guilty to the firearm-related offences. He was later returned to court after indicating that he wished to change his plea to guilty.

However, the Chief Magistrate declined to accept the guilty plea, finding that the prosecution’s account did not contain sufficient facts to establish the offences. The court noted that no urine or blood test had been obtained to prove that Smith was under the influence.

Police alleged that at approximately 1:26 a.m. on Monday, August 3, officers pursued a white Chevrolet Equinox that was reportedly travelling at high speed in Belize City. The vehicle was eventually stopped on Heart Street.

During a search, officers found a licensed firearm fitted with a drum magazine. Smith subsequently produced a valid firearm licence, but officers alleged that his speech was slurred and that they detected a strong smell of alcohol on his breath.

He was taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where police said he refused to provide a urine or blood specimen. Officers later removed and counted 43 live 9mm rounds from the firearm’s magazine.

The court raised several procedural concerns, including whether Smith was provided with a suitable private facility to give a urine sample and whether he had been clearly informed that refusing to provide a specimen constituted an offence.

The Chief Magistrate ruled that a guilty plea could not be accepted where the underlying facts failed to establish the essential elements of the charges. Both matters were consequently dismissed and Smith was released.

World.title: UDP raises concerns over BTL’s reported acquisition of SMART
World.content:
UDP raises concerns over BTL’s reported acquisition of SMART

By Zoila Palma: The United Democratic Party (UDP) has criticized the decision by Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL) to proceed with the reported BZ$80 million acquisition of Speednet/SMART, saying the move lacks sufficient transparency and due diligence.

In a statement, the party said, “The acquisition of a strategic national asset using public resources should never proceed under a cloud of uncertainty,” adding that “Belizeans deserve to know whether this transaction represents value for money.” The UDP also argued that the Board ignored concerns raised by the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the National Trade Union Congress of Belize, and other stakeholders.

The UDP announced it will hold an urgent meeting with the NTUCB and called on the Public Utilities Commission to ensure a transparent review of the proposed acquisition. The party added it “will continue to hold the Government and all public officials accountable” over the transaction.

World.title: Honours Overdue: The music icons Jamaica still hasn’t recognised
World.content:
Recipients of the National Honours and Awards will be announced this week by the government of Jamaica. Today, we look at stalwarts of the country’s music industry whose contributions have never been recognised.

Earl “Chinna” Smith

Arguably the most prolific session musician in the history of reggae, Smith has played on classic songs by Dennis Brown (Westbound Train, Cassandra), Bob Marley (Rastaman Vibration), and Burning Spear (Marcus Garvey). His licks can also be heard on Grammy-winning albums by Ziggy Marley and The Melody Makers and Lauryn Hill, as well as Amy Winehouse’s first album. In October 2023, Rolling Stone Magazine named Smith at #182 on its 250 Greatest Guitarists of All Time.

Lynn Taitt

The Trinidadian guitarist is credited with starting rocksteady. He reportedly directed the 1966 recording session that resulted in Take it Easy by Hopeton Lewis, the song many musicologists believe launched that genre. Taitt played on numerous hit songs including the Shank I Sheck rhythm; (007) Shantytown and Israelites by Desmond Dekker and The Aces; Stop That Train by Keith and Tex; and Walk The Street at Night by Derrick Harriott. Lynn Taitt — who was named at #204 on Rolling Stone Magazine’s 250 Greatest Guitarists of All Time in 2023 — died in 2010.

The Abyssinians

The legendary roots trio are best known for the seminal Sata Masa Gana, the 1971 song considered by many to be reggae’s official anthem. Bernard Collins, Donald Manning and Lynford Manning comprised the most famous version of the group, which still tours with Donald in its lineup. Declaration of Rights and Forward On To Zion are other famous songs by The Abyssinians.

Tenor Saw

Maybe the most original dancehall singer. His unique yodel made songs like Pumpkin Belly, Golden Hen and Ring The Alarm standards. That sound influenced singers such as Anthony Redrose and King Kong. Tenor Saw died in 1985.

Sister Nancy

A pioneer female deejay who made her name on sound systems before rocking the mic for producer Winston Riley in the early 1980s. It was Riley who produced Bam Bam, the 1983 song that remains her signature. Bam Bam has been used in ads by major companies such as Reebok, and sampled by heavyweight rappers including Jay Z.

Stanley Beckford

The four-star general of mento! Stanley was not only a fixture of the Festival Song Competition (which he won three times), but he had hit songs during the 1970s when mento was shunned as ‘old people music’. Soldering (recorded with The Starlights), Broom Weed and Brown Gal were some of his popular songs. He died in 2007.

Sanchez

The dancehall Sinatra, Sanchez ruled the roost during the 1980s and 1990s with a series of hit songs. They include Loneliness, Baby Can I Hold You, I Can’t Wait, Here I Am and Brown Eye Girl.

Flabba Holt

Bassist and founder of The Roots Radics Band, he is a ‘foundation’ of contemporary dancehall. Gunman (Michael Palmer), Big Ship (Freddie McGregor), Night Nurse (Gregory Isaacs), Police In Helicopter (John Holt) and Wa Do Dem by Eek A Mouse are some of the songs he played on. He can also be heard on albums by Bunny Wailer and Israel Vibration.

The first winner of the Best Reggae Album (then known as Best Reggae Recording) Grammy, this group earned their stripes with edgy Sly and Robbie-produced songs like Plastic Smile, Abortion, General Penitentiary and Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner. Mykal Rose, Duckie Simpson and Puma Jones (who died in 1990) comprised the most successful version of the group.

Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson

One of the godfathers of digital dancehall, this talented keyboardist was a member of The Roots Radics Band before forming a mega partnership with drummer Cleveland Browne, known as Steely and Clevie. They played on and produced countless hit songs including No, No, No by Dawn Penn; Love Is The Answer by Garnet Silk; Fast Car by Foxy Brown and Trailer Load A Girls by Shabba Ranks. Steely died in 2009.

The Grace Thrillers

Formed in the early 1970s by Noel Willis, this group were the first successful exponents of what became gospel-reggae. Spiritual songs like Can’t Even Walk, Jesus and He’s Alive were played in dancehalls and drew ‘forwards’ from the most hardened ‘rude bwoys’.

Winston Wallace

This former educator and trade unionist wrote Land of My Birth, the unofficial national anthem of Jamaica. That song, by Eric Donaldson, won the Festival Song Competition in 1978. The previous year, they won that contest with Sweet Jamaica. Land of My Birth transcends ‘Festival’, and is played at national events in Jamaica and its Diaspora.

World.title: CLA weeds out high fees
World.content:
From left: Walter Melbourne, Cannabis Licensing Authority’s (CLA) director of licensing and applications; CLA board chair Dr Nadeen Spence; Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake; and Simoy Brown, director of public relations and communications, address journalists at yesterday’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange.(Photo: Joseph Wellington)

A craving for traditional marijuana farmers to be included in the regulated industry locally has prompted the Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) to relax and reduce some entry requirements, including the cost of registration, for easier access to the system.

The registration fee for ganja farmers, which was US$3,000, has been slashed to US$150 under a Cultivator’s Transitional Special Permit Programme introduced by the CLA.

This provides a phased pathway for traditional cannabis farmers to transition into the regulated industry while working toward full licensing compliance.

Addressing this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange at the newspaper’s head office in St Andrew, senior members of the CLA, including board chair Dr Nadeen Spence and Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake, were adamant that the new moves are intended to open the doors to the regulated industry for traditional ganja farmers, and were in no way an attempt to shut them down.

Spence told Observer editors and reporters that there are many traditional ganja farmers who yearn to be a part of the regulated industry and the CLA is ready and willing to assist them in doing so.

“Those who want to do business in the medical cannabis industry, we will give them the information to do so if they want,” Spence said.

“The CLA processes licences for those who would like to conduct business, conduct operations [under the Dangerous Drugs Act]. For those who want to be involved, we want to provide as much information and guidance as possible,” added Spence.

She pointed to an ongoing roadshow which forms part of the initiatives that the CLA has embarked on to attract small farmers.

This is designed to expand participation in the sector as well as to guide applicants and promote the medical cannabis special permit programmes, such as the community and transitional cultivators’ permit.

Meanwhile, Blake said the roadshows are a source of education for the public and an opportunity for officials of the CLA to meet face-to-face with people who want to enter the regulated industry.

“There is going to be, maybe, some apprehension about engaging us through these programmes. The islandwide road tour is to ensure that we have that face-to-face interaction. If there’s assistance needed to complete the forms, we’re there to do that. If there’s assistance needed to determine whether or not these farming programmes are for you, we can give that advice. We can also give advice about the existing licensing products that we have,” said Blake as she underscored that farmers who are not currently regulated will not be reported to law enforcement agencies.

“You have to understand that me asking you to come into the legal space is not to try to burn down your farms or anything like that. The law of the amended Dangerous Drugs Act provides for the religious side and it provides for the commercial side. That is where the CLA operates, within the commercial space. So we try to encourage the public to stay on the right side of the law, come into the legal framework, and operate there. These farming programmes are created to further engage traditional farmers who might not have wanted to participate as of 2015 to now. We’re not planning to report you. We’re not calling the police on you,” insisted Blake.

She was supported by Walter Melbourne, the CLA’s director of licensing and applications, who scoffed at claims that there is no room for small ganja farmers in the regulated industry.

“That is why we have the cultivators’ permit. Those persons who would not have the necessary skills and requirements, moneywise as well, you could come in, and we’ll accept you into the programme. There’s a US$150 application fee and there are no more [fees] once you’re qualified,” said Melbourne.

“It is actually creating a pathway for the small man,” added Melbourne as he indicated that the CLA is prepared to hold the hands of people who want to enter the formal system and guide them through the entire process.

For the people concerned about whether they will be able to continue to operate their farms while they transition through the programme, Melbourne said they would be given special permits once they meet the requirements, which, he pointed out, are no longer very strict.

“You would have to make an application to come into the system and [the programme] is for two years. It is meant to allow you to transition. We’ll hold your hand, show you what to do. We have a Cannabis Specialisation Unit within the CLA that will assist you in terms of growing techniques, everything that you need to assist you to ensure that it’s viable. We have the requisite resources within the authority to assist you. You just have to make the application. We will assist you in guiding you in setting up your home, to set up your farm, and all of that, and you make the transition.

“We’ll go through line by line with you. I’ve seen situations in which a person cannot read or write, and I’m not mentioning this to be discriminatory or anything, but to show that we are very inclusive, in the sense that if persons cannot read or write, we’ll hold your hand. People will actually fill out the form and show you where to sign. So you take in stuff to us, like what area of land are you going to use… do you have a lease agreement? Do you have a title? Land is not a sore issue, in the sense that if you don’t even have title to it, we will say, if you have been farming the land for some time, occupying the land, we’ll take declarations from persons who have known the land for several years, just to verify and just to authenticate the fact that you have been occupying the land,” added Melbourne, as he explained that the process to become registered could take up to five months.

World.title: Gateway to Africa
World.content:
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama (left) shakes hands with Prime Minister of Jamaica Dr Andrew Holness following their media briefing at the Office of the Prime Minister on Monday. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

JAMAICAN manufacturers and exporters could soon gain easier access to a market of 1.4 billion people worth nearly US$3 trillion after Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama announced on Monday that he intends to push for the Caribbean’s inclusion in Africa’s free trade area next year.

Mahama also said Ghana would fast-track parliamentary approval of the air services agreement to allow direct flights between its capital, Accra, and Montego Bay, a move expected to strengthen trade, tourism and investment between the two countries.

Speaking during a media briefing with Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness as part of his four-day state visit to Jamaica, Mahama said discussions between the two leaders had focused on moving the long-standing historical relationship between Ghana and Jamaica beyond shared heritage and towards deeper economic cooperation.

He said Ghana intends to use its chairmanship of the African Union (AU) next year to pursue closer trade ties between Africa and the Caribbean, arguing that stronger commercial partnerships must become the next phase of Pan-African cooperation.

“When I was speaking with Mr Prime Minister, I said that one of the things that I would champion when I become AU chair next year… is to expand the remit of the African continental free trade area to include the Caribbean. We set up the African continental free trade area that allows us to export goods duty-free and tariff-free into each other’s markets. That’s a 1.4 billion population market, and that also is a 1.3 trillion GDP economy, and so we can plug the Caribbean in so that we can exchange goods between Africa and the Caribbean duty-free, tariff-free,” he announced.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which came into force in 2021, is the world’s largest free trade area by the number of participating countries and is designed to boost trade by reducing tariffs and other barriers among African nations. Mahama suggested extending that framework to the Caribbean would significantly broaden opportunities for businesses on both sides of the Atlantic.

He added that improved transport links would be critical to making those ambitions a reality, revealing that Ghana intends to move quickly to activate the air services agreement negotiated between the two countries.

“We have to activate the bilateral air services agreement between us, and it’s currently before our Parliament, and we’ll fast-track it so that it becomes operational, so that either national carriers between Jamaica and Ghana or third-party carriers can fly direct flights from Accra to Montego Bay,” he said.

Holness welcomed the commitment, saying direct air links would represent one of the most tangible outcomes of the state visit and could help unlock greater tourism, trade and investment between the two countries.

“Africa is the fastest-growing continent both in terms of demographics and in terms of their economies. It is an area which we have paid as a people great rhetoric, we’ve always been speaking about south-south cooperation. What I try to do is to find meaningful, tangible ways in which we can bring this cooperation to fulfilment. Clearly, Marcus Garvey set the foundation, connecting us intellectually, connecting us as a people. We now must take that and create… the economic emancipation of our people,” he said.

Holness noted that the state visit should not be viewed as merely symbolic, stressing that both governments are seeking practical outcomes capable of generating jobs, investment and long-term economic growth.

“We have focused primarily on, from a tourism perspective, trade and services, heavily on North American and European markets of late South American markets. But now we have to turn our attention to the African continent where there is a growing middle class who wants to travel, who wants to experience the world and who could be right at home and comfortable right here in Jamaica. So we see these visits as not just courtesies; these visits are important to set the foundation for the trade in goods and services that will come,” he said.

Beyond aviation, both leaders outlined plans to strengthen logistics and maritime cooperation, viewing their countries as strategic gateways to their respective regions.

Holness pointed to Jamaica’s continued investment in expanding the Port of Kingston, while noting Ghana is pursuing similar ambitions in West Africa. He said connecting the two logistics hubs could create more efficient trade routes for exporters and investors.

Mahama echoed that view, saying the Atlantic should become a conduit for commerce rather than a barrier separating the two regions.

World.title: Ras Ajai gunned down
World.content:
Ras Ajai (left) accepts his Grammy Certificate from Stephen Stewart for appearing on Buss A Bubble, a song from Live N Livin, Sean Paul’s 2022 Grammy Award-nominated album. Occasion was the August 2024 Grammy Certificate Ceremony at the ATL Automotive Audi Showroom in Kingston..

When British music publisher Kennedy Mensah and reggae artiste Ras Ajai recently spoke to each other the latter expressed a desire to record songs that honoured the music’s legacy. He never got that opportunity.

Ras Ajai (real name Brian Todd Boucher) was killed in Waterford, Portmore, St Catherine, on August 1.

The 43 year-old singjay/actor and another male victim were shot by gunmen in an area of that community known as Third World.

At press time, the police had reported no arrests being made in relation to the incident.

The other man remains in hospital.

“One of our last conversations, he was talking about wanting to do a strong reggae project, he described it as a real reggae project, because he believed the youths nowadays not dealing with the real reggae thing,” Mensah, who is based in England, recalled. “He wanted to put out some serious messages, and also to capitalise on the notoriety he got from being in the One Love movie.”

Ras Ajai, who was from Waterford, lived in New York City and toured for several years with Sean Paul. He made his acting debut in Bob Marley: One Love, the 2024 biopic based on the reggae legend.

The dreadlocked artiste had a small role as Claudius Massop, the West Kingston enforcer who was Marley’s close friend. Massop was controversially killed by police in February 1979.

Known for songs like Well Misbehave and Vice Grip, Ras Ajai is also featured on Buss A Bubble, Sean Paul’s 2019 single. That track is from Live N Livin, Sean Paul’s album which was nominated for a 2022 Best Reggae Album Grammy Award.

In August 2024, Ras Ajai was presented with a Grammy Certificate for appearing on the album at Mensah’s Grammy Certificate Ceremony in Kingston.

Mensah said he first met Ras Ajai in 2019 during a music publishing workshop he conducted at Jamaica Promotions (Jampro) in Kingston. Shortly after, Ras Ajai became a client of Mensah’s Back 2 Da Future Limited.

“To say that the news of his passing came as a shock would be a total understatement. I can’t imagine how his family must be feeling,” said Mensah. “We’re going to miss Ras Ajai, but at least we have a body of music to remember him by.”

World.title: Infantino’s re-election bid hit by Welsh withdrawal
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) and US President Donald Trump hold the FIFA World Cup trophy moments before presenting it to 2026 World Champions Spain after the final at New York/New Jersey Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, on Sunday, July 19. (Photo: AFP)

PARIS, France (AFP) — Wales on Monday became the first national football association to publicly withdraw support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid, piling pressure on the Swiss administrator after the collapse of his controversial plan to sell private investment stakes in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions.

The Football Association of Wales (FAW) said it would not support Infantino’s candidature in the FIFA presidential election in Rabat, Morocco, in March 2027.

“The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino, for re-election as FIFA president for the 2027-2031 term,” the FAW said in a statement.

“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgement have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football.

“Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

The English Football Association is also understood to have informed FIFA it no longer supports Infantino. It said on Saturday it fully backed UEFA’s position after European football’s governing body declared it had lost confidence in the FIFA president.

Concacaf has called for “a comprehensive reckoning” with Infantino’s leadership, while the Asian Football Confederation has urged greater transparency.

The backlash followed Infantino’s decision to abandon plans for the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would have brought private investment into FIFA’s flagship tournaments, including the men’s and women’s World Cups. The proposal, announced last week, was withdrawn within days after opposition from three continental confederations.

The collapse of the plan has left Infantino facing the biggest political challenge of his decade in charge of world football.

The 56-year-old, first elected FIFA president in 2016 and re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023, had appeared politically stronger than ever after overseeing expanded editions of the Club World Cup and men’s World Cup while increasing revenues distributed to FIFA’s 211 member associations.

But critics say the FFE debacle reinforced concerns that FIFA has become increasingly centralised under his leadership.

Former UEFA president Michel Platini, under whom Infantino served as secretary-general from 2009 to 2016, has been among his sharpest critics.

“Unfortunately Infantino has become more of an autocrat since the [COVID-19] pandemic,” Platini told

The Guardian in January.

“I think he lost the game. There is less democracy than in Blatter’s time.

“He was a good No 2, but is not a good No. 1.

“He worked very well at UEFA but he has one problem — he likes the rich and powerful people, the ones with money.

“It’s his character.”

Infantino’s close relationship with US President Donald Trump has also drawn scrutiny. The investment proposal involved a firm led by Joshua Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

“Josh Kushner’s firm has a legitimate track record,” former World Cup bid strategist Terrence Burns told

AFP.

“But the association was always going to be read politically… We’ve understood in sponsorship for 40 years that a partner brings their whole context with them.”

Following the collapse of the investment proposal, Infantino pledged to restore unity within world football.

“Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together… in the spirit of shared interest in our game,” he said.

“And with the objective to continue growing football everywhere.”

Nominations for the FIFA presidential election close on November 18 ahead of the vote in Rabat next March.

World.title: DAY TO FORGET
World.content:
Abdullah Shafique (right) of Pakistan scores runs off Kemar Roach (left) of West Indies during the second day of their second Test match at Queen’s Park Oval in Port of Spain, Trinidad, and Tobago, on Monday. (Photo: AFP)

PORT OF SPAIN, Trinidad (CMC) — A superb batting display by Abdullah Shafique and Babar Azam has left Pakistan in firm control of the second Test against West Indies at the close of play on the second day here on Monday.

Shafique’s unbeaten 107 off 185 balls coupled with Captain Azam’s 86 not out off 126 balls powered the visitors to a formidable 266 for two in reply to the West Indies’ total of 344 at the Queen’s Park Oval.

The pair has so far added 168 runs for the third wicket to put Pakistan on course to post a mammoth first innings total and give their side a hefty lead as they trail by just 78 runs heading into Tuesday’s third day of play.

West Indies contributed to their own demise with their wayward bowling gifting Pakistan’s batsmen free runs, with wicket-taking deliveries few and far between.

The home side’s opening pace attack of Kemar Roach and Jayden Seales were surprisingly inconsistent, with Azan Awais hitting Roach for three consecutive boundaries in the third over of the innings.

Together, with partner Imam-ul-Haq, they put on 34 runs inside eight overs before Shamar Joseph produced a snorter off a good length that hit the top of his bat and ballooned to gully for Jomel Warrican to take an easy catch.

Awais continued to take advantage of the slack bowling on offer, hitting Joseph for four fours in the 12th over to move into the 40s, while Shafique wasted little time in joining in on the action by blasting Warrican for sixes in successive overs.

Awais eventually brought up his maiden Test half-century off 61 balls by driving Warrican down to long on for a single.

It was Warrican who broke their 64-run partnership, with the West Indies needing to review an lbw decision against Awais after he was initially given not out, to dismiss him for 55 and leave the score 98 for two.

Azam joined Shafique at the crease, and for the next three hours, they neutralised the home side’s passive bowling attack, which was without the services of first match hero Justin Greaves.

The skipper showed his aggressive intent early on by bludgeoning Seales for three fours in the 24th over.

Pakistan went to tea at 139 for two, while scoring at just over four runs an over, and the same continued after the break, with Shafique getting to his seventh Test half-century off 79 balls with an exquisite straight drive off Roach for four.

Azam followed in the same vein by notching his 33rd half-century as Pakistan tightened their grip on the contest at 184 for two.

Azam was lucky not to have been dismissed almost immediately after, but Joseph failed to hold on to a difficult one-handed catch on the long on boundary, with the ball going over the boundary ropes for six.

With the close of play looming, Shafique reached his sixth Test century by pulling Warrican to the midwicket boundary, his first time scoring three figures since 2024.

The duo then navigated the remaining overs of play to ensure Pakistan remained in complete control of the contest.

Earlier, resuming the day on 239 for five, the West Indies’ last five wickets added 104 runs, with spinner Sajid Khan responsible for three of them to fall.

Justin Greaves only added nine runs to his overnight score of 64 before driving a delivery from spinner Ali Usman straight into the hands of point.

Captain Roston Chase reached his 12th Test half-century and added 35 runs with Roach until he was bowled off his pads by pacer Ubaid Shah for 70 to leave the Windies 304 for seven.

Khan then wrapped up the tail by dismissing Joseph, Roach, and Seales to end with figures of 4-85, while Shah (2-66), Mohammad Ali (2-67), and Ali Usman (2-80) took two wickets apiece.

World.title: WATCH: Waves of excitement at Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Emancipation Day
World.content:
Crew members of 'Empress' pose with the coveted Yamaha engine prize after winning the Yamaha Engine Race at the 43rd annual Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Saturday, August 1, 2026.

Sutania Beckford beamed with joy after her boat crew guided ‘Empress’ to a thrilling victory in the Yamaha Engine Race which brought an exciting close to the 43rd annual Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Emancipation Day.

It was sweet triumph for the crowd favourites and their supporters after losing the marquee event in the six-race boat competition to rival ‘Father’s Day’ last year.

“Every year, people come just to see [Empress] because it’s like we are up against everybody,” Beckford said.

“However, Empress decided this time not to have any boyfriends, she was under proper supervision this time, so she came out victorious,” she added with a smile.

Each Emancipation Day, hundreds of residents and visitors converge at the Old Harbour Bay Fishing Village to participate in what Jason Fuller, the president of the Old Harbour Bay Community Development Association, calls “the premier boat racing competition in Jamaica”.

It was another massive turnout on Saturday, with numbers estimated to be in the thousands.

“They love it, they live for it every year,” Fuller said about the lure of the event. “This is their passion, this is their love. And we just try each and every year to ensure that we improve and make it a memorable one.”

In addition to the races, the residents also unite for food, entertainment, and other competitions – including fish scraping, cook-offs and beer drinking – at the regatta. Due to the event’s massive growth, the organisers introduced live streaming at last year’s edition to share the experience with persons who are unable to physically attend.

“Remember, it’s the largest fishing village in Jamaica. So almost everyone have some interaction with fishing, whether you’re a fisherman, a family of fishermen, or so on,” Fuller said. “So, that is one of the main reason why the regatta means so much to the community.”

Noting that a number of fisherfolk in the community were affected by Hurricane Melissa last October, Fuller said the regatta organisers partnered with sponsors this year to give away nets and other items to help affected persons get back on their feet.

“So, even though they were affected, we are trying our utmost best to make it a seamless transition to getting back to what they were before,” he said.

Social Development Commission’s parish manager for St Catherine, Shana-Lee Archibald hailed the event for the economic activity it generates for small businesses in the community.

“The regatta is a great event, it provides an opportunity for our small businesses to benefit and that’s one of the main reasons the SDC is a part of the activities,” Archibald said.

In the meantime, spectators commended the organisers of the regatta while expressing their satisfaction for the fun and entertainment provided.

“Good energy, good vibes, super lit,” said spectator from Canada who goes by the name “Breezy”.

“I just like the view, the people, the music, it’s very nice,” he said.

– Julian Richardson

World.title: Europe’s Palantir problem
World.content:
Europe wants to kick its U.S. tech habit, but it’s struggling to detangle itself from American data analytics firm Palantir.

The problem is, the company’s tools are already deeply embedded in critical sectors across the bloc like policing, national defense and health systems. A report released today also shows that the tech firm has found ways to pay minimal taxes in Europe. On the show, hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart discuss European alternatives and why detaching is easier said than done.

Next, our colleague Seb Starcevic has interviewed Mediterranean Commissioner Dubravka Šuica. The role that was originally thought to be low profile has instead thrust the Croatian official into the limelight as various crises hit the Middle East and the Mediterranean.

Plus: Three new foods are being added to the EU’s list of products with geographic indicators. These are the labels given to products that can only be made in a specific region, like Champagne or … yes, you guessed it, halloumi.

World.title: Electricité : à gauche, Bernard Cazeneuve joue sa propre partition
World.content:
En 2011, il n’avait rejoint l’équipe de François Hollande pendant sa campagne victorieuse qu’à la condition que le candidat retire de son programme l’arrêt annoncé de la production de combustible MOX en France — suivant une recommandation d’Areva, son producteur.

Dans la Sarthe fin juin, invité par son ancien collègue de gouvernement Stéphane Le Foll, actuel maire du Mans, à s’exprimer sur son programme en matière de nucléaire, l’ancien Premier ministre n’hésitait pas à critiquer La France insoumise et les Ecologistes qui se “trompent” en ne voulant pas faire comme lui. Surtout qu’il peut se prévaloir de sa constance sur la question, quand d’autres membres de son camp ont viré de bord.

Lorsqu’il quittait le pouvoir en 2017, en même temps que François Hollande, la France était engagée dans une trajectoire de réduction de sa production d’électricité nucléaire (une décision qu’il ne cautionne pas), avec une planification à mettre en œuvre pour fermer des réacteurs. Mais depuis, l’heure est à la relance : le prolongement de la quasi-totalité des réacteurs est examiné par le gouvernement, et de nouveaux doivent voir le jour dans une dizaine d’années.

Des conseillers pronucléaires

Pour élaborer son programme, Bernard Cazeneuve peut compter sur les éclairages de Marc Fontecave, chimiste et professeur au Collège de France, ou de Louis Gallois, ancien dirigeant de plusieurs entreprises publiques, ont confirmé les intéressés à POLITICO — le second n’a pas souhaité entrer dans le détail “d’échanges privés”.

Marc Fontecave, qui préside également le conseil scientifique d’EDF, se penche depuis plusieurs mois sur la stratégie énergétique du pays dans ses cours ouverts à tous au Collège de France. Le scientifique est un opposant aux “catastrophistes” du climat, le surnom qu’il donne aux militants Cyril Dion, Greta Thunberg ou Aurélien Barrau, auxquels il a consacré un livre.

Il siège également à l’Académie des sciences, qui a rendu un avis assez sévère — mais “équilibré”, selon Marc Fontecave — sur la feuille de route du gouvernement, notamment sur le soutien au développement des énergies renouvelables.

World.title: Spain sweats over its isolated territories in Africa
World.content:
But, more alarmingly for Madrid, that argument is no longer coming exclusively from Rabat. Questions over Spain’s centuries-old control of the fortress cities have also been raised in a U.S. Congress report, and by Israel’s ambassador to the U.N.

It is a sign of the level of concern in Madrid that the government is now having to make public declarations on a point of international law that — only a week ago — it would have thought was self evident.

“Ceuta and Melilla are not to be touched,” Defense Minister Margarita Robles said during a press conference on Monday. “Everyone must be very clear that Spanish territorial integrity and sovereignty are not up for debate.”

The government’s rejection of Morocco’s claims has done little to reduce concerns in Spain over what would happen if Rabat dials up the pressure. This week, national newspapers have been filled with columns expressing fears of a “Green March 2.0” — pointing out the parallels with Morocco use of a mass popular mobilization to take over the province of Spanish Sahara in 1975.

José Manuel García-Margallo, who served as Spain’s foreign minister between 2011 and 2014 and is a member of the center-right People’s Party, said it was vital for Spain to show its control over the cities is not negotiable.

“Do you think the British would have allowed 60,000 Spaniards to enter Gibraltar?” he asked. “I’d encourage this government to be a little bit more British.”

World.title: Palantir funnels earnings to US to avoid European taxes, report finds
World.content:
Palantir pays no U.S. federal income tax because previous losses, tax credits, and R&D deductions offset its taxable income; and virtually no state income tax, with the exception of Maryland, which levies a digital services tax.

The profit gap between the U.S. and Europe is stark. In 2025, Palantir’s American business pocketed 47.7 cents in profit from every dollar of revenue — more than double the previous year’s 22.5 cents. Outside the U.S., the profit margin was just 6.3 percent. In some European subsidiaries, it fell to around 3 percent, according to the new report.

CICTAR argues that Palantir "intentionally and artificially" shrinks European profits — and therefore its European tax bills — to concentrate profits in the U.S. There is no claim in the report that such arrangements, often referred to as "profit shifting," are illegal. Multinational companies often reduce reported profits by paying subsidiaries or other related entities for intellectual property, loans or expertise.

In Sweden, for example, Palantir reported €13.7 million in revenue in 2024, but only €1.1 million in profit. At Sweden’s 20 percent corporate tax rate, that left the company with a tax bill of just €424,000.

In its Q2 earnings report on Monday, Palantir made no explicit reference to earnings from its European subsidiaries. Instead, it highlighted its U.S. business, where revenue rose 115 percent year-on-year to $1.57 billion (€1.36 billion), and boasted of its 62 percent profit margin.

A U.K.-based Palantir spokesperson said that the majority of the company's 2025 revenue and profitability was driven by its U.S. business. "Our tax position in each jurisdiction reflects the level of economic activity there, and we meet our tax obligations in every market in which we operate," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Channel rescue brings Burnham’s border pledge into focus
World.content:
On Tuesday morning, French maritime authorities said in a statement that the boat’s engine “caught fire” and its structure “deteriorated very rapidly,” triggering an immediate mayday call.

All 157 people on board were brought to safety and returned to Boulogne-sur-Mer in France.

The French maritime prefecture added that when migrants are “determined to reach the United Kingdom” they often refuse assistance and accept it only in “situations of extreme urgency.” No deaths were reported.

The incident “underlines the terrible dangers of small boat crossings,” a U.K. government spokesperson said in a statement seen by POLITICO on Tuesday. Britain will “continue to work relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys,” the spokesperson added.

Burnham visited Dover on Monday, saying his two-week-old government was already making progress in tackling irregular migration. “People want to see this issue addressed,” he said, pointing to a doubling of enforcement officers targeting smuggling gangs on both sides of the Channel. But he also called for “a system that offers safe routes for people.” More than 2,000 migrants have reached Britain by small boat since Burnham entered Downing Street.

The rescue came as migration climbed back to the top of Europe’s political agenda following the arrival of 72,000 people in Ceuta last week. After days of governments trading blame, EU interior ministers closed ranks behind Spain at an emergency meeting Tuesday, insisting the Schengen zone had never been at risk and calling for closer coordination in responding to future border crises.

World.title: Kyiv’s former top commander says NATO is too outdated for Ukraine
World.content:
Russia has made deep changes to its forces under pressure from the war, and many politicians and intelligence officials worry it could be ready to attack a NATO country by the end of the decade.

Zaluzhnyi's unusual rebuke underscores a growing change in the alliance's relationship with Ukraine. The country has shifted from relying on European military support in the early years of the war to becoming one the continent's most powerful and technologically advanced militaries — far ahead of Western forces in the mass production of drones, missiles and other key systems.

"Ukraine contributes to transatlantic security," said NATO's 32 leaders in a joint declaration at the alliance's Ankara summit last month. In recent military exercises where NATO has invited Ukrainian troops to participate, allied forces have repeatedly been surprised by their tactics and drone use.

The comments are also notable given Zaluzhnyi's widely rumored political ambitions. He was replaced as Ukraine's top commander by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in 2024.

"Most likely, NATO will remain in the same form as it is, and will spend 12 years, like Ukraine, transitioning to the standards that need to be achieved in order to be at least half the level of the Russian Federation," said the retired general.

Zaluzhnyi's remarks also reflect an enduring Ukrainian frustration with the alliance for stalling its application to join despite officially floating the prospect of eventual membership in 2023. The U.S. and other allies remain opposed.

World.title: EU ministers close ranks behind Spain after Ceuta migration crisis
World.content:
The meeting followed days of unusually public anger at Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. In a letter signed by 22 EU leaders, governments demanded tougher action to stop irregular arrivals, while Italy suspended air and sea transit with Spain over fears that migrants could move onward through the Schengen area. Sánchez hit back by urging his counterparts to show “understanding” rather than turn Spain into a scapegoat for a crisis on the EU’s external border.

By Tuesday, ministers were keen to close ranks. The EU’s Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said the influx had been “instrumentalized” by smugglers and human traffickers, while French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said ministers had condemned efforts to use images of the crossings to divide the bloc.

“The divisions that we have heard over the weekend were not welcome and they were exploited by foreign countries,” Nuñez told reporters. “But what I heard this morning reassured me.”

EU countries that had publicly called out Spain over its migration policies took a more conciliatory tone in the meeting, apparently appeased by the speed and effectiveness of Madrid’s response to the crisis, three EU diplomats with knowledge of the meeting said. They were granted anonymity to discuss the confidential talks.

Matteo Piantedosi, Italy’s interior minister, praised Spain’s efforts to control the unrest, the diplomats said. Rome clashed with Madrid on Friday, calling for Spain to be kicked out of the Schengen zone.

Another diplomat referred to the past 24 hours of diplomacy as EU “couples counseling.”

World.title: Safe glasses to watch Spain's total eclipse: where to get them for free
World.content:
Make a note of this number for the eclipse that will cross the Iberian Peninsula on 12 August. With that date in mind, the ISO number (International Organization for Standardization) of the special glasses that must be used to view this unique event of the century safely should be easy to remember: 12312-2015.

 

Without them, ultraviolet radiation will damage the eye’s photoreceptors (cones and rods), while infrared energy will have a direct thermal effect on the retina, causing solar retinopathy. The symptoms of this condition, which may take some time to appear, can include blurred vision, spots or scotomas at the point of greatest visual acuity, metamorphopsia (distorted perception of shapes) and reduced tolerance to light, or photophobia, which can trigger headaches.

The total phase of the eclipse will not exceed one minute and 48 seconds anywhere along its path across Spain, and the closer you are to the line of totality, the longer you will be able to enjoy the spectacle. Only during that brief moment will lucky observers be able to take off their certified glasses.

The ISO 12312-2 standard applies only to certain products designed for direct observation of the Sun, or what astronomers call the photosphere: the bright face of the Sun. These glasses ensure that no more than 0.00032% of visible sunlight gets through. The Ministry of Science explains that "you must put the glasses on before looking at the Sun, look briefly for a few seconds and then look away, repeating observation of the eclipse always with pauses". You must not take them off until you have stopped looking at the Sun.

The standard applies only to glasses without adjustable power or focus. It does not apply to ordinary sunglasses (ISO 12312-1), which let through hundreds or thousands of times more light than is safe for looking directly at the Sun, nor to solar filters designed for devices such as telescopes or binoculars. Nor does it apply to solar filters designed to be placed over the (front) aperture of optical devices such as camera lenses, binoculars or telescopes.

The key requirements are transmittance (the ratio between transmitted and incident light) at ultraviolet, visible and infrared wavelengths that reach our retinas; the uniformity of that transmittance; and the appropriate quality of the material. The Scientific and Advisory Commission of the Eclipse Trio adds that, if they are sold in the European Union, the glasses must also bear the CE mark.

The Ministry and ONCE are to distribute two million certified glasses free of charge at ONCE stands and at research centres, science museums and other public institutions. Several regional governments will also hand out approved viewing equipment at sites set up to watch the astronomical event. Here is the list of places where you can obtain the glasses free of charge (source in Spanish).

World.title: Iran and Oman draft waterway deal while Trump rejects Tehran's control and transit fees
World.content:
Iran and the Gulf Arab state of Oman are progressing on a deal to reopen shipping through the disputed Strait of Hormuz and potentially help wind down the war in the Middle East.

 

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the bilateral talks with Oman are focused on “establishing safe inbound and outbound shipping lanes,” routes that “uphold sovereign rights while also addressing the national security considerations of both Iran and Oman.”

“The final results of these negotiations will be announced once concluded,” he added, in remarks carried by Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.

The emerging agreement calls for ships to enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through an Omani-controlled route, with service fees charged for providing security and preserving the maritime environment, according to two regional officials who spoke to AP on condition of anonymity.

They said negotiations are still underway and that the final agreement could take a different form; however, any deal seems to depend on the US lifting its blockade on Iran’s ports, and the Trump administration has previously ruled out any deal that would give Iran control over the strait.

Any agreement formalising Iran’s control of the strait would mark a significant strategic victory for Tehran. For that reason, the US could seek to block the deal by refusing to lift the blockade. The strait was an open international waterway before the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

Washington aims to return to status quo

A US official who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity said Washington remains committed to returning to the status quo in which “no party controls the lanes or the ability to transit through them.”

In an exchange with reporters on Monday, Trump reiterated his public stance that he’s opposed to tolling in the strait. “I’m not going to let them charge,” Trump said. “Anybody’s going to charge, we’ll charge.”

In his latest statement on Wednesday, Trump threatened Iran once again, saying, "Strait of Hormuz will open 'very soon', or Iran will be 'hit very hard'.

World.title: Netanyahu rejects Gaza withdrawal until Hamas disarms
World.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Tuesday that Israel will not withdraw from its current lines in Gaza until Hamas has completely disarmed and pushed back on a recent deal announced by US President Donald Trump.

 

Netanyahu's remarks cast more doubt on the deal to disarm Hamas, which was seen as a potential breakthrough for ending the war. It also marked a rare public display of friction with the Trump administration.

The agreement called for Hamas to begin disarming and for Israel to halt its strikes and begin withdrawing from the roughly 60% of Gaza it currently controls. It was based on an October ceasefire agreement that ended major military operations and brought about the release of the remaining hostages held in Gaza but has stalled on other fronts.

Netanyahu, who faces a tough battle for reelection in October, reiterated his stance that disarmament should come first. He said Israeli forces would continue to “do whatever is necessary to protect themselves, our territory, and our citizens.”

The Trump administration “sent us a draft. We did not agree. It is not our draft. We sent our comments. … This is our position,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on social media.

"President (Donald) Trump and his team think they can get Hamas to disarm and demilitarize Gaza, we are examining this, they sent us a draft, we did not agree, it is not our draft, we sent our comments. By the way, we sent our comments before receiving any media campaign on the matter, because this is our position. We stand firm on our interests, I believe both wisely and firmly."

The US-backed ceasefire agreement last October called for Hamas to be disarmed and for Israel to withdraw. An International Stabilization Force was to be deployed, and an independent Palestinian administration was to oversee governance and reconstruction.

Israel says everything hinges on Hamas giving up its weapons, while Hamas says Israel must end its strikes and begin withdrawing from the territory. Each side accuses the other of violating the truce.
