“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: Georgian PM: ‘Opposition’s current Russophobia is dictated by Global War Party’
World.content:
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has published a lengthy social media statement linking Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine to Georgia‘s domestic politics and the country’s opposition.

According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Kobakhidze writes that after the war in Ukraine began in 2022, the “opposition’s pseudo-liberal minority” in Georgia adopted a radical stance towards Russia. He argues that such attitudes had not existed even after the August 2008 war, despite the fact that Russia continued to occupy 20% of Georgia’s territory.

In his statement, the prime minister recalls the consequences of the 2008 war. He says Russia’s military aggression killed 412 people, injured 2,232 others and displaced about 30,000 people. More than 120 Georgian settlements also remained beyond the occupation line.

Kobakhidze argues that the United National Movement, which was in power at the time, did not pursue a hard-line policy towards Russia. Instead, he says, it encouraged Russian tourists and investors to come to Georgia, promoted cultural and economic ties, facilitated Russian investment in various sectors and later unilaterally abolished visa requirements for Russian citizens.

According to the prime minister, neither government officials nor their supporters protested against that policy at the time. In this context, Kobakhidze names several current opposition politicians and public figures, including Elene Khoshtaria and Zurab Japaridze, and claims they supported closer relations with Russia during that period.

According to the prime minister, the opposition, along with affiliated NGOs and activists, turned into an “externally controlled network of agents” and adopted a sharply anti-Russian stance only after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Kobakhidze argues that the Georgian opposition’s current “Russophobia” is not genuine but stems from “directives issued by external forces”. He says that if anyone were to develop a truly radical attitude towards Russia, it should have happened after the August 2008 war, not after Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine.

The prime minister concludes his statement by asking why this “network of agents” did not display the same attitude towards Russia after the 2008 war, but only after the war in Ukraine began. Kobakhidze says society “will easily find a logical explanation” for that question.

“I believe there is a question that must be asked and carefully considered by society. We all know that, both in the past and today, this network of agents in Georgia has acted on instructions from external forces, and that its homeland is not Georgia but the ‘deep state’.

Against that backdrop, it is worth asking why they were not instructed to promote Russophobia when there was the strongest possible reason to do so – after the August 2008 war – and why they have been instructed to do so now, when the victim of Russian aggression is not their formal homeland but another country, albeit a friendly one. I believe society will easily find a logical explanation for this contradiction,” Kobakhidze wrote.

Kobakhidze on Russophobia in Georgia

World.title: Diaspora youth: Patriots or ‘information soldiers’? The hidden mission of camp in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan. More than 120 young people from 64 countries gathered in Zangilan under the slogan “Reviving Cities”. Officials told participants they should defend Azerbaijan’s achievements and push back against what they described as “biased campaigns”.

Against the backdrop of protesters calling Ilham Aliyev a “dictator” in Berlin, that message raises another question: is the state seeking to foster independent thinkers or “information soldiers” who will promote its official narrative abroad?

What was discussed at the 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp?

The 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp, which opened in Zangilan on 2 August, is officially presented as a platform for “patriotic education”, learning about “the realities on the ground” and rejuvenating the Azerbaijani diaspora. More than 120 young people from 64 countries are spending a week visiting reconstruction projects in the territories retaken by Azerbaijan, meeting government officials and learning what organisers describe as “Azerbaijani realities”.

A closer look at the speeches by Fuad Muradov, chairman of the State Committee for Work with the Diaspora, and other officials, however, reveals a more pragmatic objective. The government appears to see young people living abroad not simply as members of the diaspora with ties to their homeland, but as active participants in the information battle.

Muradov said the participants should be able to “respond with well-founded arguments to biased campaigns”. He said they should “represent” Azerbaijan’s interests with dignity in their countries of residence, on international platforms and within their own communities.

Another message struck an even tougher tone. Officials said that although their number was small, some people living abroad who called themselves Azerbaijanis did not welcome Azerbaijan’s successes. They urged participants to know who these people were, be familiar with their statements and respond to them with well-reasoned arguments. Officials also said “black PR”, “distortion of facts” and “organised campaigns” were unacceptable. At the same time, they said they remained open to “well-founded criticism”.

Elvin Aslanov, a representative of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, acknowledged that defending Azerbaijan abroad was “far from easy”, saying it required confronting double standards and disinformation. According to him, the young participants’ mission is to “convey the truth accurately and objectively”.

From the authorities’ perspective, such rhetoric may appear defensive and entirely legitimate. However, the broader context allows for another interpretation. Critics argue that the programme goes beyond patriotic education and instead systematically prepares “information soldiers” – young people expected to promote the official narrative on social media, in online discussions and in international debates. In other words, they see it as an attempt to build a state-directed “soft power” network.

What happened in Berlin, and why does it matter in this context?

The timing of these appeals is no coincidence. During Ilham Aliyev’s official visit to Germany on 21 July, Azerbaijani expatriates gathered on the streets of Berlin and chanted: “Dictator!”

Around the same time, Germany-based exiled blogger Alemdar Bunyatov approached Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev on a street in Berlin. He questioned them about political prisoners and allegations of torture.

Official media immediately described the incident as a “provocation” and portrayed Bunyatov as someone “known for his close ties to the Iranian intelligence services”. Responding to his questions, Bayramov dismissed the allegations of torture as “a personal opinion”.

Hajiyev, for his part, questioned Bunyatov about his sources of funding, his legal status in Germany and his reasons for leaving Azerbaijan. He stressed the importance of sovereignty and national security. The incident triggered a strong reaction in pro-government media, which portrayed the blogger’s questions as “provocative”.

The events in Berlin further illustrate the practical meaning of the messages delivered in Zangilan. In the official narrative, criticism is often framed as a “biased campaign”, “black PR” or the result of “external influence”.

As a result, the authorities themselves largely determine the line between “well-founded criticism” and a “biased campaign”. Young people, in turn, are expected to accept that distinction and challenge those whom the state places on the other side of it.

A method of training trolls?

Opposition figures and independent observers have long described such camps as a form of “troll factory”. Critics argue that their purpose is not to encourage independent thinking but to prepare young people to defend the official position on social media, in online discussions and before international audiences. They say that, under the banner of patriotism, organisers cultivate emotional attachment and ideological loyalty while encouraging participants to view critical voices as “hostile”.

Every country seeks to use its diaspora as a tool of soft power, and Azerbaijan is no exception. The problem, critics argue, is that the shrinking space for domestic criticism places a disproportionately heavy burden on young Azerbaijanis abroad to “defend” the official line. They must adapt to societies where freedom of expression is a fundamental principle while remaining loyal to Baku’s official narrative. For many young people, that contradiction can create genuine tension.

Muradov says, “We are open to dialogue”, while also insisting, “We will not tolerate black PR.” This raises an obvious question: what qualifies as “well-founded criticism”, and what counts as a “biased campaign”? If official media portray the questions and slogans heard on the streets of Berlin as a provocation, where is the line for young people who raise the same issues in international media or at academic forums?

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament holds first session as opposition, as expected, makes its presence felt
World.content:
First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

Armenia‘s newly elected parliament convened for the first time on 2 August. Three political forces won seats in the ninth National Assembly: the Civil Contract, Strong Armenia and Armenia factions. During the opening session, lawmakers managed only to appoint members of the Counting Commission. Heated exchanges between the ruling party and the opposition prevented them from addressing the rest of the agenda.

The opposition’s main grievance was the absence of the Catholicos from the opening session. The authorities did not invite him, and he did not bless the work of parliament. Opposition lawmakers described this as an unprecedented event in the history of independent Armenia.

Under the constitutional law governing the National Assembly’s rules of procedure, both the president and the Catholicos of All Armenians have the right to deliver opening remarks at parliament’s first session. This time, however, only President Vahagn Khachaturyan addressed lawmakers. Earlier, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said it had received no invitation for the Catholicos. When journalists asked Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan about Garegin II’s participation, he replied: “I do not know such a Catholicos.” The incident reflects the long-running dispute between the Armenian authorities and Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II. More than two years ago, Prime Minister Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He initially argued that Garegin II could not lead the Armenian Apostolic Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and fathered a daughter. Pashinyan later accused him of links with foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party also included the removal of “the de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Lawmakers also fiercely debated the nomination of Ruben Rubinyan, the ruling party’s sole candidate for speaker of parliament.

Opposition MPs repeatedly referred to his research work at Istanbul Policy Center in Turkey in 2017–18. They asked whether he had interacted with local residents and even questioned what they looked like.

“Ask me directly whether I met representatives of the Turkish intelligence services in Turkey and whether they recruited me. Ask me: ‘Is that true?’ And I will answer: ‘No,'” Rubinyan said.

Parliament resumed its first session today. Lawmakers have already settled one of the main items on the agenda. In a secret ballot, they elected Ruben Rubinyan as speaker with 63 votes in favour and 28 against.

The opposition Armenia bloc boycotted the secret ballot. MPs from the second opposition force, the Strong Armenia faction, voted against Rubinyan’s nomination.

In the previous parliament, Rubinyan served as deputy speaker. Between 2022 and 2026, he also acted as Armenia’s special envoy for the normalisation of relations with Turkey. A few days ago, Rubinyan said he would be unable to continue in that role if parliament elected him speaker. The ruling party has not yet announced who will succeed him.

“Where is the Patriarch?” Opposition MPs visit him to receive his blessing

On the opening day of the session, opposition MPs began chanting, “Where is the Patriarch?” after the president’s address. During the oath-taking ceremony, they pointedly refused to stand or recite the oath. They said they were protesting the Catholicos’s absence. However, they signed the written text of the oath, allowing them to take office formally.

At the end of the first working day, MPs from both opposition factions visited the Catholicos’s residence.

The Mother See’s information service said Garegin II blessed the opposition lawmakers. He spoke of an “alarming situation and serious problems” facing the country. He also criticised what he described as the authorities’ “illegal and unconstitutional actions” against the Church.

Catholicos receives opposition MPs at the Mother See

The Catholicos praised what he described as the opposition MPs’ “devotion and filial love for the Church”. He said their stance was especially important at a time when “the authorities continue their campaign of repression, while national benefactor Samvel Karapetyan remains under arrest for speaking out in defence of Holy Etchmiadzin”.

In June last year, Armenian authorities opened a criminal case against Russian businessman and billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. Prosecutors accused him of publicly calling for the seizure and usurpation of power. In an interview with local media, Karapetyan discussed the escalating conflict between the government and the Church. He said he supported the Church and added: “If Armenia’s political forces fail to resolve this situation, we will have to intervene in the campaign against the Church in our own way.” His supporters founded the Strong Armenia party after his arrest, and he has remained under house arrest since December last year.

105 MPs in the new parliament

The three political forces that entered the National Assembly secured the following number of seats:

The ruling Civil Contract party – 64 seats

The Strong Armenia faction – 29 seats

The Armenia bloc – 12 seats

Strong Armenia leader and businessman Samvel Karapetyan did not enter parliament. During the election campaign, his allies confidently predicted victory and even said Karapetyan would become prime minister. However, he is ineligible to serve either as an MP or as prime minister. Under Armenia’s constitution, anyone holding citizenship of another country cannot hold either office. Karapetyan holds Armenian, Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

Former President Robert Kocharyan headed the electoral list of the Armenia bloc, making him its candidate for prime minister. However, Kocharyan declined to take up his parliamentary seat. His son, Levon Kocharyan, who also ran on the bloc’s list, accepted a mandate and has already joined parliament. He also served as an MP for the Armenia bloc in the previous legislature.

“I will do everything to ensure our children never experience war”

Rubinyan thanked the more than 700,000 voters who backed Civil Contract. He said they had given the ruling party “a mandate to continue Armenia’s democratic reforms and peace agenda”. According to Rubinyan, those voters had defended the country’s sovereignty and independence.

He said the time had come for Armenians to enjoy peaceful lives, have children and raise them without fear.

“My son, who is almost two years old, and children of his age have never experienced war. I will do everything to ensure that my children, your children and all our children never have to learn what war is,” he said.

Rubinyan also thanked those who voted for opposition parties out of conviction rather than in exchange for election bribes.

“It is time to change the political discourse,” Rubinyan says

Addressing opposition MPs, Rubinyan raised the issue of the tone of parliamentary debate. He said society, political circles and journalists had formed a common view of parliament in recent months. According to him, many now see the National Assembly as a place for pointless arguments, slander and insults.

“They say this parliament will be even worse than the previous one in that respect. It seems everyone expects exactly that from us. I want to propose that we break this curse together,” the speaker said.

He argued that the opposition factions had largely stayed away from the work of the previous, eighth convocation of parliament.

“All we saw here was political confrontation, shouting and radical speeches. It is time to change the narratives that have dominated Armenian politics over the past six years. I propose that we make this parliament a place for vigorous but respectful debate that never crosses the boundaries of decency.”

At the same time, he warned that if the opposition rejected his proposal and continued “down the well-trodden path”, the ruling party was ready to respond “in the toughest possible way”.

“Why did we take our seats?” Opposition MPs explain

Ishkhan Saghatelyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, argued that neither the opposition nor the ruling party had truly won the election.

He again claimed that the authorities had used administrative resources during the campaign and imprisoned opposition figures.

“This parliament has a serious legitimacy problem. We are here to organise political struggle and advance national goals. We are here to raise the concerns of Armenia’s citizens, speak about the prisoners held in Baku and Armenia’s occupied territories, and, yes, defend the people of Artsakh’s right to a collective return.”

Hayk Farmanyan, an MP from the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that message.

“We accepted our mandates to remain true to our Armenian identity, to fight for our national values, and to defend our dignity, our identity and our Church.”

Comment

Political analyst Lilit Dallakyan shared her impressions of the new parliament’s opening session on social media:

“Well, I ‘congratulate’ the Armenian people on the start of work by a new, high-quality, substantive parliament that is supposedly ready to tackle Armenia’s complex challenges.

The daily exchange of ‘Your father is a murderer’ [directed at MP Levon Kocharyan, son of former President Robert Kocharyan] will now gain a new, equally substantive argument: ‘Your uncle is a Russian oligarch’ [directed at MP Narek Karapetyan, nephew of Strong Armenia leader Samvel Karapetyan]. That will, in turn, prompt the reply: ‘You are Turkish dictators’ [directed at the authorities].

The only positive aspect is that this season of the series is unlikely to interest anyone or distract people from the real problems that are rapidly emerging.

At a time of profound change across the world, Armenian society and every individual will have to look for solutions to their own problems. Ultimately, that will bring about the changes the country needs.”

First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

World.title: Opinion: ‘Abkhaz diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive’
World.content:
Against the backdrop of the Pacific island nation of Nauru withdrawing its recognition of Abkhazia’s independence, prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania reflects on what Abkhazia’s foreign policy doctrine should look like.

Nauru, a small island nation in the Pacific region of Micronesia, recognised Abkhazia’s independence in 2009 but withdrew that recognition in late July 2026. The move reduced the number of countries recognising Abkhazia’s independence to four. Abkhazia’s foreign ministry said Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure”.

Akhra Bzhania said: “Around 230,000 irregular migrants crossed the EU’s borders in 2025–26 alone. All of them fled countries that enjoy broad international recognition.

Why didn’t they stay in Morocco, Mali or Afghanistan? Presumably because having a flag outside the UN headquarters does not automatically mean you live in a genuine state – one where you can influence public life, where your voice matters and where your dignity will never be trampled.

Being a recognised country and being a country where people want to live and are willing to die for it are two different things.

You may achieve the first and never attain the second. But if you have the second, then you have accomplished the most important task: building a country that belongs to its citizens. That is what defines a modern state. And that is precisely what should become the main instrument for Abkhazia’s integration into the international community.

Bzhania continued: “We must send a clear message to the international community that, despite sanctions, isolation and the threat of war, the people of Abkhazia have built a society based on the rule of law and freedom. Without being members of international institutions, we have incorporated the core principles of international conventions on civil and political rights into our system of governance.

We see ourselves as part of the international community and believe we deserve our rightful place within it. To achieve that, our diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive. It should focus not on waiting for or preserving acts of recognition, but on consistently demonstrating our statehood and expanding our international contacts.

No one else is obliged to do this for us. By recognising our sovereignty, Russia effectively made Abkhazia a subject of international law. But it cannot solve our problems on our behalf.”

Bzhania continued: “We must use every tool at our disposal to achieve our goals: the resources of the diaspora, cultural, trade and sporting ties, personal connections, migration policy and regional logistics. In this game, we need to keep raising the stakes.

Today, there is a window of opportunity for such an active policy. It is no secret that relations between Georgia and the West are at their lowest point since the 1990s. Those on whom Tbilisi relied to promote its anti-Abkhaz agenda have become disillusioned with Georgia, and we should take advantage of that. That includes reviving the active dialogue with European countries that existed in the late 1990s. After all, the hopes the West once placed in Georgia as a bastion of the free world in the Caucasus have, to a greater extent, been realised in Abkhazia.

Another key asset, which has remained almost entirely outside our foreign policy efforts, is the Circassian diaspora. Four million people spread across 50 countries represent a powerful resource we can genuinely rely on. More importantly, we should offer them the prospect of political cooperation.

Abkhazia can and should become the centre of the Circassian world as the only independent state of this sub-ethnic group. Our country can become the same kind of homeland for Circassians worldwide that Israel has become for Jews. If every Circassian, wherever they live, knows they will find protection and support for their interests in Abkhazia, it will create a strong foundation for advancing our shared interests.”

Bzhania concluded: “It will probably not happen tomorrow, no matter how much effort we put in. But it can happen within a foreseeable future if those efforts remain consistent and systematic.

In 2017, I had the honour of welcoming a delegation from Nauru’s parliament to Abkhazia on behalf of the Abkhaz parliament. They were wonderful, warm people. Unfortunately, ships at sea do not only meet – they also part ways. Today, Nauru has set a course away from Abkhazia, apparently believing it to be the safer option. I wish them well. As for us, we will continue on our own course.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nauru’s withdrawal of recognition of Abkhazia

World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: Breaking: Allegedly stolen car involved serious Cairns crash
World.content:
Police say a driver has been arrested after an allegedly stolen car was involved in a multi-vehicle crash north of Cairns.

Police and paramedics were called to the scene on the Smithfield Bypass just before 1:30pm.

The Queensland Ambulance Service said multiple patients were being taken to hospital.

Police said a male alleged to have been driving a stolen car was taken into custody at Reservoir Road.

Officers said he was assisting with investigations.

The Smithfield Bypass remains closed in both directions. Motorists are urged to avoid the area and drive with caution.

Investigations are ongoing.

World.title: Deer stranded on rock shelf highlights looming urban pest problem
World.content:
It was a regular a sunny winter morning on Wollongong's Blue Mile as people walked their dogs, swam in the ocean rock pool and rode their bikes along the popular shared pathway.

The only difference was groups of people stopping to take photos of a stranded deer on the ocean rock shelf.

Small waves lapped at the legs of the animal as firefighters, police and council officers deliberated over what to do.

NSW Invasive Species Council CEO Jack Gough said it was the latest example of the pest's urban encroachment.

"It's maybe funny to see one near the Continental Pool, but it's not funny when you're driving at night and see a 200-to-300-kilogram stag on the road and crash into it," he said.

" The road toll is huge, and the cost to the environment and agriculture is enormous. "

Emergency workers gather at North Wollongong's Blue Mile to discuss what to do about a stranded deer. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Population growth, mismanagement

Illawarra residents have been reporting regular sightings of deer in unusual places, including along streets, in backyards and on rail lines.

"It is widely agreed in the community that deer are an absolute scourge," Wollongong Greens councillor Jess Whittaker said earlier this week.

Mr Gough said deer numbers were out of control due to years of mismanagement.

"The reason we're seeing more deer is because of its exponential population growth," he said.

"The reality is we have been on this pathway since the 1990s.

"There's unfortunately been decades of protections for deer as a hunting resource, and there's a real patchwork of biosecurity rules about access to land for people to be able to do deer control in NSW."

Emergency workers were called to the scene. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Mr Gough said deer populations in Wollongong and Victoria's East Gippsland were among the worst in the country.

"They trash and trample streams, they prevent regeneration particularly after fire, they strip the bark off trees," he said.

"They get into people's gardens and are responsible for multiple road and rail strikes.

"Unfortunately we don't have a scaled-up level of funding or ambition across state and local government, local land services and the rail and road authorities in a coordinated fashion that could actually start to reduce the animal's population density."

Deer cull underway nearby

The NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) is this week conducting its second deer cull of the year in the Royal National Park near Helensburgh, north of Wollongong.

The program, which has no fixed target number, aims to reduce the impact of deer on native plants, animals and threatened species.

There were 48 animals killed in May, of which 36 were killed through aerial shooting and 12 using ground shooting.

Jess Whittacker says culling deer in urban areas presents a major safety challenge. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Wollongong City Council has signed a two-year contract with South East Local Land Services to cull feral deer appearing on streets and beaches.

The move came two months after Lord Mayor Tania Brown wrote to the state government to sound the alarm over feral deer running rampant on major roads, residential streets and beaches in Wollongong.

Peri-urban areas a major challenge

Cr Whittacker said that while deer culling in the Royal National Park was a useful exercise to reduce numbers in that area, controlling deer in Wollongong suburbs was extremely difficult.

"The peri-urban and urban areas [are] such a challenging problem because you're managing safety and community and how do you cull them there?" she said.

Jess Whittacker says controlling urban deer will require a coordinated effort from all levels of government. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

"The cull in the national park will probably reduce the number of deer coming out of the national park and into the Illawarra, but we already have so many deer in the escarpment around Figtree, Farmborough Heights, Bulli and Woonona.

"That's going to need more scientific research and a strategic approach for all levels of government to work together on a coordinated approach to get the numbers down."

A council spokesperson said in a statement the deer at Wollongong's Continental Pool this morning made its way north and was last seen heading into Puckey's Estate where it no longer posed a direct risk to the public.

World.title: Mandatory domestic roaming to be key focus of mobile coverage inquiry
World.content:
Australia's competition regulator will consider whether it should force telcos to allow all mobile users to use their network if their own is not available, as part of an inquiry into regional mobile coverage.

Calls for domestic roaming had been growing amid concerns about a lack of competition particularly in regional areas.

Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email pezet.lauren@abc.net.au or laurenpezet@proton.me

In 2024 the Regional Telecommunications Review recommended the federal communications minister direct the ACCC to conduct a fresh inquiry on the issue, after a previous 2017 inquiry found roaming would reduce incentives for telcos to invest in the network.

A ministerial directive was never made but the ACCC today announced it would instigate a new inquiry of its own accord.

It will also consider if providers should be directed to share the radio access network, which includes infrastructure such as towers and radio equipment.

"We have seen that there's a lot of change in the market, that the emergence of the satellite services provides the opportunity for direct to device services to mobile phones," ACCC Commissioner Anna Brakey said.

"There's also a lot of calls for domestic roaming, we have heard those.

"What we want to do is work through in a really carefully and consultative way so that we understand all the issues, we understand the needs and that we make decisions and regulatory settings that will serve customers well into the future."

Anna Brakey says conditions have changed since the competition regulator last looked at domestic roaming. (ABC News: Michael Nudl)

The inquiry will take around 12 months and hold forums in regional and remote parts of the country.

The ACCC will consider how mobile use is changing, the current state of competition, how regulation could impact investment and competition, and the increasing role of low earth orbit satellites.

The Australia Communications Consumer Action Network (ACCAN), a strong proponent of domestic roaming, said the government had all the evidence it needed to mandate now.

ACCAN was among several groups including the National Farmers Federation and National Rural Health Alliance that called on the government to intervene and force the issue.

"There is a bill before parliament — the Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation Bill — which, with simple amendments, would allow the ACCC to declare domestic mobile roaming and get on with the job of implementation," ACCAN chief executive Carol Bennett said in a statement.

"For consumers, a reliable mobile connection means being able to stay in contact with family, friends, clients and emergency services.

"A lengthy review risks delaying these benefits by years we don't have."

Carol Bennett says the federal government should intervene and legislate mandatory domestic roaming. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Federal Minister for Communications Anika Wells was not available for an interview but in a statement said the inquiry was "timely".

"The work the ACCC is doing will complement and inform the implementation of the Albanese government's Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation (UOMO), which will require Telstra, Optus and TPG to provide reasonable outdoor access to SMS and voice calls throughout Australia," she said.

'Dragging the chain'

Kristy Sparrow from volunteer advocacy group Better Internet for Rural, Regional and Remote Australia welcomed the inquiry given it would look at all wholesale services.

"We would also be encouraging them to look at coverage maps and adopt national maps similar to what is seen in other countries like America, Europe and New Zealand," she said

Kristy Sparrow says domestic roaming is just one part of the solution to improving services in the bush. (Supplied: Lisa Alexander Photography)

In regards to domestic roaming, Ms Sparrow said consideration needed to be given to existing congestion on towers in some rural areas.

"We encourage that if there is a decision on mandatory roaming that it comes with appropriate resilience and capacity investments."

She also warned roaming would not increase the coverage footprint, only competition, and that Australia was still "dragging the chain" on access more broadly.

"Whatever the decision is it mustn't stop investment in terrestrial coverage particularly in the regions.

"(Roaming is) part of a solution but what's needed is a long-term strategy and plan and leadership in the space."

World.title: No dog poo or tea bags in surprise change to WA FOGO bin rules
World.content:
The state government authority that overseas local council waste collection has changed the rules on what can go in green FOGO bins, excluding previously allowed items including pet poo, tea bags, paper towels and used pizza boxes.

The rules have been updated online in a move the Waste Authority says will simplify sorting for households and specifies that only garden waste, unpackaged food waste and certified compostable bin liners can go in bins.

The change is likely to cause consternation for local councils, which have been grappling with considerable community resistance to the FOGO (food organics, garden organics) program as it has been rolled out over the past two years.

There have been changes to what is allowed in green-lidded bins. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

The program reduced collection of red-lidded general waste bins from weekly to fortnightly, with the trade-off being that households could put more items in their green-lidded bins, including food waste and some cardboard items, which would be collected weekly.

Creating 'pure' compost

Mark Irwin, who is Mayor of Perth's largest council, the City of Stirling, and president of the WA local government association (WALGA), told Nadia Mitsopoulos on 102.5 ABC Perth there were sound reasons for the changes, which would mean the FOGO material could be composted effectively.

"What we've seen through [implementing] FOGO is it's so important that these waste streams are pure in what they're intended to be, otherwise they're contaminated and they can't be used for their intended recycling purpose," he said.

"The changes that are being implemented are effectively to make sure that the waste is more pure."

Mark Irwin says a bigger communication strategy is needed for FOGO. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

He said many takeaway containers and cups labelled as compostable were not compatible with current systems, and neither were a number of cardboards.

"It doesn't take a lot [of contamination]," he said.

"If you put the wrong forms of waste into these waste streams, they can actually create an exploding effect across the volume that's collected, and most of these are around the chemicals that are involved."

Forever chemicals 'infect everything'

He said a number of products, including some bin liners and takeaway containers labelled as compostable, contained PFAS, known as forever chemicals.

"PFAS is an acronym for polyfluoroalkyl substance — basically synthetic chemicals," he said.

"They just don't break down and they basically infect everything in that waste stream."

FOGO bin liners are compostable. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

The food-soiled packaging items also cannot be recycled.

People have been advised to place them into the red general waste bins.

Mr Irwin said further changes to FOGO would likely lead to calls from residents to reinstate weekly general waste collection.

"People are struggling to understand," he said.

He said some people were reporting that putting food waste in a green bin was not freeing up enough space in their general waste bins.

"One of the things that's evident with the FOGO or the food organics is that while they're dense and they're heavy, they're not always voluminous," he said.

"Some of those other things that people collect in their households, like packaging, take up a lot of room in a bin, so to remove the red bin from weekly collection has been proving difficult in many councils."

Call for leadership in waste

The rule changes have taken many people by surprise. They were quietly updated on the waste authority website on July 10 and have begun to be shared by local councils on social media.

Mr Irwin said the state government needed to implement a more comprehensive communication strategy.

"This needs a really strong state-led waste strategy and it needs really strong leadership in this space to make sure that there's consistency across our state," he said.

"What we will continue to do though is talk to the minister and talk to the state government about leadership in this space."

The lids of council-supplied caddies show what can go in FOGO bins. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

The changes also mean that some of the information printed on the bins and kitchen caddies supplied to households by councils when FOGO was rolled out is now incorrect.

"It's certainly a challenge for councils," Mr Irwin said.

"They're seeing a lot of pushback from their communities and they're looking, again, for really strong leadership and sufficient funding.

"Anything we do in the waste space is not in the hundreds of thousands, it's in the tens of millions of dollars."

The WA Waste Authority has been contacted for comment.

World.title: EV sales keep nudging record high as market hit 'new phase'
World.content:
Australian drivers have entered "a new phase", experts say, with electric vehicles accounting for one in five new car sales for the third consecutive month.

July sales data published today shows the share of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) easing slightly from the record set in June, with 23,510 vehicles sold, claiming 21.7 per cent of all new vehicle sales.

It means the sales share of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) tripled year-on-year in the wake of the war in Iran and the ensuing fuel crisis.

After the June record of 23.3 per cent, many were tipping a drop with the financial year ending.

But with conflict in the Iran war again heating up and the return of the fuel excise, the price of petrol jumped again, and Australian drivers are looking to cut ties with the servo.

"It's incredible what a year in a war will make," said Rebecca Huntley, a social researcher who recorded a significant jump in support for EVs.

"If you were to have a poster of the greatest influencer when it comes to EV take-up in Australia, it'd have Donald Trump."

Toyota remains the most popular brand of new cars being sold overall with more than 115,000, but Chinese EV maker BYD is on its heels, selling more than 60,000 cars in July.

"What the numbers are telling us is that we are actually moving into a new phase," said Andrea Pellegrini, a lecturer and researcher at the Institute of Transport and Logistics Studies at the University of Sydney.

"Now actually we are kind of going into a phase where the market is becoming more mature."

The Federal Chamber of Automotive Industry (FCAI) acknowledged electric cars played a part in record sales for July, but sounded a warning that charging infrastructure needed to keep pace.

"Accessible and dependable charging will be critical to maintaining consumer confidence as electric vehicles become a larger part of Australia's new-vehicle fleet, "FCAI chief executive Tony Weber said.

Changing EV attitudes

In years gone by, some politicians have said EVs would "end the weekend" by sidelining SUVs, once considered necessary for towing boats and caravans.

But the capability of hybrids and EV options is catching up, and with the price of fuel firming above $2, and much higher for diesel, the tables have turned.

"People started to go, oh my God, I might be going away on a weekend and I might not be able to get petrol," Dr Huntley said.

Rebecca Huntley says the war in Iran has played a big role in the shift in consumer behaviour towards EVs. (ABC News: Adam Wyatt)

"Suddenly, that kind of reliability factor of combustion engines started to feature in people's minds."

Past concerns about range and charging limitations of EVs are also fading, according to Dr Pellegrini.

"General overall concerns about the electric vehicle, kind of the ease after they purchase the vehicle," he said.

"They are less concerned about the waiting time, the driving range, but also they think that it is good value for money once they start driving the vehicle."

Energy independence

Dr Huntley and her team have just published the second Clean Energy Solutions Index, a national research project that surveys thousands of people and ranks public support for the renewable energy transition.

Overall, the index recorded a modest one-point increase in "deep support" for the energy transition to 61 out of 100.

Many of the 11 clean solutions it tracks have remained either unchanged or, in the case of some infrastructure projects like onshore wind, dipped slightly.

However, the stand-out in the 2026 report was support for EVs, which rose six points.

"That insecurity around the technology of combustion engines has, I think, accelerated the consideration of EVs for a lot of people," Huntley says.

"And when we talk to people who've made the switch, it's a bit like taking back control, having agency, feeling like if something like this happens again, which a lot of people expect that it might, it's just not going to affect me as much."

For about a decade, Margaret Killen had a sticker on her old diesel car that proudly claimed her next car would be an EV.

A year later, she finally made the switch.

"It's been going really well, and I'm really pleased with my purchase," Mrs Killen said.

Margaret Killen is happy with her EV ownership experience. (Supplied.)

It was an expensive outlay, but with solar on her home, her vehicle running costs are now much lower.

"The benefits are now playing off, you know, playing out as in we've got a charger at home, we pop it on when it's low peak or sometimes we have free power hours in Tassie."

More support needed for renters

Buying and charging an EV is a much simpler proposition for someone who owns their own house and has rooftop solar.

But more than 10 per cent of Australians live in an apartment, and more than 30 per cent are renters. It's an area Pellegrini said needed greater consideration and investment.

"If you're a renter, it makes it very complicated to have a private charger installed at your property because you do not actually have a say in it," Dr Pellegrini said.

"That segment of the market is actually really crucial because we know that if people live in apartment units and they want to buy an electric vehicle, currently they mostly rely on the public infrastructure system.

Australians renting or living in apartments can often not just plug in at home to charge an electric car. (ABC News: Alex Lim)

Charging EVs everywhere A lack of charging infrastructure across the country is often cited as a barrier to the transition to electric vehicles. But soon, EV charging could be a simple as finding a car park.

But according to Dr Huntley, politicians and leaders sometimes underestimate the enthusiasm for new technology.

"There's so much opportunity in the renewable energy revolution at the household level that can lean into Australia's love of technology, love of being able to control the things that you're doing," she said.

"The biggest question is not, we don't want this; the biggest question is, is everybody going to get to share equally in this opportunity we have?"

World.title: NSW Police update body-worn camera policy after ABC investigation
World.content:
Thousands of NSW Police officers will from Wednesday be required to switch on their body-worn cameras when exercising their powers, following a Four Corners investigation and repeated calls by the state's police watchdog.

The new policy requires all officers to immediately commence recording when working in an "operational capacity", such as when using force, attending a serious crime or engaging in a police pursuit.

If officers do not use their camera, they will be required to provide a written account explaining why.

The change is being promoted to NSW Police officers via the slogan, "When the job's on, switch on."

In June, Four Corners aired an investigation into shocking cases of police brutality, and concerns that NSW Police body-worn cameras were not being used appropriately.

The decision follows a Four Corners story revealing allegations of a culture of impunity within the police. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

The investigation documented cases where officers did not turn on their cameras until after people were arrested, did not wear a camera at all, or in one instance, repeatedly muted the audio while brutally assaulting a woman experiencing a severe mental health episode.

The program was described by NSW Assistant Commissioner Peter Cotter as "confronting" and a "highlight reel of use being at our worst".

At the time, Assistant Commissioner Cotter said a review of the standard operating procedures for body-worn video was underway and would lead to change.

Change comes after years of advocacy

Until now, NSW and WA were the only states where the use of body-worn cameras by police was discretionary rather than mandatory.

The change was welcomed by the NSW police watchdog, the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (LECC).

LECC Chief Commissioner Peter Johnson described the move as a "very important development in policing in NSW".

The LECC has advocated for the mandatory use of body-worn cameras since 2023.

Police body-worn camera changes flagged NSW Police will move to the mandatory use of body-worn cameras for sworn officers in the wake of allegations of a culture of impunity within the police force.

The change was a key recommendation of a 2025 review which found a "number of serious police incidents in which officers did not activate available body-worn cameras," and another case in which an officer allegedly destroyed incriminating footage by throwing his camera in a "body of water".

"The knowledge that interactions between police and community members are being recorded helps to keep both the officer and the community safe," Chief Commissioner Johnson said in a statement.

"The use of body-worn cameras also promotes officer accountability by enabling the NSW Police Force and the Commission to effectively scrutinise officers' actions where there are allegations of police misconduct."

NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson said "the public can certainly take some relief knowing it is now in the standard operating procedures".

"It's quite shocking that it took a Four Corners episode with such harrowing footage and revelations to see this," she said, also crediting the "sustained efforts of the LECC and advocates with lived experience of harm".

A spokesperson for the Police Association of NSW said the union was working collaboratively with NSW Police on body-worn camera policy matters.

NSW Police was also contacted for comment.

World.title: NRL club claims player Keith Titmuss contributed to training death
World.content:
A rugby league player who died of heat exhaustion at pre-season training contributed to his own death by not managing his weight and diet in the off-season, his former club says.

The family of Keith Titmuss, who died in November 2020 after collapsing during pre-season training, is suing the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles for damages owing from negligence in his death, including failing to implement the NRL heat policy.

In a defence filed in the NSW Supreme Court the club has claimed it was not responsible for the death of the young man because he did not inform coaching and medical staff of his worsened physical state through the off-season.

"NRL training is inherently dangerous," the club wrote in its defence.

"Any injury, loss and damage suffered by [Titmuss's family] … was caused or contributed to by the deceased's own negligence."

Former NRL player's mother speaks on lawsuit The mother of Manly player Keith Titmuss, who died of exertional heat stroke following a 2020 Sea Eagles training session, breaks her silence on her family's multi-million-dollar lawsuit against the NRL club.

Manly Warringah alleged Titmuss failed to properly train or diet during the off-season and put himself in danger by not stopping training when he felt sick.

"Players were instructed … if they were feeling ill or feeling like they were not coping with the physical demands [that] they were to inform coaching staff," the club said.

The club also filed in its defence that it conducted a fitness test on the 20-year-old four days before he died and found "no red flags".

The session at the Sydney Academy of Sport at Narrabeen involved outdoor sprint tests before moving inside for an intense cardio session.

A 100-passes drill and a cardio circuit involving up-downs/burpees, bear crawls and "fireman carries" was conducted inside the facility's dojo, the parties agree.

The temperature was about 21 degrees Celsius during the session but the humidity was 92 per cent, court documents state.

Manly Warringah admitted the dojo was not fitted with air-conditioning but said there were multiple floor-standing fans, the back doors were open and hydration breaks were enforced.

The player's family alleged the fans were not switched on during the session.

There were 10 staff to monitor the 15 players inside, the club said.

NRL player Keith Titmuss died after 'inappropriate' training session, magistrate finds A magistrate who oversaw the inquest into the death of a young Manly Sea Eagles player recommends the NRL consider mandating a two-week period of controlled training acclimatisation after off-season breaks as part of an existing review.

A 2024 coronial inquest into his death concluded the budding NRL player died of exertion heat stroke, with a pre-existing heart condition unlikely to have played a part.

The work-out at the club's Narrabeen gym, which followed an outdoor session, was "more likely than not inappropriate", the coroner found.

Evidence at the inquest was that paramedics at the scene noted Titmuss's temperature at 41.9C, while his heart rate was more than 140 beats per minute.

Titmuss's family claimed the precautions instituted by Manly Warringah were not sufficient to meet its own heat policy guidelines, alleging the club is liable for the young man's death.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"[Manly Warringah] owed a duty of care to the deceased as an employee and … breached the duty of care owed," the statement of claim said.

Titmuss's family alleged the player started to struggle physically after an outdoor sprint test three days prior, which the club denied.

The club instituted a heat policy after former prop Lloyd Perrett said he was planning to sue the club over a training session in late 2017 which left him hospitalised with heat stroke after suffering a seizure.

Manly Warringah and the NRL were contacted for comment.

AAP

World.title: Councillors to be reinstated after private prosecution charges dropped
World.content:
Charges laid by a private resident against five central Victorian councillors and a council chief executive have been dropped after the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) intervened in court.

Last month, Hepburn businessman David Penman levelled charges against five Hepburn Shire councillors in a rare private prosecution.

Mayor Tony Clark, Don Henderson, Shirley Cornish, Pat Hockey and Lesley Hewitt, along with chief executive Bradley Thomas, were charged with misuse of public office offences.

Under the Local Government Act, all five councillors had to stand down until the matters were dealt with in court.

Opponents accused Mr Penman of weaponising a loophole in the act to effectively shut down the council, with state government announcing last week an administrator would have to be appointed.

This morning, the DPP appeared in the Ballarat Magistrate's Court to take over the charges, before successfully applying to have them thrown out.

Tony Clark says he is very pleased with the outcome. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

Councillors to return

Hepburn Shire Council confirmed that all five councillors would be reinstated to their roles.

Speaking outside the Ballarat Magistrate's Court this morning, Mayor Tony Clark spoke on behalf of his fellow councillors.

"We are extremely pleased with the outcome, and we will leave it there," Mr Clark said.

"We will have more to say later."

Bradley Thomas announced his resignation as chief executive earlier this year and is expected to finish in late August.

A statement from the Hepburn Shire noted the DPP "having reviewed all the evidence, determined that there were insufficient grounds available to proceed with the prosecutions".

"This is a great outcome for democracy and our community," the council said.

Late last week, the then-Victorian local government minister Paul Hamer announced his intention to appoint an administrator to the council, calling the matter an "unnecessary disruption".

New Minister for Local Government Tim Richardson has been contacted for comment.

David Penman says he accepts the court's decision. (ABC News: Laura Mayers)

Businessman claims 'institutional resistance'

Outside court, Mr Penman said he "was a little surprised" by the DPP stepping in.

"They [DPP] hadn't been in contact," he said.

"I thought the charges were particularly strong.

"But obviously, it's politically sensitive.

"I'm not suggesting that played a role but had I elected to play my role in the [courts] then it would've been different."

Mr Penman said he would accept the DPP's decision.

"This is a democracy. I've always said the courts are where democracy plays out," he said.

"[If] that's the decision of the DPP, then I accept that."

Hepburn Shire says the five councillors will be immediately reinstated. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Cost arguments to continue

Multiple organisations, including the Hepburn Shire Council, as well as witnesses, council CEO Bradley Thomas, and each of the councillors are seeking Mr Penman to pay their legal costs.

The court heard of the "significant costs" that were incurred by each party during the proceedings.

Magistrate Patrick Southey said there would need to be "at least a day" for each representative to quantify costs owed.

There were five different lawyers in the courtroom representing clients, while Mr Penman represented himself.

In an argument about costs this morning between Mr Penman and representative for Cr Don Henderson, David Tamanika, Mr Penman said a different magistrate "said he had done absolutely nothing wrong".

"That is absolutely not true," Mr Tamanika responded.

" I am not going to let you mislead the court. "

The dispute was broken up by Magistrate Southey.

"Look, Mr Penman, what another magistrate did or didn't say isn't going to have a bearing on the costs," Magistrate Southey told the court.

"This matter has been dragging on too long.

" And I understand there is legislation before Parliament, isn't there? To ensure this doesn't happen again? "

The state government confirmed last week that legislation to close the loophole used by Mr Penman was being considered by parliament.

All parties will return to court in late August as they continue to determine costs.

Court move welcomed

Rural Councils Victoria (RCV) welcomed the DPP's move, noting the disruption to the "lives and careers" of the Hepburn councillors.

"Sadly, this episode has already created significant disruption to local representation and the functioning of the council in Hepburn," an RCV spokesperson said.

"Until the Victorian government changes the law and closes the loophole that forces councillors to stand aside in these circumstances, the threat will continue."

"We urge the new premier, Ben Carroll, and the new minister for local government, Tim Richardson, to fix this flawed law as a matter of urgency."

World.title: Why I was locked in a bar on top of the world for 24 hours
World.content:
NationalCensus Opinion Why I was locked in a bar on top of the world for 24 hours Nick Dalziel Contributor August 5, 2026 — 3:00pm

August 5, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In recent days, you will have received an email or a letter from the Australian Bureau of Statistics with instructions on how to complete the 2026 census. Most of us will fill in the online form on August 11. It should be 20 minutes of inconvenience to be counted and avoid a fine. But until I spent a census day locked inside a hostel in La Paz, Bolivia, I’d never considered how convenient our census actually is. How do you count a population without a functioning postal service, or universal access to the internet? La Paz, Bolivia is the world’s highest capital city at 3650 metres. Getty Images La Paz is dirty, hilly and vibrant. It’s hard to breathe between the 3650-metre altitude and 1990s engine emissions on the city’s chaotic streets. But I loved it. Here is a country that’s rejected a lot of Western norms. You won’t find a McDonald’s here – the multinational tried and failed. Bolivians would much rather support a local street food vendor or “casera” trying to support their family. (It is possible, Northcote!)



Like many tourists, and even the ones who call themselves “travellers”, I was largely unaware of the daily happenings in a country where I’d only spent a week, taking each day as it came. Book a hostel a week out? Nah, that’s too rigid. But staff at the Wild Rover Hostel were imploring us to extend our bookings for March 23, 2004. I heeded. At least there was a bar: Nick Dalziel, right, locked down in Bolivia during the country’s census. From midnight, the doors were locked. Nobody, not even workers, could leave. Bolivia was taking stock of its population for the first time in 12 years, or 23 years, depending on who you asked. Myself, my hostel companions and the entirety of the 11,365,333 people in Bolivia were required to stay in the one place from midnight to midnight so they could be counted. The only exception: a medical emergency. Anyone spotted on the streets on this day would be rounded up and counted among the prison population.



Reply-paid envelopes are out of the question in a country without a functioning postal service, as is the idea that everyone can go online. Instead, 860,000 volunteer census collectors spent the day going door-to-door, counting the number of people in each of Bolivia’s 4 million households. Related Article Bolivia A gringo's trip to hell The census came about after years of protests demanding one, and people I spoke to were passionate about complying. Local governments urged Bolivians to stay home because the more people counted in an area, the greater the share of resources and political representation. Staying home was the thing to do for your region. The hostel shut its doors to the outside world for a day, with employees sleeping on the floor in the reception area. Meanwhile, guests and staff had a fiesta on a beautiful but eerily quiet March afternoon. We had a barbecue and played beer pong with plenty of local lagers. And then, at midnight, the doors were unlocked. Everyone had been counted. Life could resume. In the days that followed I heard stories of travellers getting stranded in all sorts of bizarre places, many without proper preparation or anything to eat. A full day locked in whatever room or broom cupboard or hovel they’d managed to find the night before. By sheer luck, I had been given the opportunity to stay longer in my dorm bed.



And if comparatively privileged travellers were hard done by, think about the locals what they sacrificed for census day. It evoked memories of pandemic lockdowns and the terrible situations many found themselves in: unable to travel to provide care, or stuck inside in cramped home or a dangerous domestic situation. A day of lost income is also a lot less easily absorbed in Bolivia. However, I was inspired by the dedication of the census volunteers who wanted the best for their local communities. Related Article Census From deadline to details: The six things you need to know to handle the census I’ll think about this on our own census night and the effort we take to ensure nobody is missed. There’ll be plenty of ABS staff who travel to remote locations and who head out to count those without a roof over their heads. Grumble you may, that you’re forced to log in or fill out a form for everyone in your dwelling on the night of Tuesday, August 11. But unlike Bolivia, most Australians have it pretty easy when it comes to counting population. Compared to a full day of lockdown, 20 minutes on the couch is more than manageable. Nick Dalziel is a communications manager and writer from Melbourne. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Perth boy accused of stabbing mum to death refuses to appear before magistrate
World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth boy accused of stabbing mum to death refuses to appear before magistrate Rebecca Peppiatt August 5, 2026 — 2:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 16-year-old boy who is alleged to have killed his mother and stabbed his 12-year-old sister would not appear before a magistrate in Perth Children’s Court on Wednesday as it was revealed he was being seen by a psychiatrist on a weekly basis while in custody. The teen, who cannot be named, was arrested after police were called to a Bentley address early on July 21 where they found a 35-year-old woman dead, having allegedly been killed by her son. World.title: ‘Bike Boy’ ordered to drug rehabilitation after accused carjacking of young family
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts ‘Bike Boy’ ordered to drug rehabilitation after accused carjacking of young family Erin Pearson August 5, 2026 — 2:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The man known as “Bike Boy” has been released on bail to a live-in drug rehabilitation centre after being charged with carjacking a mother and her toddlers while wearing only his underwear and a hoodie. Ryan Meuleman, 28, says his life spiralled into drug addiction and daily ice use after he was seriously injured as a teen in a crash with the family car of former premier Daniel Andrews. Ryan Meuleman, also known as “Bike Boy”. Monique Westermann However, his lawyer argued the Noble Park man is now ready to get his life back on track and undertake the hard work of rehabilitation. Melbourne Magistrates’ Court heard a woman was sitting in her idling car with her three-year-old twins outside a Pakenham laundromat on May 3 when Meuleman jumped in the driver’s seat.



The pair fought over control of the gear stick before Meuleman managed to drive the car a short distance. The woman’s husband heard her cries for help and intervened, pulling the alleged carjacker from the Kia Sportage and holding him until police arrived. The incident was captured on CCTV footage. Related Article Crime ‘Bike boy’ suing Dan Andrews to plead guilty to burglary and theft The court heard Meuleman was already on bail, charged with commercial burglary and theft when the alleged incident occurred. On Wednesday, First Constable Donovan Nortje opposed Meuleman’s release saying he had shown a blatant disregard for members of the public and the laws of Victoria. He pointed to the 28-year-old’s prior convictions for burglary, theft, car theft, drug-related matters, driving more than 45km/h over the speed limit, dangerous driving, deception and cannabis possession.



Defence lawyer Tom Smedley asked for his client to be released to drug rehabilitation centre The Cottage in Shepparton. “He wants to get his life back on track,” Smedley said. “Mr Meuleman knows it’s not a holiday and he has work to do there.” Matthew Morovan, from The Cottage, told the court Meuleman would receive treatment for his daily alcohol and drug use. He said participants were housed in three cottages on the property which was surrounded by 43 security cameras and 1.8-metre fences.



Related Article Courts Pantless, bloodied ‘Bike Boy’ accused of trying to steal car with family inside Morovan said between two and five staff were onsite during the day to help facilitate their three-phase, 12-week program, with patients only able to leave under supervision. Later, he said, they were allowed to leave alone with a 9pm curfew, and in the final stage permitted to have overnight stays outside the facility. Random drug testing also took place with “rigorous” searches of new arrivals’ belongings. However, the court heard no checks were performed between 11.30pm and 6.45am and there were no perimeter alarms onsite.



Smedley said the 2013 incident that left his client, then 15, hospitalised had been a turning point in his life and seen him move from cannabis use to methamphetamines. Carjacking carries a maximum penalty of 15 years’ jail with a mandatory sentence of time in jail. Magistrate Phillip Goldberg granted the accused man bail on the condition he stays at The Cottage and is not permitted to leave under any circumstances. “It’s recognised that a residential rehabilitation program is a benefit to the community and to the applicant. The community is better served when persons are not subject to the ravages that are brought by drug use,” he said. Meuleman launched defamation proceedings against Daniel Andrews and his wife, Catherine, in November last year, after being badly injured in the collision with the Andrews family’s four-wheel drive in 2013. World.title: ‘He’s the club’s future’: Wighton says Tallis Duncan should be Souths’ top priority
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘He’s the club’s future’: Wighton says Tallis Duncan should be Souths’ top priority Chris Barrett August 5, 2026 — 2:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tallis Duncan is South Sydney’s next captain, according to veteran Jack Wighton, who believes the rising star should be the Rabbitohs’ top priority as some of their highest-profile players approach the last year of their contracts. The 24-year-old has been a standout for Souths this season and returns from a hamstring injury against Parramatta at Allianz Stadium on Saturday night as Wayne Bennett’s team pushes to secure a top-eight berth. Tallis Duncan tries the Rabbitohs’ Indigenous jersey on for size. Sitthixay Ditthavong The Rabbitohs have injured superstar Latrell Mitchell, Campbell Graham, David Fifita and a cast of others coming off contract at the end of the 2027 season. But with Duncan likely to be heavily pursued by rival teams if he does not re-sign before the November 1 transfer window, Wighton says Souths are right to put the rising back-rower at the top of their list.



“He’s the club’s future,” the 33-year-old centre said on Wednesday. “He’s probably the club’s next captain if you ask me. He’s a great role model, he’s a great leader, and he does that with his actions and being upfront. “The club would be foolish if they didn’t prioritise him … he’d be first off the rank if it was me running the club. I think they’re definitely going down the right lines there. As I said, I can see him as the next captain of this whole club.” South Sydney veteran Jack Wighton. Sitthixay Ditthavong Souths will also be bolstered by the inclusion of their captain, Cameron Murray, for the Indigenous Round match against the Eels following a calf strain, as well as Fifita, who is back from suspension. Demonstrating his versatility, Duncan has for the sixth time in his last seven games been named in the centres, where he has prospered in the absence of Mitchell.



A member of Souths’ strong Indigenous contingent from the Wonnarua tribe in the Hunter Valley, Duncan said he was focused on helping the seventh-placed Rabbitohs make the finals for the first time since 2022 but would love to stay for good. “I love this club and if everything was the same and it was up to me, I’d be here forever,” Duncan said. “I love this club but I feel like at the moment it’s time for football and all that stuff can come later.” Loading Wighton will don headgear on Saturday after suffering a split ear against Cronulla on Sunday, adding that necessary accessory to the cast he is wearing on his right arm after surgery earlier this year. Front-rower Keaon Koloamatangi left training early on Wednesday with an apparent hip complaint, but teammates downplayed concern over his fitness.



There is less confidence about Mitchell’s recovery from a complex nerve damage that threatens to end the 29-year-old’s season. He has trained separately from the rest of the squad in recent weeks, including running laps of their Heffron Park headquarters, but was not seen at their session on Wednesday. “We are not sure as players,” five-eighth Cody Walker said when asked when Mitchell might be back. Souths five-eighth Cody Walker speaks to reporters ahead of Indigenous Round. Sitthixay Ditthavong “But I’m sure the medical staff have a really good plan in place to hopefully see him play at the back end of the year.”



Mitchell hasn’t played since round 11 in mid-May as a result of back and calf injuries and the emergence of a nerve issue which he has consulted a neurologist about. “He’s a superstar of the game,” Walker said of Mitchell. “[But] I do believe that we have the players in place to be able to still compete at a high level and win games.” While Mitchell will sit out again on Saturday, his Winmarra Foundation is displayed on the back of Souths’ Indigenous Round jersey.
