World.title: Mental health overhaul as government accepts Bondi stabbing inquest recommendations
World.content:
The NSW government will overhaul its response to mental health emergencies and strengthen support for those with complex mental illnesses after it backed all recommendations from the coronial inquest into the Bondi Junction Westfield stabbing attack. The Minns government announced on Wednesday it had accepted 11 of the 13 recommendations from the coroner in full. It offered in-principle support to the remaining two, including the provision of specialised mental health accommodation. The Minns government has backed all recommendations from the coronial inquest into the Bondi Junction stabbing attack. Dion Georgopoulos Queenslander Joel Cauchi, 40, was shot dead by NSW Police Inspector Amy Scott after he stabbed 16 people at Bondi Junction Westfield on the afternoon of April 13, 2024. Six people died of their injuries: Dawn Singleton, 25; Ashlee Good, 38; Jade Young, 47; Cheng Yixuan, 27; Pikria Darchia, 55; and Faraz Tahir, 30. A further 10 people were injured but survived.



Related Article Updated

Bondi Junction attack ‘A vast and permanent space’: Grieving families speak after Bondi stabbing inquest findings NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said the mental health reforms would “help people access the right care at the right time”. “The government’s response continues our work to strengthen mental health services, improve access to care, and ensure people with severe and complex mental illness receive the support they need earlier and closer to home,” he said. The inquest into the Bondi Junction Westfield stabbing attack urged the government to house and care for the mentally unwell, referred the killer’s psychiatrist to the watchdog over treatment “failures”, and recommended bravery awards for the heroism displayed by police, victims and witnesses to the tragedy. “His attacks were a quintessential example of an active armed offender – rapid, unpredictable and fatal within a very short period of time,” NSW Coroner Teresa O’Sullivan said, handing down her findings, with 23 recommendations, in February.



The families of those who died spoke outside the Coroners Court in Sydney of the voids that remained in their lives, while experts called for urgent changes to care and support for people with mental illness. The government stopped short of adopting a recommendation that proposed specialised short-term accommodation for those confronting mental health issues and homelessness, opting for an alternative approach to boosting housing support involving the agencies Homes NSW and NSW Health. CCTV footage of Cauchi (right) at Westfield Bondi Junction. A recommendation to make permanent the state’s “wanding” trial – allowing police special powers to search for knives and other weapons at shopping centres, transport hubs and sports grounds – was embraced by the government. It echoed the results of a statutory review into the powers, granted through legislation, that passed parliament two months after the attack. The government declined to fully endorse the inquest’s recommendations regarding a review of the NSW Ambulance’s major incident response plan. The coroner had called for the review to consider command structure within NSW Ambulance, and the adequacy of training structures for senior members of the force. However, the government said the review was already in its final stages.



Among the other coronial recommendations accepted by the government were a public safety campaign to educate those in the retail sector, including centre owners, operators and staff about how to prepare for, and respond to, future incidents. Measures to improve emergency service interoperability, communications and training, were also accepted. More to come. World.title: Forrestania clocks 131% WA gold resource uplift, haulage underway
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Forrestania clocks 131% WA gold resource uplift, haulage underway Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 5, 2026 — 2:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Forrestania Resources has more than doubled the gold inventory at its British Hill deposit in Western Australia, delivering a massive 131 per cent increase to the project’s mineral resource estimate, which now stands at 126,290 ounces. The Perth-based gold developer tabled a JORC-compliant resource of 2.62 million tonnes grading a solid 1.50 grams per tonne (g/t) gold. Notably, the company has also dramatically de-risked the project by delivering a whopping 180 per cent increase in the higher-confidence indicated resource category. That portion now makes up the lion’s share of the resource, weighing in at 1.88 million tonnes at 1.43g/t gold for 86,080 ounces. Forrestania Resources has three RC rigs operating at its British Hill gold project in Western Australia. The upgrade was underpinned by recent drilling that included a suite of high-grade hits such as 1 metre at an impressive 22.98g/t gold, 4 metres at 7.46g/t gold from 124m and a shallow intercept of 7 metres at 5.69g/t gold from surface. Forrestania is already trucking gold ore sourced from British Hill to its recently acquired and soon-to-be-refurbished Lake Johnston processing facility, 185 kilometres southwest of Kalgoorlie. The company says the recent exploration success has given it the confidence to keep the drill rods turning, with three reverse-circulation rigs on site furiously drilling as part of an approved 100-hole program to expand the resource further, both along strike and down-dip.



‘We believe there remains significant opportunity to further expand the resource base and enhance project economics.’ Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty The latest resource upgrade slots neatly into Forrestania’s aggressive regional consolidation strategy, which has seen it transform from a grassroots explorer into an emerging producer in less than a year. Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty said: “British Hill continues to expand, with a more than doubling of the previous Mineral Resource Estimate and a material increase in the proportion of higher-confidence Indicated Resources. The combination of resource growth, ongoing drilling success and excellent regional infrastructure positions British Hill as a key asset within our broader Forrestania gold strategy.” The centrepiece of Forrestania’s strategy is a classic hub-and-spoke model, with the company’s game-changing acquisition of the Edna May gold project from Ramelius Resources delivering a 2.9-million-tonne-per-annum processing plant to serve as a central hub. Operationally, Edna May complements the company’s existing Lake Johnston processing plant, where major refurbishment works are already well advanced. Once both are fully operational the company will control a formidable, combined processing capacity exceeding six million tonnes of ore per annum by early 2027.



Forrestania’s now holds a large strategic footprint comprising a dominant 623-square-kilometre contiguous tenure package adjacent to the historic one-million-ounce Bounty gold mine. This forms a key part of a broader 1000-square-kilometre statewide portfolio, with active projects located near the major mining hubs of Coolgardie and Menzies. To bankroll its ambitions, Forrestania recently locked away a massive $310 million in fresh equity through a heavily backed, institutional share placement, issuing shares at 40 cents apiece. The raise allowed it to complete the acquisition of the Edna May plant from Ramelius and will also fund its refurbishment. Over the past year, Forrestania has been on an acquisition blitz, snapping up stranded gold assets across WA’s premier goldfields. Its buying spree included a $58.9 million takeover of Kula Gold to secure the high-grade Mt Palmer project, a $24 million acquisition of Newcam Minerals’ Southern Cross assets and a $93.5 million merger with Zenith Minerals, building a total resource base approaching 2 million ounces. For an explorer, having a clear pathway to monetise a discovery is the goal. And with high-grade ore from multiple projects such as British Hill now feeding a growing network of processing plants, Forrestania appears to have exactly that. The company has pieced together a compelling regional production story in breathtakingly short order leaving its junior explorer days firmly in the rear-view mirror. With drill rods turning, ore already on the move and a war chest to fund its two-hub strategy, Forrestania would seem to have all the pieces in place to become WA’s next significant gold producer. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Judge makes non-publication order as complainant’s cross-examination continues in alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the third day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

This week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex has heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney on Wednesday. Audrey Richardson

The man, now in his early 40s, gave evidence that Jones also groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. On Tuesday, “J” told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

“I just want justice for what happened; that’s why I’m here,” he said. “I’m here because it’s the right thing to do and people need me, people need me to do this.”

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box. He will face further cross-examination by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, which started on Tuesday afternoon.

Bashir has asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020 and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to Judge Glenn Walsh.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Why I was locked in a bar on top of the world for 24 hours
World.content:
NationalCensus Opinion Why I was locked in a bar on top of the world for 24 hours Nick Dalziel Contributor August 5, 2026 — 3:00pm

August 5, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In recent days, you will have received an email or a letter from the Australian Bureau of Statistics with instructions on how to complete the 2026 census. Most of us will fill in the online form on August 11. It should be 20 minutes of inconvenience to be counted and avoid a fine. But until I spent a census day locked inside a hostel in La Paz, Bolivia, I’d never considered how convenient our census actually is. How do you count a population without a functioning postal service, or universal access to the internet? La Paz, Bolivia is the world’s highest capital city at 3650 metres. Getty Images La Paz is dirty, hilly and vibrant. It’s hard to breathe between the 3650-metre altitude and 1990s engine emissions on the city’s chaotic streets. But I loved it. Here is a country that’s rejected a lot of Western norms. You won’t find a McDonald’s here – the multinational tried and failed. Bolivians would much rather support a local street food vendor or “casera” trying to support their family. (It is possible, Northcote!)



Like many tourists, and even the ones who call themselves “travellers”, I was largely unaware of the daily happenings in a country where I’d only spent a week, taking each day as it came. Book a hostel a week out? Nah, that’s too rigid. But staff at the Wild Rover Hostel were imploring us to extend our bookings for March 23, 2004. I heeded. At least there was a bar: Nick Dalziel, right, locked down in Bolivia during the country’s census. From midnight, the doors were locked. Nobody, not even workers, could leave. Bolivia was taking stock of its population for the first time in 12 years, or 23 years, depending on who you asked. Myself, my hostel companions and the entirety of the 11,365,333 people in Bolivia were required to stay in the one place from midnight to midnight so they could be counted. The only exception: a medical emergency. Anyone spotted on the streets on this day would be rounded up and counted among the prison population.



Reply-paid envelopes are out of the question in a country without a functioning postal service, as is the idea that everyone can go online. Instead, 860,000 volunteer census collectors spent the day going door-to-door, counting the number of people in each of Bolivia’s 4 million households. Related Article Bolivia A gringo's trip to hell The census came about after years of protests demanding one, and people I spoke to were passionate about complying. Local governments urged Bolivians to stay home because the more people counted in an area, the greater the share of resources and political representation. Staying home was the thing to do for your region. The hostel shut its doors to the outside world for a day, with employees sleeping on the floor in the reception area. Meanwhile, guests and staff had a fiesta on a beautiful but eerily quiet March afternoon. We had a barbecue and played beer pong with plenty of local lagers. And then, at midnight, the doors were unlocked. Everyone had been counted. Life could resume. In the days that followed I heard stories of travellers getting stranded in all sorts of bizarre places, many without proper preparation or anything to eat. A full day locked in whatever room or broom cupboard or hovel they’d managed to find the night before. By sheer luck, I had been given the opportunity to stay longer in my dorm bed.



And if comparatively privileged travellers were hard done by, think about the locals what they sacrificed for census day. It evoked memories of pandemic lockdowns and the terrible situations many found themselves in: unable to travel to provide care, or stuck inside in cramped home or a dangerous domestic situation. A day of lost income is also a lot less easily absorbed in Bolivia. However, I was inspired by the dedication of the census volunteers who wanted the best for their local communities. Related Article Census From deadline to details: The six things you need to know to handle the census I’ll think about this on our own census night and the effort we take to ensure nobody is missed. There’ll be plenty of ABS staff who travel to remote locations and who head out to count those without a roof over their heads. Grumble you may, that you’re forced to log in or fill out a form for everyone in your dwelling on the night of Tuesday, August 11. But unlike Bolivia, most Australians have it pretty easy when it comes to counting population. Compared to a full day of lockdown, 20 minutes on the couch is more than manageable. Nick Dalziel is a communications manager and writer from Melbourne. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

But with Duncan likely to be heavily pursued by rival teams if he does not re-sign before the November 1 transfer window, Wighton says Souths are right to put the rising back-rower at the top of their list.



“He’s the club’s future,” the 33-year-old centre said on Wednesday. “He’s probably the club’s next captain if you ask me. He’s a great role model, he’s a great leader, and he does that with his actions and being upfront. “The club would be foolish if they didn’t prioritise him … he’d be first off the rank if it was me running the club. I think they’re definitely going down the right lines there. As I said, I can see him as the next captain of this whole club.” South Sydney veteran Jack Wighton. Sitthixay Ditthavong Souths will also be bolstered by the inclusion of their captain, Cameron Murray, for the Indigenous Round match against the Eels following a calf strain, as well as Fifita, who is back from suspension. Demonstrating his versatility, Duncan has for the sixth time in his last seven games been named in the centres, where he has prospered in the absence of Mitchell.



A member of Souths’ strong Indigenous contingent from the Wonnarua tribe in the Hunter Valley, Duncan said he was focused on helping the seventh-placed Rabbitohs make the finals for the first time since 2022 but would love to stay for good. “I love this club and if everything was the same and it was up to me, I’d be here forever,” Duncan said. “I love this club but I feel like at the moment it’s time for football and all that stuff can come later.” Loading Wighton will don headgear on Saturday after suffering a split ear against Cronulla on Sunday, adding that necessary accessory to the cast he is wearing on his right arm after surgery earlier this year. Front-rower Keaon Koloamatangi left training early on Wednesday with an apparent hip complaint, but teammates downplayed concern over his fitness.



There is less confidence about Mitchell’s recovery from a complex nerve damage that threatens to end the 29-year-old’s season. He has trained separately from the rest of the squad in recent weeks, including running laps of their Heffron Park headquarters, but was not seen at their session on Wednesday. “We are not sure as players,” five-eighth Cody Walker said when asked when Mitchell might be back. Souths five-eighth Cody Walker speaks to reporters ahead of Indigenous Round. Sitthixay Ditthavong “But I’m sure the medical staff have a really good plan in place to hopefully see him play at the back end of the year.”



Mitchell hasn’t played since round 11 in mid-May as a result of back and calf injuries and the emergence of a nerve issue which he has consulted a neurologist about. “He’s a superstar of the game,” Walker said of Mitchell. “[But] I do believe that we have the players in place to be able to still compete at a high level and win games.” While Mitchell will sit out again on Saturday, his Winmarra Foundation is displayed on the back of Souths’ Indigenous Round jersey. World.title: Mental health overhaul as government accepts Bondi stabbing inquest recommendations
World.content:
The NSW government will overhaul its response to mental health emergencies and strengthen support for those with complex mental illnesses after it backed all recommendations from the coronial inquest into the Bondi Junction Westfield stabbing attack. The Minns government announced on Wednesday it had accepted 11 of the 13 recommendations from the coroner in full. It offered in-principle support to the remaining two, including the provision of specialised mental health accommodation. The Minns government has backed all recommendations from the coronial inquest into the Bondi Junction stabbing attack. Dion Georgopoulos Queenslander Joel Cauchi, 40, was shot dead by NSW Police Inspector Amy Scott after he stabbed 16 people at Bondi Junction Westfield on the afternoon of April 13, 2024. Six people died of their injuries: Dawn Singleton, 25; Ashlee Good, 38; Jade Young, 47; Cheng Yixuan, 27; Pikria Darchia, 55; and Faraz Tahir, 30. A further 10 people were injured but survived.



Related Article Updated

Bondi Junction attack ‘A vast and permanent space’: Grieving families speak after Bondi stabbing inquest findings NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said the mental health reforms would “help people access the right care at the right time”. “The government’s response continues our work to strengthen mental health services, improve access to care, and ensure people with severe and complex mental illness receive the support they need earlier and closer to home,” he said. The inquest into the Bondi Junction Westfield stabbing attack urged the government to house and care for the mentally unwell, referred the killer’s psychiatrist to the watchdog over treatment “failures”, and recommended bravery awards for the heroism displayed by police, victims and witnesses to the tragedy. “His attacks were a quintessential example of an active armed offender – rapid, unpredictable and fatal within a very short period of time,” NSW Coroner Teresa O’Sullivan said, handing down her findings, with 23 recommendations, in February.



The families of those who died spoke outside the Coroners Court in Sydney of the voids that remained in their lives, while experts called for urgent changes to care and support for people with mental illness. The government stopped short of adopting a recommendation that proposed specialised short-term accommodation for those confronting mental health issues and homelessness, opting for an alternative approach to boosting housing support involving the agencies Homes NSW and NSW Health. CCTV footage of Cauchi (right) at Westfield Bondi Junction. A recommendation to make permanent the state’s “wanding” trial – allowing police special powers to search for knives and other weapons at shopping centres, transport hubs and sports grounds – was embraced by the government. It echoed the results of a statutory review into the powers, granted through legislation, that passed parliament two months after the attack. The government declined to fully endorse the inquest’s recommendations regarding a review of the NSW Ambulance’s major incident response plan. The coroner had called for the review to consider command structure within NSW Ambulance, and the adequacy of training structures for senior members of the force. However, the government said the review was already in its final stages.



Among the other coronial recommendations accepted by the government were a public safety campaign to educate those in the retail sector, including centre owners, operators and staff about how to prepare for, and respond to, future incidents. Measures to improve emergency service interoperability, communications and training, were also accepted. More to come. World.title: Forrestania clocks 131% WA gold resource uplift, haulage underway
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Forrestania clocks 131% WA gold resource uplift, haulage underway Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 5, 2026 — 2:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Forrestania Resources has more than doubled the gold inventory at its British Hill deposit in Western Australia, delivering a massive 131 per cent increase to the project’s mineral resource estimate, which now stands at 126,290 ounces. The Perth-based gold developer tabled a JORC-compliant resource of 2.62 million tonnes grading a solid 1.50 grams per tonne (g/t) gold. Notably, the company has also dramatically de-risked the project by delivering a whopping 180 per cent increase in the higher-confidence indicated resource category. That portion now makes up the lion’s share of the resource, weighing in at 1.88 million tonnes at 1.43g/t gold for 86,080 ounces. Forrestania Resources has three RC rigs operating at its British Hill gold project in Western Australia. The upgrade was underpinned by recent drilling that included a suite of high-grade hits such as 1 metre at an impressive 22.98g/t gold, 4 metres at 7.46g/t gold from 124m and a shallow intercept of 7 metres at 5.69g/t gold from surface. Forrestania is already trucking gold ore sourced from British Hill to its recently acquired and soon-to-be-refurbished Lake Johnston processing facility, 185 kilometres southwest of Kalgoorlie. The company says the recent exploration success has given it the confidence to keep the drill rods turning, with three reverse-circulation rigs on site furiously drilling as part of an approved 100-hole program to expand the resource further, both along strike and down-dip.



‘We believe there remains significant opportunity to further expand the resource base and enhance project economics.’ Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty The latest resource upgrade slots neatly into Forrestania’s aggressive regional consolidation strategy, which has seen it transform from a grassroots explorer into an emerging producer in less than a year. Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty said: “British Hill continues to expand, with a more than doubling of the previous Mineral Resource Estimate and a material increase in the proportion of higher-confidence Indicated Resources. The combination of resource growth, ongoing drilling success and excellent regional infrastructure positions British Hill as a key asset within our broader Forrestania gold strategy.” The centrepiece of Forrestania’s strategy is a classic hub-and-spoke model, with the company’s game-changing acquisition of the Edna May gold project from Ramelius Resources delivering a 2.9-million-tonne-per-annum processing plant to serve as a central hub. Operationally, Edna May complements the company’s existing Lake Johnston processing plant, where major refurbishment works are already well advanced. Once both are fully operational the company will control a formidable, combined processing capacity exceeding six million tonnes of ore per annum by early 2027.



Forrestania’s now holds a large strategic footprint comprising a dominant 623-square-kilometre contiguous tenure package adjacent to the historic one-million-ounce Bounty gold mine. This forms a key part of a broader 1000-square-kilometre statewide portfolio, with active projects located near the major mining hubs of Coolgardie and Menzies. To bankroll its ambitions, Forrestania recently locked away a massive $310 million in fresh equity through a heavily backed, institutional share placement, issuing shares at 40 cents apiece. The raise allowed it to complete the acquisition of the Edna May plant from Ramelius and will also fund its refurbishment. Over the past year, Forrestania has been on an acquisition blitz, snapping up stranded gold assets across WA’s premier goldfields. Its buying spree included a $58.9 million takeover of Kula Gold to secure the high-grade Mt Palmer project, a $24 million acquisition of Newcam Minerals’ Southern Cross assets and a $93.5 million merger with Zenith Minerals, building a total resource base approaching 2 million ounces. For an explorer, having a clear pathway to monetise a discovery is the goal. And with high-grade ore from multiple projects such as British Hill now feeding a growing network of processing plants, Forrestania appears to have exactly that. The company has pieced together a compelling regional production story in breathtakingly short order leaving its junior explorer days firmly in the rear-view mirror. With drill rods turning, ore already on the move and a war chest to fund its two-hub strategy, Forrestania would seem to have all the pieces in place to become WA’s next significant gold producer. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Judge makes non-publication order as complainant’s cross-examination continues in alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the third day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

This week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex has heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney on Wednesday. Audrey Richardson

The man, now in his early 40s, gave evidence that Jones also groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. On Tuesday, “J” told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

“I just want justice for what happened; that’s why I’m here,” he said. “I’m here because it’s the right thing to do and people need me, people need me to do this.”

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box. He will face further cross-examination by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, which started on Tuesday afternoon.

Bashir has asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020 and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to Judge Glenn Walsh.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan grills Winston Peters on 'racist' comments that were directed at him
World.content:
The Green MP who Winston Peters told to "go back to your own country" has challenged the Foreign Minister in Parliament over his comments.

Peters says his comments were not racist, and he disagrees with the prime minister's statement condemning them.

The MP, Lawrence Xu-Nan, tried about a dozen times to pin Peters down.

The pair clashed repeatedly, with Peters using Parliament's rules to avoid answering directly whether he stood by his previous comments and Parliament's Speaker Gerry Brownlee stepping in to require Peters to answer.

In the end, on the interpretation taken by Brownlee, it seems a misquote on the Green MP's part may have let Peters avoid reopening the wound.

Peters last week during a general debate speech had responded to heckling from Lawrence Xu-Nan by saying "go back to your own country ... that's where they lie like a flatfish, but they don't lie like that here, all right?"

"This is called a democracy, unlike what you're used to," Peters said.

Xu-Nan grilled Peters during Question Time on Wednesday to ask whether he stood by his statements.

"I stand by all of my statements as Minister of Foreign Affairs including those made during two visits this term to China and my numerous engagements with my Chinese counterpart," Peters responded.

Xu-Nan repeatedly put Peters own comments to him directly, but Peters repeatedly quibbled that Xu-Nan's questions to him were about his comments made as leader of the party.

"If the member would like to question my statements made as leader of the New Zealand First party, he should understand the correct place to do that is during the general debate, not during oral questions," Peters claimed.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins challenged this, saying that when a minister was making a statement relevant to a portfolio they hold, "they cannot be doing that as a party leader ... the key point here is, is it portfolio related".

"Him saying that 'I made that statement in the general debate as New Zealand First leader' cannot be allowed to stand ... when he is in this House, he is the Minister of Foreign Affairs."

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Peters and Seymour both raised points of order challenging that, Seymour pointing out that Hipkins had earlier challenged Prime Minister Christopher Luxon for using the defence force plane to fly home after a National Party event by claiming he was not acting as prime minister at the time.

Speaker of the House Gerry Brownlee said he did not have the previous rulings to hand about the matter, but it would be dealt with "at some point".

Xu-Nan asked if Peters agreed with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon that he had a "long track record of inappropriate attention-seeking comments designed to get the media and other politicians to talk about him instead of the issues Kiwis are facing".

Peters said the answer was "undoubtedly no", before also rejecting the suggestion his comments from last week had been racist.

He tried to refer to comments previously made by other MPs, but Brownlee disallowed it.

Peters eventually said what he agreed with was that "somebody who's been in this Parliament five minutes has wasted so much of Parliament's time".

Brownlee said that answer "doesn't help the order of the House" and his answer "doesn't need to be an insult to someone duly elected to the Parliament".

Xu-Nan tried again, but Peters again claimed the phrasing and forum was not correct.

Green MP Ricardo Menendez March challenged that with the Speaker, but Brownlee was having none of it.

"I know what the statement was, I know it very well, I've spent quite a bit of time on it ... it wasn't accurately given. Words matter."

When Labour's Kieran McAnulty raised a point of order about Peters' comments about Xu-Nan, Brownlee said he had given Xu-Nan licence to ask more questions, and people could "draw their own conclusions about what's happening here".

He did not think it appropriate at the time to have the person being questioned removed from the House.

However, he said he would review the Hansard - the official record of Parliament - and stood by his view that all members of Parliament "regardless of how long they've been here, are elected equally".

Xu-Nan was born in China, but migrated to New Zealand as a child and is a citizen.

The Chinese Embassy criticised Peters' comments, saying it had made "solemn representations" to the Foreign Ministry over the "negative" remarks.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon himself criticised the comments as racist, but has refused calls to sack Peters as Foreign Minister.

World.title: The House: Responses and responsible government
World.content:
All the most overdue responses to Parliament's official Written Questions are addressed to the one MP responsible for ensuring prompt answers, and for enabling a responsible government - the Speaker of the House Gerry Brownlee.

The Speaker is the head of New Zealand's legislature, the equivalent to the Prime Minister (head of the executive) and the Chief Justice (head of the judiciary). The legislature is sovereign - the most powerful of the three branches of government.

As the head of the legislature, the Speaker interprets and enforces Parliament's rules, and must also protect its 'rights and privileges', including its constitutional role in responsible government.

Responses and responsibility The House Download MP3 4m

Responsible government is not about governments acting responsibly. It means that governments are genuinely responsible to (must answer to) Parliament.

Governments are meant to be kept in check by Parliament, which includes the opposition (who are most likely to question actions, and least likely to be cowed).

In the House, true responsible government would include ministers honestly answering questions in Question Time. In Select Committees it would include ministers and officials honestly answering questions. And in the quieter Written Questions, it would mean ministers honestly answering questions.

Other than voters, only the Speaker can judge whether the government and its ministers are playing ball or dodging their constitutional expectations. Only the Speaker can pressure ministers to answer.

Each speaker has a different idea of what is required in this aspect of their role. The key sentence in the rules says: "Content of replies (1) an answer should seek to address the question…". Some speakers have focussed on the word "answer", others on the word "address".

If a government can avoid oversight, then Parliament is not really sovereign. The fewer questions ministers answer, the less responsible governments could be said to be.

While ministers in various governments often manage to dodge giving answers in Question Time most ministers make a better fist of answering Written Questions, which are asked in their thousands and must be answered within six working days. All the questions and some of the answers can be read on the Parliament website.

Just as with Question Time in the House, the person with the responsibility for enforcing the six-day rule for answers (and their quality), is the Speaker.

While speakers cannot be asked questions in the House, "written questions may be put to the Speaker relating to any matter of administration for which the Speaker is responsible". These are necessary because speakers' responsibilities go beyond managing the House to include Parliament's buildings, the Office of the Clerk, Parliamentary Service, committees they chair, and the three Officers of Parliament. This also gives Speakers the chance to set an example for the other ministers.

Not every Written Question on the Parliament website that is due an answer has received an answer. Some questions have missed the six working day deadline, a few have missed it by months.

For those keeping score at home - ministers with multiple answers a month or more overdue are:

David Seymour (as Deputy PM, and Assoc. Justice) with 90 unanswered written questions.

Simeon Brown (Health) with 16 unanswered written questions.

Chris Bishop (Transport) with 15 unanswered written questions.

Gerry Brownlee (Speaker) with 33 unanswered written questions including every question more than seven months overdue.

World.title: Christopher Luxon defends using Air Force flight after attending National Party fundraiser
World.content:
Christopher Luxon is defending his use of an Air Force flight after attending a National Party fundraiser, saying he has a "busy job" and "full schedule".

Labour on Wednesday accused the prime minister of using the Defence Force as a "personal taxi service" for campaigning purposes.

Luxon flew from Whanganui to Auckland on a six-seater NZDF King Air plane on the evening of 23 July after attending a National Party fundraising dinner.

Speaking to reporters at Parliament, Luxon said he needed to get back to Auckland for a meeting the next morning and no Air New Zealand or Jetstar flights were available.

He said he had brought the meeting forward to 7am that he could also attend the funeral of former National MP Bill Birch that day.

"I needed to get back to that meeting... I couldn't catch a commercial flight to get there after a full day in Feilding and Whanganui," he said.

"Those planes need to be flying, and the pilots need the hours and the training anyway. It's not costing the taxpayer any additional money."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said Luxon could have easily skipped the National fundraisier and caught an earlier commercial flight from Whanganui in order to make the next meeting.

He said instead Luxon appeared to be using the Defence Force like a "personal taxi service".

"It's absolutely unjustifiable. Attending a party fundraising event is a bright line," he said. "Air force planes should not be used to support that."

Hipkins said only a select group of people, including the prime minister, had access to those planes.

"It's really important for the political neutrality of the Defence Force that they are not used by those people for campaigning purposes."

Luxon has come under pressure in the past week over his use of NZDF flights. Previous prime ministers also made use of such facilities, though Hipkins argued that was never for party purposes.

Luxon said his job as prime minister was a busy one and so he used military assets "if and when it's appropriate".

"It's an extreme job. It has a lot of commitments. They're long hours. Commercial flights don't always work from different parts of New Zealand.

World.title: Justice Ministry to be reviewed, as minister's confidence in agency 'seriously shaken'
World.content:
The Minister of Justice has ordered a rapid review of his ministry following its handling of a former employee, saying his confidence in the agency has been "seriously shaken."

Paul Goldsmith said paying somebody for five years without working "cannot be justified", and he's "seriously concerned" about how it occurred.

Goldsmith, who is also the public service minister, has instructed all chief executives in the public service be given strong guidance for managing employment cases that involve criminal proceedings.

He said the issue was mishandled consistently for five years.

"We only found out about this entire episode because my office asked. My confidence in the Ministry has been seriously shaken by this," said Goldsmith in a statement.

The former Lotto presenter Russell Harrison had been arrested in June 2021 as part of a global FBI sting targeting organised crime and was granted interim name suppression.

He began working at the Ministry of Justice as a kaiārahi - Family Court navigator in 2021 when he was suspended on full pay.

Goldsmith explained he had started going through the recruitment process when the ministry received his police vetting form, which showed he had criminal charges pending, and was put on suspension.

He continued to receive his taxpayer funded salary for five years, before pleading guilty to a charge of money laundering early last month. His employment was then terminated.

"He was a lotto presenter, and he's made a fool out of the Ministry of Justice, and he probably thought that he had won the lotto," said Goldsmith.

It's not clear yet how much Harrison was paid out in total, but Goldsmith said it was "well over half a million dollars."

"It is far too much, and it is very very poor use of public money and we expect a lot better."

Goldsmith has called it "utterly unacceptable", and said New Zealanders expect the public service to be able to work their way through difficult employment matters as business owners across the country do every day.

He said he'd received an apology from the Justice Secretary Andrew Kibblewhite, but his confidence has been "seriously shaken."

In his capacity as Minister of Justice, he's directed the Public Service Commission to undertake a rapid review of the Ministry of Justice.

It would be part of a review of the ministry's overall operations and performance and be conducted by Debbie Francis and Steve Haszard.

Sir Brian Roche has been told to ensure all public service chief executives set out clear guidelines for managing employment cases that involve criminal proceedings. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In his capacity as Minister for the Public Service, he's instructed Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche to write to all chief executives, "setting out strong guidance for managing employment cases that involve criminal proceedings."

He wasn't aware of any other cases "as egregious" as this, but said "we need to ensure there are processes firmly in place to stop this from happening again."

Goldsmith said he'd be updated on both matters regularly, and expected the review to take four to six weeks.

"I recognise that chief executives must manage these matters in accordance with fair employment processes, however, that doesn't mean passive management."

"Where an employee is on pay and not working, I expect agencies to manage the matter actively, make timely decisions, and keep the interests of taxpayers firmly in view.

"Paying somebody for five years for not working cannot be justified," Goldsmith said.

Speaking to reporters later on Wednesday afternoon, Goldsmith said "we're obviously very angry about the revelations."

He confirmed the ministry recently received advice it could have removed Harrison as an employee earlier, but "they got it wrong."

"They went on misguided advice right through the five years, thinking that they couldn't get out of this."

It was only after Goldsmith's office made inquiries that the ministry looked into it "in some detail" and concluded they got it wrong, he said.

"He was put on suspension at the time," but the recent advice showed his employment could have been terminated at that point.

"How they didn't come to review that over the last five years is inexplicable, and that is why my confidence has been shaken."

He also explained the criminal record check and police vetting hadn't been received by the ministry until after Harrison started working there, but Goldsmith said that often happens.

He said the job offer is subject to the successful passing of those vettings, and that's "where the opportunity was."

"They didn't take it, and it has been - frankly - a comedy of errors over five years."

He doesn't know how widespread the practice was, of allowing people to start work ahead of vetting, but expected everybody to have full vetting in place before "they're in front of vulnerable people."

Goldsmith said he was not defending it in "any way, shape, or form."

In terms of Sir Brian's instructions, Goldsmith said the primary point he would make was that he expects if anything like this happens for more than two months, the Public Service Commissioner expected this to be elevated to senior management and dealt with in a "timely manner."

World.title: What the latest unemployment figures could mean for the election
World.content:
The release of the second quarter unemployment figures has seen political parties come out and make their election pitches.

The latest unemployment figures have seen Nicola Willis wear two different hats, releasing one response as finance minister, and another response as the National Party's finance spokesperson.

Wednesday morning's release by StatsNZ has shown unemployment rose to its highest level in nearly 11 years in the second quarter, going from 5.4 percent to 5.6 percent.

A total of 171,000 people were unemployed, a rise of 7,000 on the previous quarter and 13,000 higher than a year ago.

Speaking as finance minister, Nicola Willis said the statistics already confirmed what many New Zealanders already knew: that the second quarter was tough.

"This is exactly why our focus is on the policies that boost our economy and build business confidence, because confident businesses are the ones who hire people and grow their operations - and it's encouraging to see recent jumps in business confidence and hiring intentions," she said.

Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds says the unemployment figures were a damning verdict on Christopher Luxon's economic management. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Willis said there was more to do, which was why the government was backing tourism and international education, fast-tracking major construction projects, investing in infrastructure, and promoting its Investment Boost scheme.

Then, a short time later, in a follow-up press release as National's finance spokesperson, Willis put the boot into the opposition.

"Labour's response to all of this ranges from ambivalent to outright opposition. They can't credibly say jobs are their priority while working against the very policies driving job creation," she said.

"Then there's the tax question. Labour and its coalition partners want to load businesses up with a suite of new taxes at precisely the moment employer confidence needs protecting, not undermining."

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick says cut after cut does not grow the economy. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said the unemployment figures were a damning verdict on Christopher Luxon's economic management.

"Christopher Luxon promised he would grow the economy, create jobs, and lower the cost of living. Instead, unemployment continues to rise and Kiwis are paying the price," she said.

"Behind every unemployment statistic is a person who wants to work, a family worried about paying the bills, and a community feeling the impact. That's the real cost of National's economic choices."

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters says the rise in unemployment is directly attributable to the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said Luxon would blame the last government while taking on more debt, in order to fund tax breaks that disproportionately benefited the wealthiest.

"Political tit for tat aside, it's time for the Prime Minister to put his hands back on the wheel of this economy and invest in our country. Clearly, cut after cut doesn't grow an economy. It breaks one," Swarbrick said.

"Building a thriving economy means supporting the little guy, not patronising them as your government cuts local jobs and infrastructure investment then consolidates contracts to give them to multi-national corporations. These are political decisions, not inevitabilities."

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said the rise was directly attributable to the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, and the resulting increase to fuel costs.

"We said at the start of this conflict that this would severely impact both inflation and unemployment. This is more evidence of the need for New Zealand to find and own our own oil and gas that we hold in our deep-sea basins," he said, pointing to his party's policy to invest in surveying the country's offshore basins for oil and gas.

ACT leader David Seymour also looked to overseas events, and said the country was in a long, hard fight for recovery.

He said there were multiple factors at play, and it showed the importance of maintaining discipline on spending.

"A lot of the current economic pain has been caused by the fact that if you nearly double the oil price in a month, then that's going to suck a whole lot of cash out of people's wallets. They leave that at the petrol station, they can't spend it elsewhere. That's got to hurt."

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi said the unemployment rates was "unacceptably high," and Māori, Pasifika, and rangatahi were feeling it the hardest.

"No wonder our children are leaving for Melbourne, Paris, London, Washington. Obviously, this government is doing a really, really bad job at moving the economy and ensuring there are jobs here for our people to have."

Midday Report Essentials for Wednesday 5 August Midday Report Download MP3 21m

Meanwhile, Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said the economy was creating jobs, but not fast enough to reduce unemployment.

Another 13,000 people found work during the quarter, but that wasn't enough, he said.

The jobless rate increased because more people entered the workforce, including some who had not previously been seeking employment.

World.title: Netball NZ in talks with private investor over new league for 2028
World.content:
Netball New Zealand is in talks with at least one private investor about establishing a new franchise league in 2028, in what would be a significant shake-up of the elite domestic game.

RNZ understands the national body is exploring a private ownership model for the ANZ Premiership, as part of efforts to secure the long-term future of the game.

A source with knowledge of the talks told RNZ "a high net-worth family" with sporting links has held discussions with Netball NZ about taking over the licence to run the league. It is believed Silver Ferns greats Adine Wilson and Anna Stanley were involved in bringing the investor to the table.

Details of the proposal remain closely guarded, with both parties understood to have signed non-disclosure agreements while due diligence is carried out.

However, it is understood the model being explored would see the competition run independently of Netball NZ, with private ownership taking responsibility for the league's commercial and operational arrangements.

Netball NZ officials, including chairman Alastair Carruthers and interim chief executive Jane Patterson, were unavailable for comment on Wednesday. Both are travelling home from the United Kingdom following the Silver Ferns' gold medal-winning campaign at the Commonwealth Games.

However, addressing speculation about the future of the domestic competition last month, Carruthers acknowledged private investment was "an area the board is very interested in".

"It's not an obvious possibility for 2027, but I think all forms of investment into our league has to be looked at," he said.

The Silver Ferns' stunning win over Jamaica in Monday's gold medal match at the Commonwealth Games underlined the strength in the game in New Zealand. www.photosport.nz

The news Netball NZ officials are engaging in talks with private investors is a hopeful sign amid increasing concerns over the future of the domestic game.

Without a broadcast deal in place for 2027, the national body is yet to commit to running a competition next season as it faces losses of up to $6 million for the financial year - about $3.7m of which can be chalked up to the cost of running the ANZ Premiership this year.

The financial strain has fuelled questions over whether the current model is sustainable, with at least some form of privatisation increasingly seen as the only way forward.

New Zealand Netball Players' Association boss Pippa Moore said the athlete body are open to considering significant changes if they helped secure the future of the domestic game.

"We are open to considering all credible options, including private investment, that can better unlock netball's commercial value," Moore said in a statement.

"Any future model must provide a strong domestic competition, meaningful professional opportunities for New Zealand players, and a clear pathway that ensures future generations can aspire to play at the highest level."

But with the privately backed proposal understood to target a 2028 launch, it leaves New Zealand's top players in limbo over whether they will have a professional contract next year.

Mystics defender Phoenix Karaka defends Georgia Heffernan's shot at goal in the ANZ Premiership grand final. Shane Wenzlick / Photosport.nz

Given the ongoing uncertainty the players are facing, Netball NZ last month scrapped the final restrictions preventing Silver Ferns and other leading players from pursuing contracts in Australia and the UK, removing the requirement for athletes to receive a dispensation from Netball NZ before signing with overseas clubs.

As Netball NZ battles to secure broadcast and commercial investment for 2027, one high-profile netball identity told RNZ that Netball NZ was treating next season as a "bridging year" while it works towards a new competition model in 2028.

The source said options under consideration for next season included pausing the ANZ Premiership for a season or reverting to an amateur competition. The source warned either option risked accelerating the exodus of New Zealand's best players overseas, leaving little foundation on which to relaunch a professional competition in 2028.

World.title: Missing Auckland 6-year-old spent the night with people known to his family - police
World.content:
Police searched for a missing 6 year-old boy overnight only to find in the morning that he was with people known to the family.

There were grave concerns for the boy who went missing from his home on Tuesday evening, after an argument with his family.

When he didn't return home at 7pm, his grandmother reported him missing.

The boy was wearing just a t-shirt, track pants and no shoes.

MetService data showed overnight temperatures in the area dropped as low as 4.6 degrees celsius.

A police spokesperson said police staff searched for the boy overnight.

At 6.39am police put out a media release asking the public to report any sightings of the boy.

Six minutes later police sent out another release to say the boy had been found safe and well.

World.title: Steps the Tauranga hospital cat goes missing, community launches search
World.content:
A much-loved "community cat" who has spent years greeting staff and visitors at Tauranga Hospital is missing.

Steps, a 12-year-old tabby, affectionately known as the hospital's "patient support officer" was last seen in the hospital carpark on Monday night.

He had been curled up beside his bed by the hospital steps on Clarke St. His house near the carpark lift was also missing.

His disappearance was shared on a Facebook group set up to share posts about Steps with more than 4000 followers.

Owner Quinn Pratt said while Steps was "technically" his cat, he was much more of a community cat.

"He's more famous than I'll ever be," Pratt said.

A work ID for "Dr Steps" at Tauranga Hospital. STEPS THE TAURANGA HOSPITAL CAT / SUPPLIED

Pratt had brought Steps and his brother home as kittens after a hunting trip to Murupara about 12 years ago. He and his wife Emily had lived right across from the hospital, until about a year ago.

He said right away Steps began hanging out on the hospital steps, which led to his name.

Since then he'd become a common sight at the hospital and when Pratt's family decided to move they arranged for a neighbour, Karla Horn to watch over him.

He said Steps was loved by hospital staff and visitors and could often be found hanging out in the emergency department or taking the lift up and down.

Over the years Pratt said he had disappeared a handful of times, he was microchipped, and Pratt would normally get a call from a local vets within a few days.

People had also tried to take him home, Pratt said, but now he had his own house and signage in the carpark this happened less.

Steps in his house. STEPS THE TAURANGA HOSPITAL CAT / SUPPLIED

Pratt said what made this time different was the fact his little white plastic house was missing too.

"He's probably too friendly... I'm hoping it's someone who has taken him with good intentions.

"Unfortunately, he's the most generic looking cat on the planet."

Both Tauranga MP Sam Uffindell and Bay of Plenty MP Tom Rutherford both have appealed for Steps to be returned on social media.

Uffindell said Steps was a "friendly companion to all that come for treatment or to visit loved ones" at the hospital.

Rutherford said Steps was not a stray and was well-cared for by the community.

"He plays an important role around the hospital, bringing comfort to patients and staff.

"If you've seen him or know anything, please get in touch... let's help get him home safely."

World.title: De Minaur wins all-Australian clash as Popyrin gets through in Montreal
World.content:
Fallen star Alexei Popyrin has dug deep for a morale-boosting victory to join Alex de Minaur in the second round of the Canadian Open in Montreal.

Two years after upstaging the great Novak Djokovic in a seismic US Open triumph, Popyrin has slumped to number 139 in the world as he battles a crisis of confidence.

But after toiling through qualifying just to make the main draw, Popyrin toiled for another two hours and 12 minutes to see off Argentine Roman Andres Burruchaga 4-6, 7-5, 6-3 to notch his first ATP-level win since May in the Masters event.

The breakthrough was only Popyrin's ninth win of a lean 2026 campaign and vaulted the one-time world number 19 into a second-round contest with US seventh seed Taylor Fritz or another Argentine, Thiago Agustin Tirante.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

De Minaur, meanwhile, looked to be cruising before fellow Sydneysider James Duckworth put the world number seven through the wringer late on.

Runner-up in 2023, de Minaur was a set and 3-1 up before Duckworth fought back hard seeking a first win over his countryman in three meetings.

But de Minaur held firm to fend off six set points and progress 6-2, 7-6 (6) and book a third-round date with either Britain's Cameron Norrie or Peru's Ignacio Buse.

"In the first set everything was flowing," de Minaur said after the one-hour, 46-minute dogfight.

"I was up a break, had a couple more chances to go up by a double break and all of a sudden it slips away.

"Then all of a sudden momentum shifts and we got into a battle. So I am glad I was able to sneak through. There are a couple of things I need to tighten up on, but we live to fight another day."

While de Minaur and Popyrin move on, fellow Australian Adam Walton crashed out with a 6-3, 6-4 loss to American Jenson Brooksby.

In the women's WTA event in Toronto, Tahlia Gibson continued her stellar 2026 season with an upset 7-5, 6-1 second-round win over Polish 18th seed Maja Chwalinska.

Gibson's 28th win of a breakout year earned her a crack at Russian 16th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova.

World.title: How Australia can harness home support in lead up to Brisbane 2032
World.content:
Water Polo Australia has hailed the enormous success of the World Cup finals in Sydney, saying that it proves Australia is in an ideal position to host more World Aquatics events in the lead up to the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games.

Sydney hosted the eight-team World Cup finals over five days at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre, the first time a major global Water Polo event had been hosted in the city since the 2000 Olympics.

Australia's Stingers won a hugely impressive bronze medal, following on from their memorable silver medal at the Paris Olympics to firmly establish themselves as one of Australia's most likeable and backable teams.

Meanwhile, the Sharks finished an enormously credible fourth, beating world champions Spain in a heroic penalty shoot out in the quarterfinals to underline their status as a team that is building to be a genuine medal contender for the 2032 Games.

But more importantly, more than 10,000 spectators came through the doors across the five days, creating a memorable atmosphere at the former Olympic venue.

The Stingers won a brilliant bronze medal in Sydney. (Supplied: World Aquatics/Julius Dimataga)

And the Australian players certainly appreciated it.

"To have a whole pool full of our friends and family, and the water polo community, it's really special … this is such a huge part of our careers and something that we'll never forget," Sienna Hearn said after the semifinal loss to the USA.

"The atmosphere [in Sydney] is so special for all of us and makes us want to try even harder for our friends and family."

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

Bronte Halligan noted that it was the home support that made the difference for the Stingers as they fought back from defeat against the USA to win bronze.

"Any game on home soil is unreal. But then to win a medal, at a world event, on home soil is just phenomenal," she said.

"The crowd was epic, they got us through the game, we stayed in it, we got the result and I couldn't be prouder of the girls."

Head coach Bec Rippon agreed, calling the crowd "amazing".

"We don't get many opportunities to play in these big moments — and for this team the semifinal the other day was only the second ever semifinal that we've played in," she said.

"So to have opportunities like this, under pressure, with a crowd, you can't buy that kind of experience.

"We have such a privilege of going overseas and playing in front of other nations' home crowds, so it was really amazing to be able to do that for our fans, friends and family here tonight who follow us all over the world."

Water Polo Australia hungry for more

Teenager Bless Daly is among the new guard of Australian water polo players on the rise. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

It's not a surprise that Water Polo Australia wants to see more of that support over the next six years and beyond.

"We were really keen to make sure we leveraged the home crowd advantage," Water Polo Australia chief executive Tim Welsford told ABC Sport the day after the tournament, his voice still hoarse from cheering on during a thrilling week of water polo.

"In the early stages of planning there was a very clear line of sight on what we wanted, to have the opportunity for kids to come into the centre, to buy a Sharks or Stingers top, to put the war paint on their face, the zinc, and sit in the crowd and support their team.

"That was a very clear vision for us about what we wanted to deliver in terms of the user experience inside the venue, and I think we went very close to nailing that.

"I think anyone who was in the venue, and it probably came across on the broadcast, will tell you how electric the atmosphere was.

"And that wasn't just the Australian games, even the men's gold medal game between Hungary and Greece, we had this beautiful picture of all the Greece fans in the blue seats, all the Hungary fans in the green seats, and we had all the Aussie water polo purists sitting in the middle.

"And at 7 o'clock on Sunday night, we still had the most incredible atmosphere."

Supporters cheer on Team Australia at the bronze medal match between Australia and Russia during the 2026 World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup at Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Remarkably, Water Polo Australia was able to garner such incredible community buy-in with just eight months lead-in time.

Welsford said that if they were given longer, they could layer even more onto the event and what they could achieve.

"We've got an appetite to do more of this into the future," Welsford said.

"That's why we really sort of pushed to make every post a winner this time so that World Aquatics, considers us … a really safe pair of hands for them to be able to allocate events to, that they know they're going to get a great result here.

"I'm confident they walked away with that exact feeling.

"We talked often about what does success look like [for this event], and you've got all those [attendance and social media] metrics and I think that's a really important piece and we will measure those, of course.

"But the community-building success was just incredible — people that are reaching out saying, we need to host more of these.

"Australia is cherry ripe for this type of thing … There is a real appetite here for us to do this again. And so we want to support that community groundswell.

"We would love to have it back."

Bec Rippon led the Stingers to two major global medals in the last three years. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo )

Some of the metrics truly have been encouraging, with almost 14 million social media views in the lead up to and during the event, coupled with the huge attendances.

"Our numbers in the last three months have been bigger than our Olympic year in terms of the social media views," Welsford said.

"This is an unbelievable opportunity for us to be able to showcase the sport."

Water Polo, although a relatively niche sport in Australia, is huge in Europe.

And despite being a long way from the sport's heartland, one of the key features of the tournament was how much support other nations received — none of which was by accident.

Water Polo Australia reached out to the embassies of all nations participating in the event to help drum up support within their communities, which was realised in a vibrant, multicultural crowd celebrating the sport throughout the five days.

Even the thorny issue of Russia's involvement — the women's team qualified and became the first international Russian team to compete on Australian soil since the country was banned in the wake of the Ukraine War.

"I think everybody understandably was a little bit on edge a little bit around how that would play out, and we are continually empathetic to the Ukrainian community and what's going on over there at the moment," Welsford said, noting that Australia, as an organising committee, does not get the option to select which teams qualify for the event.

"So it's our job to then accept our lot and make the best of the situation and try and put on a great show for everyone," he added.

"We did have a Ukrainian protest, they were really well organised, extremely peaceful, they did everything they could to amplify their message and we thank them for doing it in the way that they did as well."

National Aquatic Centre essential for aquatics legacy

Australia will hope for even more events in the lead up to 2032 as the dream of a National Aquatic Centre is realised. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

A key factor in being able to host more events will be the development of the National Aquatic Centre in Brisbane, a venue that Water Polo Australia, along with their diving and artistic swimming counterparts, really lobbied for before getting Swimming Australia on board.

"The National Aquatic Centre concept was actually initiated firstly by water polo, but then in conjunction with diving and artistic swimming," Welsford said.

"Under Rob Woodhouse's leadership, [Swimming Australia] sort of joined the scheme a couple of years ago, but it was largely driven by the other three aquatic sports.

Proposed design for 2032 aquatic centre revealed The state has chosen three firms to design the aquatic centre: ARM Architecture, NH Architecture and Queensland-based Arkhefield.

"But since Rob's come on board, it's been fantastic that it's been all four of us and we've been really well united and supportive of each other, making sure that we can all get something that's really ticks the legacy box for us.

"People will talk about 2032 and what that means, but even last night talking to the Sydney 2000 crew, there were so many events in the lead into 2000 that we hosted here locally.

"People and countries wanted to come out and have that experience prior [to the Games].

"So in the context of us hosting this year, this is the start of it for us.

"We want more of these international style events here over the next six years and we believe countries will want to come, particularly given the experience they've had over the last five or six days.

"We want to do more of that as we move forward.

"The National Aquatic Centre delivers us that legacy venue that we need. I think if anybody experienced what Sydney Olympic Park was able to do for us — not that was built for the Olympics, but it was the Olympic venue — it stands up so well in terms of a legacy asset for us to be able to use.

"You know, 26 years after the Olympic Games and 30 years after it's been built, it's still being used as a world-class event for aquatics.

"It's a phenomenal opportunity that we need to make sure we get right in terms of the National Aquatic Centre."
